In the Śrī Pāñcarātra Aniruddhasaṃhitā: On the peak of the Himālaya mountain, in a sacred field frequented by all the Siddhas.
It is frequented by all the vidyādharas and by all the gandharvas. || 1 ||
It was crowded with all the most excellent siddhas and munis, as well as all the gods;
it was filled with various wild animals and abounded with various lotuses.
It was filled with various trees, crowded with various flowers, teeming with various birds, and adorned with golden trees. || 3 ||
Adorned with musk, beautified by golden grounds, and graced with betel-nut trees, coconut palms, and *ketaka* flowers; || 4 ||
It was crowded with Apsarases, graced by elephants,
and adorned with hermitages filled with the foremost of sages.
Adorned with ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, graced by lotuses,
and filled with sandalwood trees, *vakula* trees, and clusters of lotuses.
It was crowded with white, blue, and red lotuses, as well as with the jewels of the ocean.
It was filled with citron trees, adorned with jackfruit trees,
crowded with cows and elephants, and surrounded by Brahmins.
In that hermitage, seated in its center, was Bhṛgu, the best among those who know the Vedas, devoted to meditation on the Self, for the sake of the Supreme Soul.
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), proficient in the meaning of all scriptures,
resembling the rising sun, with a face like the orb of the moon.
He was endowed with a sacred grass ring upon his hand, wearing a supreme black antelope skin,
possessed of a tranquil mind, gentle, and seated in the vīrāsana posture.
All the sages standing at his side, having prostrated before the Teacher of the World, all those sages spoke these words to him without weariness: || 12 ||
O lotus-eyed one, O you who are devoted to compassion, all the Vedas—with their limbs, sub-limbs, and in full detail—were previously heard by me from you in their entirety. (13)
"We do not see the path to the highest good; tell us that, O Great Sage.
Having heard this, that highly wise great sage spoke.
Bhṛgu:
In former times, by the power of my asceticism, I went to Śvetadvīpa.
It was provided with gate-towers, endowed with many enclosures,
furnished with numerous pavilions, and equipped with many pillars.
It was established together with gardens and the like, surrounded by footpaths, and provided with stone slabs and many stories. || 17 ||
It was provided with arches and latticed windows, adorned with banners,
joined with figures of Garuḍas, and furnished with lions at the corners.
Having entered the palace, which resembled a mountain of gold,
I bowed down to that highly wise one and entered the inner chamber.
Having performed circumambulation in due order and having bowed down to the Primordial Form (Ādimūrti),
one should then bow to Aniruddha on the northern side of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Having approached him, I worship the Lord of the World according to the previously mentioned sequence of yoga, joined with the worship of the four locations.
With services such as the offering of a seat, accompanied by materials for the *arghya* and other rites,
and with offerings of cakes and the like, preceded by the *madhuparka*.
Thus, when a long time had passed, the God of gods, the Lord of the World, Aniruddha, the Supreme Person, spoke directly.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, peaceful, with a face like the orb of the moon,
he was adorned with necklaces and armlets and shone brilliantly with a crown.
His chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; he is resplendent with a forest garland;
he wears yellow garments and a wreath; and he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace. (25)
The omnipresent Lord of the world appeared out of supreme compassion;
seeing him, they were filled with wonder and praised the Lord of the universe with hymns of praise. (26)
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, whose banner is Garuḍa.
Salutations to you, the support of the worlds; salutations to you, who possess fourfold nature.
Salutations to you, O beloved of Kamalā; salutations to you, O mine of compassion;
salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds; and salutations to you, the bearer of Śrī. || 28 ||
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O Purifier of the worlds!
O best of Brahmins, by this hymn Janārdana became pleased. (29)
The Blessed Lord said: "Choose a boon; may it be well with you. I am pleased with you, O sinless one.
Bhṛgu said:
He has understood the meaning of all the scriptures and is supreme in his knowledge of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
"O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, by your grace I have previously heard [of the path], yet I do not see the way to liberation; tell that to me now. (31)
The Blessed Lord said: "Through the path declared in the Pañcarātra, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise.
O Brahmin, apart from the Pañcarātra, no other path to liberation exists. (32)
Bhṛgu said:
"O Lord, O Master of the World, what is the Pañcarātra, and by whom was it proclaimed?"
By whom has this been heard, O Hṛṣīkeśa, and by whom is liberation attained? (33)
"What is the true meaning of the word *pañcarātra*? Tell me according to reality.
"The Blessed One replied: 'The *Pañcarātra* was proclaimed by me out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (34)
On the surface of the earth, he caused Brahmā, Indra, Rudra,
and the gods to hear the great scriptures such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, even those that extend over many nights.
In his presence, that fame prevails in the world;
just as the host of moons and stars does not shine at all during the day. (36)
Likewise, the other five do not shine at all in his presence, just as the five [planets] do not shine when the sun is blazing. || 37 ||
In that same way, the nights and the other [periods] reach his presence.
Therefore, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is called Pañcarātra. (38)
The Praṇava, which arises from the five elements, is remembered as Pañcarātra;
because it is born from the fivefold nature of living beings, it is remembered as Pañcarātra. || 39 ||
Those men who shall worship according to the method of the Pañcarātra—
this scripture of the Pañcarātra bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This is my own command; accept this scripture with reverence. || 41 ||
"By my grace, may you especially reach the further shore of the scriptures.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished right there.
Taking this scripture, I shall go to my hermitage;
by relying upon this scripture, the path to liberation is successfully attained. (43)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Scripture," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the second chapter.
Bhṛgu said:
Having undertaken the Pañcarātra, one should perform initiation by that very path.
It is measured by five nights as praised by Aniruddha. || 1 ||
The Sages:
What is this Pañcarātra like? Tell us that, O great sage.
Bhṛgu:
The Pañcarātra, the great knowledge, was uttered by Nārāyaṇa. || 2 ||
(7) There has never been, nor will there ever be, a scripture superior to the Pañcarātra. Among all castes, the Brāhmaṇa is supreme; among all stages of life, the ascetic (yati) is the highest.
Just as the Gaṅgā is foremost among sacred fords, Acyuta among deities, the Aśvattha among all trees, and the Moon among the constellations; || 4 ||
Just as Viṣṇu is among the Ādityas, and Śaṅkara is among the Rudras;
so too is the Sāmaveda among the Vedas, and the lord of men among men. (5)
And likewise, among all the scriptures, the Pañcarātra shall be supreme,
just as Viṣṇu, the imperishable, is the most excellent among all the gods.
Likewise, among all scriptures, the Pañcarātra is the most excellent;
this Tantra, rooted in the Vedas, is authoritative like a Kalpasūtra.
Since the Pañcarātra was specifically spoken by Viṣṇu himself,
it is therefore an authoritative source in this world throughout all the treatises on Dharma.
In all the Dharmaśāstras, and especially in the Āgamas,
as well as in all the Purāṇas, the Pañcarātra is authoritative.
Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra; the hearers are the various manifestations and the sages who are the Grandfathers (Pitāmahas). 10.
The Vaiṣṇava teaching is auspicious, flawless, and destructive of sin;
it was proclaimed by the Primeval God for the welfare of all living beings.
(8) Endowed with four feet and bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life,
the Pañcarātra is declared to be the purifying fifth Veda.
For it is the greatest merit among merits, the most purifying among purifiers, the most ancient among Purāṇas, and the very essence of dharma among all dharmas. (13)
The scripture of the Blessed One is spoken by those born of devotion to the Blessed One; the Purāṇa known as Pañcarātra was spoken by the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa). 14.
The Purāṇa of Viṣṇu and the purifying Pañcarātra have been proclaimed;
they issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa and are practiced by the Brāhmaṇa alone. || 15 ||
One should regard a Brahmin who knows the Pañcarātra—the Veda emerged from the mouth of Viṣṇu—as being like a god. (16)
Upon merely seeing a Vaiṣṇava, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground; however, if through delusion one disregards him and sets out on a journey far away, [the following occurs]. (17)
These lead to hell; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Brahmin, this Pañcarātra has emerged from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
If, however, out of delusion one should revile him, he will certainly go to hell;
whereas the gift given to one who knows the Pañcarātra yields the fruit of giving ten million cows.
Superior to the gift of a hundred maidens and even superior to a hundred gold niṣkas [is this].
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Praise of the Scripture," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
Now begins the third chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"O bull among sages, I shall describe the characteristics of a teacher in brief."
A Brāhmaṇa who is born of pure lineage, pure, and a constant speaker of the Veda. || 1 ||
One who knows the Pañcarātra, self-controlled, endowed with virtuous conduct, youthful, delicate, peaceful, and beautiful in all his limbs. || 2 ||
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who is devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
whose mind is fixed on me, whose life-breaths are dedicated to me, and who is intent upon my worship.
One whose mind is intent on chanting my names, who is eager for stories about me,
who is virtuous, pure, skillful, truthful, and has conquered his senses— (4)

One who knows the scriptures, is skilled in ritual action, understands the meaning of the Pañcarātra, is devoted to keeping the sacred thread in hand, and is dedicated to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 5 ||
One who is engaged in the five daily rites, endowed with the five sacrifices,
knowledgeable in mudrās, mandalas, and sacrificial pits, and devoted to the worship of the mandala.
Devoted to vows and fasting, endowed with the virtues of compassion and moral conduct,
he was completely liberated from all sins and entirely free from all defects.
Skilled in activities such as plowing and the like, devoted to the daily rite of bathing,
adept in pure rituals, and intent upon the rite of consecration.
Skilled in festive rites and other ceremonies, capable in the ritual of the thousand jars,
devoted to the worship of the twelfth day, and contemplating the twelve-syllable mantra. (9)
Skilled in independent ritual action, devoted to the fire of yoga, and pure;
his arms marked with the conch and discus, and adorned with the five-fold ornaments.
One who knows the principles of consciousness, matter, and the Lord; who is devoted to the practice of mantras and yantras;
who understands the investigation of the sciences of craftsmanship; and who is skilled in the creation of artistic works. || 11 ||
He was one who spoke with a smile, devoted to the worship of his elders,
intent upon his own wife, enjoying the pleasures of life, and endowed with sons.
Free from consumption, leprosy, and other such ailments, and devoid of improper conduct; endowed with the practice of the *samaya* vows, having conquered anger and subdued the senses. (13)
Endowed with compassion for all beings, possessed of auspicious limbs, engaged in virtuous deeds, and free from desire and delusion. || 14 ||
He was devoted to the worship of the Śālagrāma, skilled in singing and dancing,
knowledgeable in the various types of musical instruments, and proficient in the art of rhythmic clapping.
An intelligent disciple—endowed with all virtues, truthful in speech, and devoted to compassion—should choose as his preceptor one who is possessed of these very qualities. (16)
Endowed with virtues such as discipline and the like, and devoted to the hearing of the Dharma—these include the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, the Śūdra, and others as well. (17)
The twice-born [preceptor] should first initiate the student who is a celibate, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant, according to the path prescribed in this scripture. (18)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Preceptor," in the *Aniruddha-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
O bull among sages, I shall now describe the procedure for initiation in brief:
one should perform the rite of initiation during the period of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa). || 1 ||
On an auspicious weekday and on a favorable day, when the disciple is endowed with virtues and his mind is delighted— that is declared to be the proper time.
One should especially initiate [the disciple] during the bright fortnight, and specifically on the twelfth day;
for here knowledge is bestowed and the accumulation of sins is destroyed.
Because it is given (dīyate) and because it causes [impurities] to perish (kṣīyate), it is therefore called initiation (dīkṣā).
Initiation is said to be of two kinds: the scripture (śāstra) and the mantra; thus it is twofold.
First, O Brahmin, O great sage, listen to the initiation into the scripture;
[seek] a Brahmin who has mastered the scriptures and is endowed with the qualities previously mentioned. (5)
The disciple, knowing the scriptures, should worship the Guru, the sage devoted to [his practice].
First, there is the formal selection of the teacher (ācārya-varaṇa), and then the procurement of the ritual materials (dravyopādāna).
Likewise, immediately following the consecration, there is the offering of the sprouts,
the binding of the blindfold over the eyes, and the consecration of the seat of the scripture.
Having first performed the worship of the deities situated within the fire-mandala of the pitcher (kumbha),
and having previously completed the worship of the door, one should thereafter perform the morning bath.
One who has mastered the Tantras should instruct in the procedure for the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
having first marked [the disciple] with the conch and discus and performed the supreme worship of the door and other parts.
Having performed the worship of the three locations and the binding of the eyes immediately thereafter,
and having performed the worship of the seat of the scripture, the wise one should address the scripture.
Then, having removed the eye-cloth, the worship of the excellent preceptor follows;
this rite has been proclaimed by me in this tantra, O bull among sages. (11)
I shall now explain the offering of the initiation-sprout; listen attentively.
One should cause it to be sown on the seventh, the fifth, or even the third day.
When the onset of night has arrived prior to the day of commencing the ritual,
one should first perform the collection of earth and then carry out the decoration of the pavilion.
The preceptor, having filled twelve excellent small pots with clay and having strewn rice over them,
should place one pot in the center of those.
To the east of that, one should place the seed-vessel (*bījapātra*), and to the west, the water-pot (*kumbhaka*).
Then, having performed the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*), one should also cause the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited. || 15 ||
Thereafter, the knower of mantras should worship the jar with the Soma mantra;
then he should worship the vessels which consist of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Likewise, one should offer Soma into the seed-vessel with the homa-mantra,
as well as sesame, mung beans, barley, black gram, mustard, and rice.
Either niṣpāva or priyaṅgu is declared to be the eight seeds;
then the practitioner should prepare a seed-vessel with the respective mantra.
Having offered the bali-oblation, one should vigilantly perform protection all around;
and until the end of the ritual day, one should properly carry out the worship.
One should perform the worship of the four locations preceded by the worship of the door;
likewise, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, the wise man should bind the protective amulet (*kautuka*),
either one located within a mystical diagram (*yantra-maṇḍala*) or that known as the *Nārāyaṇaka*.
Either the Yantra called Vāsudeva, or the Viṣṇu-Yantra,
or even a simple Maṇḍala adorned with the forest of Tantras.
Or else, the wise one should have a mandala constructed as prescribed by the divine mantra;
then, having performed the binding of the eyes, he should practice three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

14) Having then performed the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), one should carry out the deposition of the Mātṛkās. One should perform the internal deposition of the root mantra and bind the thread of Māyā. || 24 ||
Having worshipped the pedestal of the scripture, one should place it upon the bed;
thereafter, having offered an oblation (bali) on all sides, one should cover it with a cloth. || 25 ||
One should pass the night in vigilance, and in the morning, having praised Janārdana,
one should cut the thread of illusion and cast it into shallow bowls.
Then, having removed the blindfold, he should bathe the disciple along with his attendants;
having adorned him according to the rule, he should cause him to enter the pavilion.
Seated in his own place, the wise one should perform the worship of the doors and so forth;
he should worship the water-pot (kumbha), and immediately thereafter the mandala.

Then, having performed the fire sacrifice (homakārya), one should perform the worship of the seat of the scripture (śāstrapīṭha), after having completed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites preceded by the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). || 29 ||
Having brought the disciple to his side and seated him near him,
the teacher brought forth the seat of the scriptures and instructed him.
One should explain the beginning and end of all the Saṃhitās without exception, or else this Tantra alone, according to the requirements of the task at hand. || 31 ||
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, offerings for the fire-sacrifice,
and rings, as well as with cows, land, gold, jewels, and so forth, according to the extent of one's wealth.
(15) The initiation into the Śāstra has been declared by me, and likewise the initiation into the Tantra;
this rule is proclaimed specifically for the Brāhmaṇa. || 33 ||
For a Kṣatriya, there exists no initiation into the scriptures up to the lowest Śūdra;
the best of teachers should awaken him solely by means of a yantra and mantra.
Or even merely a mudrā, or likewise a mantra or a yantra.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation into the Scripture," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā within the Śrī Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Now begins the fifth chapter. The Blessed One said:
"O best of sages, listen as I now describe the Viṣṇu yantra."
Especially in fields of merit and in temples of the deities.
On a mountain peak, by a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or even in a pure house,
the wise man should have a pavilion constructed, provided with sixteen pillars.
Having constructed an altar according to the prescribed measurements either in the center of the completed pavilion or elsewhere,
and having smeared it with cow dung, one should draw the yantra in its center.
First, one should draw the Praṇava according to the measurement of a palm;
outside of that, one should fashion a hexagon, which is further encircled by a circle.
Having drawn a circle with a measurement of half a finger-breadth as before,
the practitioner should then delineate a circle with a measurement of four finger-breadths. (5)
Upon that very same [space], one should specifically draw an eight-petaled lotus;
by that same measurement, one should draw an eight-cornered figure outside it.
The six syllables are in the inner corners, and the eight syllables are in the outer corners;
beyond that, the filaments (kesara) are prescribed, and beyond those, the sixteen petals.
One should draw a twelve-sided figure on the outside and write the twelve syllables;
likewise, one should provide filaments and draw thirty-two petals.
O Brahmin, the filaments are proclaimed to be a hundred times the size of the petals;
one should fashion a wheel outside that, complete with a hub, spokes, and a rim.
One should draw the navel and the rim with a measurement of one finger-breadth;
the field of the spokes is proclaimed to be four finger-breadths in measure. || 10 ||
One should fashion it with twenty-four spokes, each measuring one finger-breadth;
having arranged the outer pedestal and so forth, or alternatively, [the mandala] may consist of simple triangles.
Having written the vowels upon sixteen lotuses, I shall briefly describe the syllables;
one should likewise draw a thirty-two-petaled [lotus] for the Nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubh.
All the lines are said to be white, and the space between them yellow;
the hexagon is red-colored, and the pigment (varṇaka) should be white.
The space between the corners should be black, and the filaments pale red; one should make the eight petals white and the spaces between them black. (14)
The eight outer corners should be yellow and the center dark;
outside of that, one should know the filaments to be filled with the color red.
One should fill the sixteen lotuses with a pale red hue;
the interior space with blue color, and the outer corners with yellow.
The interior should be dark-colored and the exterior filaments white;
one should make the interior black and that petal red-hued.
The region of the hub should be golden-hued, while the spoke is indeed black in color; the intermediate space should be yellow, and its rim (nemi) should be dark blue.
The other pedestal should be red; now hear what follows the pedestal.
Specifically outside the yantra, there should be either thirty or twenty [units]. (19)
The width is proclaimed to be either seven or five [units];
one should mentally delineate the pedestal, the pathway, and the door in their proper sequence.
One should cast [the colors] white, red, and so forth, ending with yellow;
however, by way of inversion, according to the division of their respective parts, in accordance with what is beautiful.
Or, even without the *pīṭha* and other parts, one should draw five lines on the outside;
O Brahmin, the lines should have three colors each, following the sequence of the five colors.
(18) A wise person should especially worship Viṣṇu by means of the *praṇava* (Om),
and one should worship all the syllables in their respective places. || 23 ||
The wise one should worship the rim (nemi) joined with the noose and goad;
then, one should fully worship Dharma and the other [virtues] at the corners of the pedestal's body.
One should place Ananta in the middle of the path and Caṇḍa and the others at the gate;
thus, O great sage, the Viṣṇu-yantra has been fully explained.
Bhṛgu said:
O Lord of the World, please explain the ritual procedure for the yantra known as Nārāyaṇa.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having first performed the *praṇava* as before, one should write the eight-syllable mantra within the eight petals starting from the east; one should inscribe it in all the corners. (26)
Outside of that, one should properly draw a circular whorl of filaments, and outside that, a circular eight-petaled lotus; beyond that, one should fashion a wheel.
In the center of the eight-petaled [lotus], one should write the eight-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha;
one should draw the wheel as before, provided with a hub and a rim.
The eight-syllable [mantra] is as before; outside is a twelve-pointed wheel, and within that [wheel] is a twelve-sided figure; outside its corners is a lotus with filaments.
That petal is declared to be the twelfth; one should place the twelve-syllable [mantra] there.
Outside of that, there should be a sixteen-sided figure; one should fashion the wheel outside of that.
(19) One should fashion a lotus as before, provided with sixteen spokes, complete with a rim and a hub, and endowed with twenty-four petals.
One should draw an outer wheel joined with twenty-four spokes;
the exterior shall be a square provided with thirty-two flames.
Having arranged the seats and so forth as before, one should perform the ritual of the marakṣetra;
the entire interior space should be black, and all the lines should be black.
The pericarp is yellow in color, the intermediate space has a white luster,
the filaments are yellow, and the lotus itself is pale red.
The two navel-rims are yellow, while the protective field (rakṣetra) is red;
it has the shape of a lotus petal and is adorned with a black color. || 35 ||
The entire field of the filaments is filled with pale red;
its petals are pale red, while the outer corner is yellowish.
And on the outside, it has the luster of a citron, resembling yellow saffron;
beyond that, the collection of petals is mixed with yellow and red.
The space between the petals is dark blue, and the outer circle is as before;
it has the shape of a blue lotus petal and is colored with the hue of blue.
The intermediate space, however, should be red; one should draw the wheel as before and especially adorn it with a garland of flames of red color. (39)
All the external seats and so forth should be as they were in the previous maṇḍala.
One should worship Nārāyaṇa in the center and place the maṇḍala in its own proper place. (40)
But especially during the Arātrika rite, the wise one should worship the image;
at the time of initiation, he should place the yantra known as Nārāyaṇa.
O Brahmin, when diseases arise, and again when there is a need for expiatory rites and the like,
as well as upon the invasion of a foreign army and the occurrence of the defect of the new moon (kuhū-doṣa), [one should perform these].
O Brahmin, when planetary afflictions have arisen, especially in rites for protection, during the procedure for drought, and likewise in the rite of ritual bathing; || 44 ||
The Blessed Lord said: O great sage, I shall describe the Yantra known as Vāsudeva.
Having performed the Praṇava as before, one should project a twelve-sided figure on the outside. (45)
Having likewise drawn a filiform lotus, one should write the syllables of the mantra in the corners;
on the petals, one should draw the twelve forms, and outside, one should draw the wheel.
One should draw it four times, joined with the hub, the spokes, and the rim;
outside, one should draw a twenty-four-sided figure and the Gāyatrī.
As before, one should fashion a lotus and draw it with twenty-four petals;
one should likewise fashion a wheel as before, provided with twenty-four spokes.
Outside [the inner circle], one should draw a thirty-two-cornered figure with the *nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubh* mantra;
outside that, one should fashion a lotus provided with thirty-two petals. (49)
Likewise, one should draw an outer wheel provided with thirty-two spokes;
on the portion of the rim, one should depict a noose and a goad, and outside that, one should draw flames.
One should arrange it according to the sixty-four-fold sequence, or even half of that;
outside of that, one should draw a square and the seats (pīṭhas) and so forth as previously described.
In the east, it has the appearance of a lotus petal; in the center, it is like a mātuluṅga fruit; and in the west, it is especially like a wheel. || 52 ||
Likewise, there should first be the lines and then the intermediate spaces;
the pericarp is yellow in color, while the corner is indeed white in color.
The two naves and the rim should be dark green, while the hub-field (arakṣetra) should be white;
the spokes should indeed be yellow in color, and the outer corner red.
The entire field of filaments (kesara) is filled with red and yellow;
the petals, however, are pale-red, while the rim and the nave should be white.
The inner space should be black in color, while the intermediate space is yellow;
the outer corner should be yellow, and the intermediate space there is black.
The outer petals should likewise be red; the hub and the rim should be white.
One should know that the spokes are variegated, while the mass of flames is red.
The *pīṭha* and so forth are declared as before; however, the syllable should be white.
Thus, O Great Sage, the great *yantra* has been fully explained. (58)
He who worships the great yantra attains the supreme state;
he obtains incomparable prosperity, and it shall yield the fruit of ten million sacrifices. || 59 ||
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of all forms of giving.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Yantra," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, which is part of the Mahopaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: I shall describe the procedure for the mandalas; listen to it in brief.
One should divide that field, which has been made square, into thirty parts.
In this case, there shall be one hundred parts for the nine divisions;
in the midst of that, by means of ten rows, the lotus-field is produced. || 2 ||
One should determine a separation equal to one-twelfth of the field;
having divided that separation into three parts, the circle of space (vyomavṛtta) shall likewise be formed.
One should divide the remainder into four parts: the first portion is the pericarp (*karṇikā*), the second is said to be the filaments (*kesara*), and the third and fourth are likewise [the petals].
One should fashion the tip of the petal by means of one-fourth of a part; by the remaining collection of parts, one should fashion a single petal. (5)
The entire space between the petals is measured by the length of the little finger;
likewise, there are three lines and five lines in the middle of each petal.
One should make it raised by the measure of a barley grain and then bring forth the base of the petal;
the tip of the petal attains width, or else it becomes a portion of the filaments.
Alternatively, one may determine the height of the pericarp according to one's preference as being equal to a portion of the tip;
the height of the machine (yantra) is the measure of the petals, while the filaments are a portion of the petal-measure.
Having thus formed the lotus, one should rotate it outwardly as a circle of space (vyomavṛtta).
Outside the circle of space, one should fashion a square.

One should purify the remainder, beginning with the pedestal (pīṭha), by means of the *paṅktipada* itself; thus, the pedestal is formed by the *paṅkti*, moving two [units] in each of the four directions.
In the intermediate directions, one should lead [the lines] for three squares and two squares within;
one should fashion the excellent pedestal (pīṭha) with four rows as the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha).
In the middle, one should fashion the body using twelve [units]; by means of the two circles at the front and back, there shall be two [parts] each.
One should erase the eight [squares] by means of the two middle rows;
then, having unified all of them, [one should place] that eight [square] on both sides of it.
Three [syllables] each at the beginning and end, two in the middle of the two lines;
having wiped away eight [syllables] from those positions, and three each in the middle. (14)
Thus, having unified [the area] by means of the first and last rows, one should sweep around the exterior of the lotus-field in five [strokes]. || 15 ||

The remaining space is declared to be the enclosure (koṣṭhaka), and the pathway (vīthikā) is made with two parts; in the region called the limbs (gātraka), one should fashion the conch and other [ornaments]. || 16 ||
One should draw the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus in the order of the directions;
likewise, the club, the noose, the Śārṅga bow, and the forest garland.
One should install [the deities] in order all around, starting from the southeast corner and ending at the northeast;
the remaining [deities] should be assigned according to the sequence of rows, beginning with the gates.
One should purify the main gate by means of two sets of four [squares] each;
the *śobhā* should be formed with nine squares, and the side-gate (*upadvāra*) should be like the main gate.
With six steps, one should fashion the subtle beauty of the remaining corners;
then, with a measurement equal to one part of the outer row, one should draw three lines.
One should especially draw eight auspicious symbols (maṅgalāṣṭaka) at the entrance;
afterwards, one should fill them with various pure powders (rajas).
The pericarp is said to have the luster of gold, the filaments the brilliance of blood,
the mass of petals white, and the supreme interior black.
One should likewise fashion the outer circle as a sphere of space with a beautiful reddish glow;
one should make the corner of the pedestal white, and the body should appear dark blue.
The interior of the limbs is red, while the exterior of the limbs is blood-red;
the remaining three [colors]—white, black, and yellow—occur in sequence.
One should draw the conch and other symbols in white color in its center;
the pathway should be filled with the luster of emerald, and the door with white.
Yellow, red, black, and dark blue are for Śobhā and the others in sequence;
likewise, the three unsurpassed lines are white, red, and black. (26)
The Blessed One said:
"Listen to the mandala named 'Bestower of Desired Accomplishment' (iṣṭasiddhiprada).
By means of worshipping it for the sake of desired accomplishment, one shall indeed attain that desired accomplishment. (27)
Having first made it square according to the measurement of the arms and hands,
one should specifically divide the middle of the field into forty squares.
Where there are one thousand six hundred parts, by means of worship for the attainment of desired goals, there shall be one thousand six hundred [repetitions]. || 29 ||
O Brahmin, one should draw a ten-petaled lotus in the center as before;
having prepared the pedestal as before, one should form a pathway with an outer row [of squares].
Outside of that, one should purify the Gātrāgāra (the body-chamber) with five rows;
then, by means of three middle rows, one should create the eight corners in the center.
The fourth [line] should be at the front and the back, and likewise four-footed in the middle;
having thus combined these eight [parts], one should smear [the area].
One should mark out the circumambulation path using exactly eighteen steps;
then, one should mark out a space of five squares in the middle of the corner.
One should smear the outer sixteen squares in a clockwise direction;
having combined all the remaining groups of squares into one, one should smear them as well.
The pathway shall consist of a single row; hear now the sequence for the remaining rows.
O best of Brahmins, one should wipe the inner doorways and so forth with three rows.
One should lead [the lines] with two preceding rows, adorned with beauty and sub-adornment;
one should then polish the fine ornamentation on the sides of the four corners.
At the second and a half corner, one should sweep out exactly one square;
thus the pathway (vīthī) shall be formed in a single row, which one should clear by proceeding clockwise.
Outside of that, one should fashion a Vidhīka with a row of squares;
the remaining portion, consisting of three rows, should be made as before, including the gateway and the pathway.
Having fashioned the door-decorations, the side-doors, and the subtle ornaments as before, one should likewise [fashion them] in the corner regions as before.
One should sweep the outer path outside the row of the learned as before;
one should draw three lines on the exterior, or even just five.
Having thus performed the ritual procedure, O Brahmin, listen to the method for the vessel of colored powder (rajas-pātra). One should arrange it with its pedestal and lotus as before. (41)
The boundary line should be like a bee, the middle of the body yellow,
the exterior clockwise [line] dark blue, and the ground of the corners likewise.
One should fill the space between the corners and the sides with red color;
the outer path (vīthī) with white alone, and the inner path with dark blue.
One should create the four [squares] in sequence according to the distinction of colors, white and so forth;
the pair of squares situated within the corners should be red, black, and white, respectively.
One should fill the outer path with yellow, that which is outside it with red, and the five [sections] with the five colors beginning with white. || 45 ||
Likewise, O Brahmin, two corners are proclaimed to be white and dark;
one should likewise draw three lines, consisting of five groups of five colors.
Furthermore, O bull among sages, I shall describe the locations of the deities:
one should worship the limbs and sub-limbs at the tip of the pericarp and on the petals.
O Brahmin, one should worship the three qualities in the filaments, as well as the three mandalas; and in the eight directions of the pedestal, one should worship the lords of the directions.
One should worship Śaṅkha and the others specifically in the middle of the body;
the Ṛgveda and the others in the intermediate spaces, and the Vedas and so forth in the center of the corners.
And in all the processional paths (vīthikā), one should worship Ananta and the others:
Ananta, Vāsuki, and likewise Śaṅkhapāla. || 50 ||
In the upper door and the others, one should worship all [the deities] beginning with Āditya;
likewise Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Pūṣan, and Garuḍa. (51)
O best of Brahmins, having worshipped the attendants of Vighna in the corners and likewise Kumuda and the others within,
one should worship Satya and the others at the outer doors.
Likewise, Satya, Suparṇa, Tārkṣya,
and Garuḍa [should be placed] at the primary and secondary gates, as well as the lotus, discus, mace, and other emblems.
And in all the corners as well, one should worship Agni and the others in order:
Agni, Pāvaka, Citrabhānu, and Vibhāvasu. (54)
O best of Brahmins, one should worship Sudarśana and the others upon the three lines,
and worship Caṇḍa and the others upon the sacrificial grass strewn around.
Bhṛgu:
O best among speakers, tell me, what is the time for the worship of the maṇḍala?
The Blessed Lord:
During initiation, at festivals, during ritual bathing, and at the festival of fruits; || 56 ||
And likewise during the investiture of the Damanaka plant and the great festival of flowers.
Especially during the Pavitra festival, likewise on the Jayantī day, at the time of the Kṛttikā festival, and during eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 57 ||
On the equinoxes and solstices, especially on the twelfth lunar day, during all rites of expiation, and likewise at the spring festival (Vasantotsava). (58)
One should perform the worship of the maṇḍala; otherwise, it would result in fault.
Worship of the maṇḍala is superior, while the worship of the image is inferior. (59)
Worship in the fire of the pitcher-maṇḍala image shall be supreme;
by this very supreme propitiation, all defects come to an end.
It removes all sins for men and increases the prosperity of kings and kingdoms;
yet, a ritual performed without worship at the four locations leads to fruitlessness.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform worship at the four locations;
the four locations are the most excellent, while the three locations would be middling.
The inferior [practice] consists of two locations, while the supreme is that which illuminates a single [object].
One is declared to be the image (bimba), and the other is the image-and-fire located in two places.
One should worship [the deity] facing west, situated within the fire of the pitcher and the mandala— the pitcher being joined with three locations and the mandala with four.
O Brahmin, one who acts otherwise toward the god Nārāyaṇa incurs fault;
one should worship all the deities situated there facing the west.
One should worship all the deities beginning with Varuṇa and ending with Nirṛti;
O Brahmin, [the rite] would be incomplete without the deities and without the door-guarding deities.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Yantras," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, a Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Bhṛgu said:
O Supreme Lord, tell me what the mandala of the discus and lotus is like.
The Blessed One said:
"I shall describe the mandala of the wheel and lotus; comprehend it in detail. (1)
The procedure for laying the foundation lines, as well as the increase of the manas, the filling with colored powders, and likewise the fruit of the worship of the mandala. || 2 ||
Having constructed a pavilion as before and adorned it according to the prescribed rules,
one should construct an altar in its center measuring five cubits.
Having made it firm, with an equal form on all sides, and extending [eastward] from the northeast, one should make it four finger-breadths wide; the base should be two finger-breadths,
and the altar for the jar (kumbha-vedi) should specifically be one cubit in height.
The width, however, should specifically be four cubits, three cubits, or even five cubits; the base, moreover, should be three finger-breadths thick.
The sacrificial altar (homavedī) should likewise be equal in width and length;
alternatively, it may be one palm in width and three finger-breadths in height.
The wise one should draw the mandala known as the Cakra in the center of the altar.
The Cakra is declared to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling. (8)
I shall now describe the supreme method as it has been taught; listen attentively to this summary.
One should draw a lotus in the field of the eyes (akṣakṣetra) according to the previous measurements of the palm (tāla).
Everything is born from the *vṛtta*; the *vṛtta* is produced from the center.
Outside the lotus, there is the navel and the rim, whether as one, two, or three [circles].
But that which is outside of it is the non-field (arakṣetra); the outer rim (bahirnemi), however, is as before.
The navel-rim (nābhinemi) is proclaimed to be four finger-breadths in measure. || 11 ||
The field of the spokes is proclaimed to be six finger-breadths in measure; one should place a thread, which is one-third of a spoke, on both sides.
The best of mantra-knowers should rotate [the cord] with a cord measuring two parts;
others, however, should likewise do so below, so that it takes the shape of a mātuluṅga fruit.
The wise one should draw a leaf-and-creeper design on the path outside the rim;
the measure of the creeper should be three finger-breadths, and the outer rim should be three finger-breadths [in width].
The non-field (arakṣetra) should be cast outside with a measurement of sixteen finger-breadths;
in the place of the spokes, one should draw a wheel of twelve or sixteen [spokes].
The wheel is fourteen finger-breadths in size and adorned with four parts;
the axle, the nave, the spokes, and the rim—these are known as the four parts. (16)
The axle and the hub are said to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and likewise the rim;
the area of the spokes, however, is produced with a measurement of four finger-breadths. || 17 ||
That [cavity] should be like a wheel, or even shaped like a conch,
or having the form of a lotus petal, with petals like the leaves of a blue lotus.
It should be shaped like a half-moon or like a bird's egg;
thus, specifically within the field of the spokes of the twelve-spoked wheel. (19)

Outside of that, the portion of the ground for the rim (nemi) and the field for the spokes (valli) should be made as before; likewise, one should fashion the outer hub (nābhi), and the field for the spokes (araka) shall be formed in the same manner.

One should perform that rite as before; the measurement is prescribed to be as before. One should fashion the area for the rim (nemi) on the outside, and likewise the spokes (pradhayaḥ) on the outside.
The circle of the path (vīthi) should be drawn twice as large, and the outer circle of the sky (vyoma) should be made so;
then one should make it square and draw the pedestals (pīṭha) and other features as before.
O Brahmin, one should subsequently fill it with two kinds of radiant powder;
the lotus is as before, while the hub and the rim are yellow.
The rim should be red, while the spoke indeed resembles black;
the leaf-patterned vines are white, and the hub and felly are dark blue.
One should fashion it with a single opening at the edge of the spokes,
resembling an *indīvara*, a *mātuluṅga* fruit, a lotus petal, or the interior of a barley grain.
(33) Furthermore,
[the shapes] are like the interior of a *pippala* fruit, an axe, resembling a thunderbolt,
square, circular, crescent-shaped, and like a *kūrpara* (elbow). 26.

The preceptor [should place] these twelve, beginning with the conch and the discus, in the directions starting from the east; however, the axle is declared to be yellow, which is the consensus for all wheels.
One should fill the area between the navel and the rim with various colors;
one should fill it according to its beauty and according to one's own preference.
As before, there should be a leaf-vine; it should be white at the navel and the rim. The circle of spokes should be black, while the intervening space is yellowish.
One should especially fill the outer assembly with various colors;
likewise, the circle of space (vyomavṛtta) is black, and one should perform the rites for the pedestal and so forth as before.
One should especially draw three lines— white, red, and black—
and fill the interior of the pedestal specifically with white and red [pigments].
That which is endowed with three wheels is proclaimed as the most excellent;
that which is endowed with two wheels is declared to be middling.
Even a single [deity] is said to be inferior; thus, this [classification] becomes threefold.
One should worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment, in the center of the maṇḍala.
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others on the petals, and Soma in the sky;
one should worship Śrī in the region of the nave and Sarasvatī in the region of the rim.
In the *ara*-field, one should worship Jaya, and in the *ara* [itself], one should worship Mūrti. Likewise, in the *ara*-fields and in the limbs, one should worship the twelve Ādityas. (35)
On the outer rim, however, one should especially worship Keśava and the others;
and in the Pradhikṣetra, one should especially worship the oceans and other such features.
One should worship Indra and Agni upon the pedestal and other sites as before,
either with numerous ritual offerings or with thirty-two.
One should perform the sprinkling and bathing especially with sixteen [mantras];
the wise man who worships in the Cakra shall also attain that state.
One who seeks wealth obtains wealth; one who seeks victory shall obtain victory;
one who seeks desire obtains desire; and one who seeks a son obtains a son. (39)
By worshipping the discus, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices,
as well as the fruit of a hundred Prājāpatya penances and a thousand cows.

And likewise during the rite of offering the sacred grass (pavitrāropaṇa), as well as in the ritual of ceremonial bathing (snapana), in all rites of expiation (prāyaścitta), and in the case of ill omens and the like. || 41 ||
When afflictions such as diseases of the king arise, when one is oppressed by enemies,
or when drought and other calamities occur, one should worship the Lord within the lotus of the wheel.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Mandala of the Discus and Lotus," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, which is part of the Mahopaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"O great sage, listen as I describe the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), which is a secret matter."
Everything is born from conduct; conduct is born from the middle [of the body]. || 1 ||
One should construct the altar for the water-pot (kumbha) in the northeast corner of the mandala;
one should construct the altar for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the southeast direction of that [mandala].
In the Daṇḍaka [region], however, there is a special [arrangement]: the Kumbhavedī in the eastern part, the Maṇḍala in the middle portion, and that known as the Kumbha in the western part.
O Brahmin, if a gentle site cannot be found, one should then arrange for the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and so forth;
however, the image should always be installed in the western part.
O Brahmin, at the end of the southern [side], it is situated as a reflection in the north;
it is joined with the navel of the womb and endowed with lotus-girdles.
The measurement of ninety-six finger-breadths applies to all fire-pits (kuṇḍas) that are without a rim;
these may be angular, bow-shaped, circular, conical, disc-like, or lotus-shaped.
The triangle, the pentagon, the hexagon, the heptagon,
the octagon, the nonagon, and thereafter the mace-shape and the womb-shape are declared.
Thus, in this tantra, the fourteenth pit was described by the Supreme Lord;
its measurement shall be half that of the altar of the pit-maṇḍala, or one fist-breadth.
Three *muṣṭi*s or two *tāla*s are considered one *hasta*;
two of those are called a *daṇḍa*, and two of those are said to be a *dhanus*. (9)
A yuga and a gocarma are proclaimed to be its measure; the measurement of both the square and the circle is determined by the middle [line]. (10)
One should rotate the measuring cord according to the palm-measure from the central line;
then, one should strike that cord against the side of the circumference of that circle.
By the application of four cords, a square is produced;
one should drop [the cord] at the middle neck with a cord measuring half [the length]. || 12 ||
By means of the application of movement in the four directions, a square is produced;
either by virtue of the square itself, or else by virtue of the circle.
One should construct all other sacrificial pits according to those same measurements;
one should dig a square pit in the ground measuring one cubit in size.
The measurement for the [central] part is one *tāla*, while the measurement for the navel is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
outside of that, there should be three girdles (*mekhalā*) each measuring one *tāla*.
One should fashion the yoni above it, four finger-breadths in width and raised by that same measure, in the middle of the pit toward the west.
It is proclaimed to be ten finger-breadths in length, either according to the measurement of the *catur-aṅgula* or according to the [specific] style (*vṛtta*).
O Brahmin, one should specifically draw a crescent moon with a width of ten [units] on the back and sides, measuring six, four, and two finger-breadths respectively. (18)
One should fashion its stalk like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, four finger-breadths in length;
the binding at the base should be three finger-breadths, and the opening itself six finger-breadths.
O twice-born one, the hollow of the middle girdle should be equal in measure to the circumference;
in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
In the upper corners of the Mekhala, one should draw the discus, conch, and other symbols;
these should be fashioned from clay alone, measuring one finger-breadth in height.
Thereafter, the wise one should smear it with clay and cow dung,
and having adorned the pedestal with lime powder, it should be made according to the measurement of a palm (tāla).
This square has been described; now the bow-shaped pit (cāpakuṇḍa) is explained. According to the measurement of the previous circle, the best of teachers [should take] half of that.
One should cause that measuring cord to revolve around the bow with the string fixed;
the girdle (mekhalā) must be exactly the same as the shape of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O best of the twice-born, one should fashion a yoni-shape in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
by means of a yoni-pit, the yoni [of the deity] is attained, and by a lotus-pit, the lotus.
O Sage, the bow is said to be six finger-breadths long, and when strung it is thirty-six;
by means of these very finger-breadths, one should fashion every sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The tip of the bow should be twenty-four finger-breadths long, and the bow itself sixty finger-breadths;
when strung, it is said to be thirty-six [finger-breadths], and the half-circle [of the bow] sixteen finger-breadths. (27)
That very [shape] shall be the lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa), and likewise the disc-shaped pit (cakrakuṇḍa);
the triangular pit (tryaśrakuṇḍa) specifically, O Sage, measures thirty-two finger-breadths.
The measurement for the length of the cloth is proclaimed to be thirty-two finger-breadths;
one should then stretch a thread across its southern and northern sides.
Next, I shall describe the womb-pit (yonikuṇḍa), which arises as a square;
it measures ten finger-breadths at the corners of Vāyu and Nairṛta.
One should place the cord at the tip of the corner and rotate it to form a half-moon;
from the lunar horn of the half-moon and from the center of the east, one should drop [the marks].
On the right and left sides, however, it should be shaped like the tip of an aśvattha leaf;
its arrangement should be like a womb, yet one should not fashion an actual womb.
Now I shall describe the lotus-shaped pit (abjakuṇḍa): one should first draw a circle;
then, above it, the middle girdle, and then the lower girdle, which is half [the size] of that.
In this manner, one should fashion the lotus petal with a measurement of exactly eight finger-breadths;
one should then gradually form the *praṇava* (syllable Om) like the petal of the lotus on the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*).
One should likewise have it made with eight petals or twelve;
now I shall describe the conch-shaped pit (śaṅkhakuṇḍa), which is long from east to west.
Having drawn a circle as before with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths,
one should draw a half-moon on the eastern side of that circle's circumference.
One should fashion the lotus of the eyebrows with a measurement of four finger-breadths;
then, on the western side, one should fashion the tip of the conch.
One should make the tip like a vulva, measuring six finger-breadths;
on the northern side of the girdle, one should fashion a slight depression for the navel.
One should likewise fashion three girdles on the right side,
and one should especially arrange some kind of flame in the four directions.
Now I shall describe the *cakrakuṇḍa*: one should draw it as circular as before;
one should properly fashion two girdles (*mekhalā*), one below and one above, each measuring two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In the center of that, one should fashion the *arākṣetra* measuring eight finger-breadths;
it should be twelve or eighteen [finger-breadths], resembling the egg of a bird.
O best of sages, let the axle be the center of the fire-pit, the nave the navel, and the two girdles the rim; having thus fashioned the four flames, it should be like a crest of fire.
Now I shall describe the five-pointed [star]; attend closely to it now.
Having made a circle as before, one should divide its circumference into five parts.
Having drawn the ear-line (karṇasūtra) outside, and specifically outside each fire-line,
one should draw the cloth-line (paṭṭasūtra) using nine threads (half of eighteen).
The middle of the silk thread should be made slightly inclined; one should perform [the drawing] accordingly.
Based on that, one should fashion the girdle (*mekhalā*); now the hexagon is described. (45)
One should perform the drawing as before, measuring fifteen finger-breadths;
one should fashion it above the thread with a measurement of fifteen finger-breadths.
One should perform the drawing as before and mark it with half-measures;
O Brahmin, six marks arise, and one should extend six threads outward from them.
Having then measured the length of the cloth, one should cast out the marking-thread on the outside;
likewise, one should fashion the girdle, and understand it to be seven-cornered.
One should mark the circle in seven ways and cast out the corner-lines to the exterior;
one should draw lines from corner to corner, which is proclaimed as the length of the cloth-strip.
The procedure for the eight-cornered [mandala] is likewise, and so too is the procedure for the nine-cornered one;
now I shall describe the form of the mace (gadā), which is long from east to west.
As before, it should be joined with the [preceding] section, but reduced by two *aṅgulas*;
from one element to the next, it should be made [to decrease] by six, four, two, and one *aṅgula* respectively.
In the western part of that pit, measuring eight finger-breadths [in width],
it should be joined with a slight *praṇava* and specifically shaped like a staff.
Thus, O best of sages, the fourteenth pit in this tantra [is described];
however, during a festival, one should have it made either nine-cornered or eight-cornered.

O Brahmin, for the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), one should have it performed either in a square or even in a single-cornered [shape], and one should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
One should arrange either four fire-pits or even a single pit;
one should likewise arrange them specifically for the rite of consecration.
O twice-born one, the ritual procedure for the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) has been declared for the festival of leaves and flowers, as well as for the final pitcher;
now hear the method for the installation of the water-jar (kumbha).
A great pitcher (mahākumbha) is proclaimed to be complete with two measures (khāri);
a secondary pitcher (upakumbha) is half of that, and a side-pitcher (parikumbha) is half of that again.
One should wrap that measure and the vardhanī vessel with a cloth;
there should be a space of one finger-breadth, or it may be the size of an axle-pin.
Having placed upon a heap of rice a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay, according to one's means. (59)
Thereafter, one should wrap it in cloth, cover it with earthen bowls, and surround it with bundles of flowers,
coconuts, betel nuts, and various fruits.
With various kinds of fruits and even coconut fruits,
it was provided with jewels and gold, and endowed with the eight auspicious marks.
It should be provided with small vessels, equipped with oil-lamps,
adorned with golden bands, and covered with linen cloth.
One should place the *parikumbha* within the *kumbha*, the *maṇḍala*, and the *kuṇḍas*;
it should be provided with banners and arches, and adorned with the *dvārakumbhas*. (63)

Thus, in the case of the ritual of initiation (dīkṣā), as well as in the festivals of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and so forth, one incurs fault if it is done otherwise; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sacrificial Pit," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall now describe the consecration, specifically for the preceptors."
Especially for Kṣatriyas, and particularly for practitioners.
A wise man should especially have a pavilion constructed at a temple of Viṣṇu;
having fully decorated the pavilion, it should be adorned with arches and other ornaments.
Having adorned it with canopies and the like, one should beautify it with garlands of darbha grass;
and having offered the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) on the previous day, one should do so on the day of the rite.
It may take place on the seventh, the fifth, or even the third day;
or, having first prepared a site with an eastern gate, one may perform the entire rite immediately.
On the preceding day, at the onset of night, the wise man should tie the protective thread (kautuka).
O Brahmin, he should cause the worship of the four locations to be performed as prescribed by the rules.

O Brahmin, one who is most proficient in the scriptures should perform the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which bestows the attainment of desired goals, or else have a mandala of a lotus within a wheel constructed. (6)
One should perform the consecration of the jar at night while staying in the bedchamber;
one should prepare the bed for the deity situated within the cage in the western direction.
One should fully provide five bhāras of grain;
half of that amount in rice, and half of that again in sesame seeds.
Having placed a new cloth and likewise a tiger skin upon it,
and having laid a woolen blanket over that, the practitioner [should sit] upon the pedestal.
Placing a finger-mark above that, as well as a variegated cloth,
together with five pillows and likewise a covering cloth.
One should prepare a bed provided with soft coverings;
one should worship Ananta, who resides in the ocean of milk. || 11 ||
One should perform the worship in the fire of the pitcher-mandala as before;
the wise one should offer oblations everywhere and cause the Purāṇa to be recited.
Having risen at the time of dawn, one should perform the ritual bath as before;
having worshipped the door and other [entrances], one should fully worship the water-pots and other [vessels].
Having lifted up all those pitchers— either twelve or four—
one should place the group of four in the center and the group of eight in the eight directions.
Having placed upon a mound of rice a shallow bowl (śarāva) wrapped in thread and cloth, provided with a tuft of grass (kūrca), and filled with pure substances; || 15 ||
One should offer flowers in the east, a collection of leaves in the southeast,
fruits and water in the south, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the southwest.
In the northwest is the water of the sacred ford (tīrtha), in the north is the fragrant water,
in the northeast is the water of unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and in the southeast is that known as the ash (bhasma).
O Brahmin, in the center of the four [vessels] is water with gems; in the southeast, water with iron; in the southwest, water with grains; and in the northwest, water with rice.
In the northeast, one should gradually arrange all the items and place the substances:
three blue lotuses and likewise two ketakī flowers. (19)
A hundred-petaled lotus, a pair of *jāti* flowers, and likewise two *nandyāvarta* flowers— one should place these ten flowers into the center of the jar.
In the absence of flowers, however, one should use *jāti*; then the filling with leaves is described:
two *tulasī* plants and likewise two *damanaka* plants. (21)
One should cast into the water of the fire *saṭābhadra*, *dūrvā*, likewise *sahadevī*, and the *bilva* leaf. (22)
In the absence even of leaves, however, the leaf of tulasī is excellent;
likewise, the leaves of the plantain, breadfruit, mango, bilva, and āmalaka [are suitable]. (23)
The coconut, the *havya* fruit, the *likuca*, and the pomegranate—these should be placed in the southern direction;
however, in the absence of these fruits, the pomegranate alone may be used. (24)
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter as the fifth—these are the five products of the cow.
However, if these products of the cow are unavailable, clarified butter alone is recommended. (25)
[Water] from a river, from a waterfall, from a pool, as well as from the ocean, from a lotus pond, from a golden [well], and likewise from a rain-cloud, as well as camphor and agallochum. || 26 ||
The one who has mastered the tantras should place cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, bamboo manna, and camphor into the fragrant water. (27)
In the absence of ela and the other [ingredients], they prescribe camphor;
likewise, rice, *taṇḍulaka*, *priyaṅgu*, and that which is called *kambu*. (28)
Kalamā rice, red śāli rice, bamboo grain, and likewise barley—these are prescribed as substitutes for unbroken rice (akṣata) when it is unavailable. || 29 ||
The splendor of the three sacrificial fires, the splendor of the fire for daily oblations, the splendor of the fire for sacrifices, and the splendor of the fire for festivals. || 30 ||
But even if sacred ashes are not obtained, one should always apply vibhūti from the sacrificial fire-pit;
likewise, [one may use] emerald, lapis lazuli, and topaz.
Gomedha, indranīla, vajra, and likewise pearl;
coral, crystal, and also puṣparāga and brahmarāga. (32)
But even if gems are not obtained, a single pearl is recommended;
likewise gold, silver, copper, iron, and tin. (33)
One should place these metals—copper, lead, and iron—as well as śāli rice, vrīhi rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, barley, and bamboo seeds. (34)
O best of sages, one should place wheat, sesame, green gram, peas, black gram, and horse gram into the water-pot for the wind humor (vāta).
The master who has reached the further shore of the tantra should deposit all the ritual objects in the northeast;
the sequence of extraction is held to follow precisely the sequence of the placement of the yantra.
One should install [the deity] according to the prescribed rites with mantras beginning with "Keśava" and so forth;
the bathing should be performed with the Puruṣasūkta or the Viṣṇusūkta.
And at intervals between the baths, O Mahāmati, one should offer water for the guest-offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, and incense. || 38 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon the seat, one should perform the consecration;
then, having performed the pure bath, one should carry out the lustration ceremony (nīrājana). || 39 ||
Having adorned [the image] according to the rule, one should enter the sacrificial ground;
then, having seated it upon a throne, one should perform the binding of the turban.
And by means of that [initiation], one should regard the Teacher—the Guru of the World—as being the Bhaṭṭamācārya himself; as soon as he is seen, one should perceive him as a god.
(47) A seat, sandals, an umbrella, and a fly-whisk; a vehicle, a banner-staff, insignia, and a trumpet. || 42 ||
One should present the sound of conchs and kettledrums, the doorkeeper, ornaments,
the bronze cymbals, and the insignia in the presence of Viṣṇu.
One should offer the time-sign and the *kala* in the presence of Viṣṇu;
and here, the king in particular should perform the consecration.
One should perform the consecration with one hundred and eight *niṣkas* joined with the nine gems and combined with tin and gold. (45)
Thus, having performed all the preliminary rites as prescribed for the twice-born, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) when an auspicious moment has arrived. || 46 ||
By means of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, accompanied by dance and song, and joined with shouts of "Victory! (47).
Then, having performed the consecration accompanied by the sound of the Vedas and joined with the blowing of conchs, one should likewise offer water for sipping (ācamana).
Then, having bound his eyes, he should touch the weapons;
he should also show the vessels placed upon raised stands and auspicious objects.
Accompanied by all the royal insignia and preceded by the offering of an excellent seat, he should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground before all the people without weariness.
O Brahmin, if he is a Vaiśya, he should especially use the word "pāla" (protector) even without the consecration and other rites; if he is a Śūdra, he should use the word "dāsya" (servant).
The Brāhmaṇa is the cause of all social classes, and the king is the cause of the kingdom.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall now describe the duties of a king; listen to them in brief."
For the kingdom is the body of the king; the king is said to be its life. || 1 ||
Therefore, both the king and the kingdom must be protected by the wise;
however, it is said that the king’s importance is especially greater than that of the kingdom. (2)
The king is the teacher of the people, and the Brāhmaṇa is the teacher of the social classes;
because he protects living beings from injury (kṣata), he is declared to be a Kṣatriya. || 3 ||
Because of his affection for his subjects, he is called "Rāja" (King); and because he is devoted to the protection of the earth, he is known as "Bhūmipāla" (Protector of the Earth). || 4 ||
Because he is not subject to the constraints of others and because he is the leader of men, he is called the Lord of Men (nareśa).
One should display the binding of the turban (paṭṭabandha) for him above all other living beings.
And the birth and duties of the social classes, beginning with the twice-born, are proclaimed.

One born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is declared to be a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, those born of a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriyā mother are specifically called Kṣatriyas, O rulers of the earth.
Nevertheless, the attainment of birth for Vaiśyas and Śūdras is described [in this way]:
teaching, studying, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise performing sacrifices. (8)
Giving and receiving are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa); for kings, however, [the six duties] are studying, sacrificing, giving, protecting the earth, punishing, and adjudicating.
He possesses heroism, splendor, fortitude, and dexterity; he does not flee in battle, and he is expert in sacrifice, charity, ritual acts, and in the discernment of reasoning and refutation.
Endowed with the three powers, he is strong and increases his treasury;
he is possessed of the sovereign, the minister, the ally, the treasury, the kingdom, the fortress, and the army. || 11 ||
He was long practiced in the art of governance, skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, devoted to the science of polity (Nītiśāstra), virtuous, and fond of Brāhmaṇas. || 12 ||
Endowed with all constituent parts, he is the cause of all that is auspicious;
intent on protecting his own kingdom, he afflicts the kingdoms of others. || 13 ||

Skilled in mounting vehicles, proficient in the meaning of the treatises on statecraft (Arthaśāstra), a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas), and one who views all deities with equal regard. || 14 ||
Devoted to the propitiation of the deity and always intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu,
he is accompanied by kinsmen and servants and is ever devoted to his guru. (15)
He was devoted to the acquisition of wealth, intent on protecting his children, skilled in riding horses, and an expert in duels. || 16 ||
He was devoted to wrestling, diligent in the study of the treatises on subjugation, and intent upon all mantras according to the authority of his guru’s words. || 17 ||
He was devoted to song and dance, intent upon hearing the Purāṇas, faithful to his own wife, and avoided the wives of others. || 18 ||
He was endowed with manifold acts of charity, refined by the playing of stringed instruments,
skilled in the splendor of song and proficient in instrumental music and dance.
One should consecrate as king a person endowed with these very qualities.
Now, I shall describe the conduct of the virtuous, specifically that of the Kṣatriyas.
At dawn, having been awakened by attendants and having risen from his bed,
he should then offer gifts of food, especially to the Brāhmaṇas.
He gave a prastha of ghee, a goblet, and likewise gold and garments;
having discharged his urine, feces, and other waste in secret. (22)
Then, one should always perform the morning bath with warm water,
provided with bathing substances and accompanied by anointing and other such rites.
Before the rising of the sun, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana).
Having performed the recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī, one should perform the ritual of standing in attendance (upasthāna). || 24 ||
One should perform sacrifice for one's own sake, or worship Viṣṇu by means of a yantra,
or indeed do both, always preceded by libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites.
One should properly perform the gift of betel-leaves to Brahmins, the gift of cows, the gift of a maiden, as well as the gift of sesame seeds, red cloth, and gold. (26)
Having received the blessing from the twice-born with consecrated unbroken rice grains purified by mantras,
and having taken the sacred remains (prasāda) from the holy sites located within the temple, [he departed].

Having heard the purpose of the rite for the gods and the Brahmins, one should perform everything accordingly, having adorned [the image] with ornaments, unguents, and other decorations as prescribed by rule. (28)
Having reached the assembly hall, the king should take his seat and constantly attend to legal cases together with Brāhmaṇas.
He was fanned with conch shells and the sound of kettledrums, amidst a tumultuous clamor of shouts of victory,
and with yak-tail whisks, palm-leaf fans, and other fans.
It was joined by a multitude of excellent women, accompanied by the sound of kettledrums,
provided with many lamps, and adorned with canopies and other ornaments.

Having observed the enemies who have entered the king's own kingdom as if they were his daughters-in-law, the best of kings should cause the messengers arrived from the enemy king to hear [the following]: 32.
Having understood what is to be accepted and what is not to be accepted, the king, together with his ministers,
O Indra among kings, should take up that which is to be taken and completely avoid that which is not to be taken. (33)
Having discerned friend and foe, one should perform the respective duties;
then, having dismissed all people, one should enter the inner courtyard of the house. (34)
Having gone to the home of his parents, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff;
having heard their words and accepted them, he should perform each respective duty.
Having personally arrived at his own home, he should perform each respective rite;
he should perform worship of himself, or of the Yantra, or of Viṣṇu.
At dawn, one should perform the morning ablutions and carry out those respective duties;
then, having discarded the outer garments and the like, one should put on fine clothes.
Having reached the resting place, one should perform the necessary tasks of rest;
then, having laid down supine, one should discard all ornaments. (38)
Then, having performed the ritual bath, one should cause [the image] to enter the temple;
and having worshipped the Lord of Gods and offered sacrificial food (haviṣya), [one should proceed]. || 39 ||
Seated upon his meal-seat, O king of kings, he should properly partake of his food; he should eat together with the physicians and his own troops.
At the time of meals and while seated, one should likewise cause the conch and the kettledrum to resound, together with one's sons, kinsmen, and servants.
At the time of holding the meal, one should likewise proclaim it;
first, one should purify the food, leaving no remnant of the substance already eaten. (42)
On Saturdays and Wednesdays, one should perform an oil massage;
especially on the day of one's birth-star (janma-ṛkṣa), one should perform the gift of gold.
Then one should apply fragrant ointments, especially at the time of enjoyment;
on the day of the planet Venus, one should perform the vision of Viṣṇu.
He should travel two *krośas* outside the village together with his retinue;
every day, and especially so, he should inspect the elephants and horses. || 45 ||
While moving about his retinue, he should deliberate on the affairs of state;
likewise during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun. (46)
One should especially perform the gift of gold on one's birth-star;
by means of giving, everything is consumed [by its merit], therefore giving is preeminent. (47)
One should govern the kingdom according to dharma; otherwise, one becomes a creator of evil. When evening has arrived, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
The king should have the rite performed like that of a deity together with his family priests;
when the assembly of women has arrived in the pavilion, he should observe the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having caused [the deity] to eat, he should place [the image] upon the bed;
then, together with his protective retinue, he should deliberate upon the affairs of state. || 50 ||
In this manner, the king should perform [this] daily, always free from sloth.
For the sake of the prosperity of the kingdom, the king should practice the worship of Viṣṇu. (51)
For the sake of its special worship, one should cause a city, village,
or town to be built in a pure location, and have the plowing and other preparatory works carried out.
The residence of Brāhmaṇas is called an agrahāra;
that of kings is declared to be a pura; and the residence of Vaiśyas is a pattana. || 53 ||
One should cause a city to be constructed, joined with three types of people, and provided with forts, dwellings, and towns, villages, and ports.
A wise man should especially establish a village on the bank of a river,
consisting of either one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight [houses].
Or even four thousand [verses], whether superior, inferior, or middling;
or half of that, or half of that again, according to one's means.
A wise king should cause learned Brahmins, who are knowers of the Vedas and well-versed in the scriptures, to receive [the offerings]; he should never examine the Brahmins along the royal road.
A wise person should cause a village or similar settlement to be built in a pure and delightful location.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Kings," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā of the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
(p. 55) Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall now describe the layout of a village; listen attentively.
It may be established in a sacred field, on a riverbank, on a mountain peak, or at a junction of three paths.
One may construct a temple for the sake of a deity, or a temple for the sake of a village;
that which is to the east of the village should be independent, while that which is to the west should be dependent.
One should construct a street twenty-one *ayanas* long and one *krośa* wide, woven back and forth; thus, the village shall become excellent.
Half of that is declared the middle [size], and half of that would be the lowest. It should be provided with either an odd number of walkways or two walkways.
Having performed seven, five, or three repetitions according to the sequence of *otaplota*,
one should cause the prosperity of the village to be brought about by this very same procedure.
The Brahma portion is the middle one; immediately after that is the Daiva;
