the Mānuṣa should be the third, and the Paiśāca indeed the fourth.
In the Paiśāca style, one should provide a dwelling for the deities; in the Brāhma style, indeed, a temple for Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, in the outer circumambulation path, one should cause a walkway to be constructed.
O Brahmin, one should construct a temple of Viṣṇu to the east or west of the village, having either a single pedestal, or two, or even three.
Whether it be a seat, a bed, or even one mounted upon a vehicle,
the Vārāha [form] is in the eastern direction, and the Nṛsiṃha [form] is indeed in the southeast.
In the south, Hayānana is proclaimed; in the southwest, there should be Śrīdhara;
in the west, Vāsudeva; and likewise, in the northwest, Vāmana.
The wise one [should place] Rāghava in the north and Mādhava in the northeast;
having reached the pathway outside of that, he should place Ravi and Soma in the east.
In the southeast is the station of Bhairava; in the south is indeed Makaradhvaja;
Ṣaṇmukha is declared to be in the southwest; and Kanyakā is in the west.
Madana is declared to be in the northwest, and likewise the abode of the Mothers in the north;
having placed Śaṅkara in the northeast, Viṣṇu’s temple is in the center alone.
One should construct a pond in every direction, as well as a trench and a well;
however, one should build the royal palace in the central part of the city.
Outside the palace, however, one should provide a residence for the queen;
one should construct a wall all around it, adorned with gates and gate-towers.
Or else, that [area] should not exist outside; one should arrange for a stable for horses, a stable for elephants, and also a kitchen. || 16 ||
Outside was the residence for the guards, provided with its own transport personnel,
as well as chariot-makers and perfumers.
One should arrange the marketplaces, the internal streets, and the outer streets,
as well as the dwelling for the distribution of gifts, according to one's preference. (18)
One should construct the outer fortress beyond the city, and outside of that, a water-reservoir;
it should consist of stone walls and earthen walls, equipped with mechanical engines and turrets.
One should create a garden on all sides and cause a well to be constructed everywhere; the construction of palaces and villages should be planned according to the auspicious signs.
Having heard the whispered advice, let the auspicious words be accepted;
having abandoned inauspiciousness, let the cowherd go to the right for his welfare. || 21 ||
If [the omen] is on the left, there will be the destruction of horses; one should thus determine the fault.
At the time of setting out on an expedition, a woman carrying a full jar is auspicious.
One should display the sounding of drums and conchs, as well as the clapping of cymbals,
and show jars of milk and jars of liquor in an auspicious assembly.
When an ill omen occurs, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations to Brahmā, or alternatively, perform ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in front of the hole. || 24 ||
The king should perform the rite of site-inspection according to the path prescribed in the scriptures:
if the ground is elevated, it is excellent; if level, it shall be middling. (25)
If it is deficient, one should avoid the lower ground;
then the preceptor should perform the entry-offering (praveśabali) with rice seeds.
Accompanied by the sounding of conch shells and joined with the Svasti-sūkta,
[he should proceed] from Indra up to Brahmā along the path of the Pañcarātra. (27)
One should perform the installation of the conch in the cardinal or intermediate directions;
likewise, the wise man should fashion the pathway and the temple.
At the time of installing the conch, one should place gems, metals, and so forth;
especially in a temple, one should properly perform the ritual of plowing.
One should till the ground seven times and construct a basin for irrigation;
then, having sown the seeds, one should perform the watering.
And at the conclusion of the ripening of the fruit, one should perform protection on all sides;
at the conclusion of the ripening of the fruit, however, one should cause the cows to be satisfied with fodder. || 31 ||
Then, having made it four-cornered, one should properly perform the excavation;
afterwards, one should fill the earth and fill it with large boulders.
Thereafter, one should fill it with sand and then proceed to fill it with water;
having made it firm with hands and feet, one should place a small stone upon it.
Having placed it upon the foundation, one should fashion the temple; or else, one may have it constructed upon a secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), or even independently. || 34 ||
One should cause the city to be built as either Drāviḍa or Kesara;
it may be circular, oval, or rectangular.
p.
59) Or else, it may have a peaked roof entrance or even a hall-like chamber;
it is provided with sandals and the like, and adorned with footstools. || 36 ||
It was equipped with various celestial chariots, adorned with halls and latticed windows,
and provided with arched gateways and pavilions.
It was provided with walls and gate-towers and joined by an inner pathway;
in the southeast was the Mānasa-sthāna, and in the south the supreme Gandhālaya.

Śrīsthāna is declared to be in the southwest (Nairṛti), the supreme Pānīya in the west (Vāruṇa), [the seat] of the Nāga kings in the northwest (Vāyavya), and the supreme [seat] of the devotees in the north (Saumya). 39.
One should place Viṣvaksena between the lords of the north and the northeast;
subsequently, one should station Garuḍa facing toward the Lord.
One should station Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the two sides of the entrance;
one should place Durgā and Gaṇapati in the northeast and the southeast.
O Brahmin, one should construct the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha) in front of the gopura; furthermore, the wise man should have a well made to the east of the kitchen.
O best of Brahmins, one should place the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) in the south, the treasury (kośasaṃgraha) in the northeast,
and the Form of the Directions (diṅmūrti) on the side of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Or likewise, [the image] of Vāsudeva and others, or indeed of Varāha and others;
or a triad of stūpas, or a pentad, or even a heptad.
Or even one [image], O best of the twice-born, by the power of the sacred site;
having performed it thus according to the rule, one should properly carry out the consecration. (45)
Then, having performed the placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa), one should fashion a pair of bricks;
one should carry out the installation of the temple (vimāna) according to the procedure of the Pañcarātra.
A wise person should construct the temple to the east of the *taruṇālaya*;
however, one who is most skilled in the ritual manuals may perform it with the *mūla* [mantra] even without a *taruṇālaya*.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Construction of Villages," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā of the Mahopaniṣad within the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O great sage, listen as I declare the measurement of the image, which is a secret."
Whether seated, lying down, mounted on a vehicle, or standing; || 1 ||
Whether it be Vāsudeva and the others, or Keśava and the others, or especially the Fish-incarnation and the rest—the sacrificer as well as the preceptor [should worship them]. (2)
Or it may be according to the height of the sacrificer, or by the power of the door of Bharga;
or it may be the measurement of the pedestal, or even the measurement of a cubit.
Furthermore, it may be measured by the tāla, or else according to the number of finger-breadths (aṅgula);
three finger-breadths are declared to be the measure for the middle [finger] and the fist.
Direct measurement, indirect measurement, weighing, measuring by capacity, comparison,
and hanging measurement— these six types of measurement I shall now describe. (5)

It is said that "high" refers to measurement by height (unmāna), while "broad" refers to measurement by width (vistṛta). Measurement by depth (nābhimāna) would be the standard (pramāṇa), and the intermediate [measurement] would be by comparison (upamāna). || 6 ||
The cord should hang down, joined with these measurements;
likewise, it is said that it should be six measures, for otherwise it would cause defects.
It may be a complete painting (citra), or a half-painting (ardhacitra), or even a mere appearance of a painting (citrābhāsa).
A complete painting is that which is seen in its entirety, whereas a half-painting consists of one and a half [parts].
The image situated upon a cloth or wall is proclaimed to be of three kinds:
made of gem, metal, stone, wood, or even clay.

That which has a single root, that which has many roots, that which is independent, that which is dependent, that which is supported, as well as that which is a combination, and furthermore, enjoyment and union. (10)
An image situated in the place of Brahmā is declared to be a *ekabera*; an image situated in the divine portion (*divyabhāga*) is remembered as a *bahubera*.
The independent [deity] is to the east of the village, while the dependent is to the west;
established at the Ālaya on the side of the wall, it becomes supported.
Whether accompanied by Śrībhūmi or even devoid of it, it is known as Yoga.
It is said that Śrīkara brings about enjoyment, while Yoga becomes a means for subjugation (vaśyakara). || 13 ||

One should have [the image] made with a height of ten *tālas*, endowed with the proportions beginning with the *ayā*; having made a *tāla* consist of one hundred finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), it shall be one hundred and twenty-four. (14)
The worship and other rites for the Goddess, performed at a height of nine palm trees and accompanied by the six auspicious marks (ṣaṭkautuka), is declared to be "with many enemies" (bahuvera). 15.
Thus has been declared the procedure for the two [types of worship], excluding the stone-worship (śilārcā);
likewise, the ritual worship (karmārcā), the ceremonial bath (snapanam), and the rite for the marriage-thread (karmakautukam) during the installation (sthāpane). || 16 ||
The installation is of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
That which is installed in houses is the former, and that which is in the temple is the other. (17)
For one's own sake, there should be a guardian of the house and a protector of the dwelling;
but the deity stationed in the principal place is the protector of the king and the kingdom. (18)
If there is mutual attachment, however, there will be a disturbance in the kingdom according to one's desire.
Likewise, there shall be worship through ritual action, worship through festivals, and worship through offerings. (19)
The bathing, the sacred ford, the dual worship, along with the worship at the time of sleep and awakening—
these are declared as the sixfold image, which is described as the most excellent.
The middle [line] is said to consist of three [syllables], and the final one shall be a single [syllable];
it is joined with Kṛṣṇa, Rāghava, Siṃha, and Vārāhaka.
It should be joined with the Sudarśana [discus] and accompanied by the image of Lakṣmī;
or it may have eight arms, or one may perform it according to one's preference.
On the bed, the principal [form] is two-armed; at that time, Kṛṣṇa becomes Rāma.
Likewise, there may be the Vārāha, the Vāmana, and the Traivikrama;
or the Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha, the Vārāha, or the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
It is declared that the Śrīkara and Vijaya [mandalas] are for use in cities, villages, and towns;
thus one should fashion the groups of images and perform the consecration properly.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Bera," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā of the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: O best of sages, I shall fully explain the installation of the images.
The image (bera) is said to be of two kinds: stationary and mobile. || 1 ||
The northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is the primary [time], while the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is secondary;
one may perform the mobile rite during either the secondary or the primary period.
One should avoid performing a consecration in the months of Māgha and Bhādrapada,
as well as during the setting of Jupiter or Venus, and likewise in the vicinity of an eclipse.
The best of preceptors should avoid the installation of the Lord of the gods on an inauspicious weekday, at an inauspicious ascendant, as well as under an inauspicious lunar mansion or lunar day.
The most excellent teacher, together with an astrologer and a craftsman, should properly perform the installation according to the treatises on architecture (śilpaśāstra). (5)
Accompanied by the patron and all his attendants,
and having gathered all the necessary materials, he should thereafter perform the ritual act.
On the seventh, fifth,
or third day prior to the commencement of the rite, the wise man should perform the ritual and offer the sprouts.
Then, when evening has arrived, one should perform the collection of clay;
accompanied by attendants, one should go toward either the eastern or the northern direction.
Whether it be a garden, a riverbank, a wall, or even a place made of that [same material],
O Brahmin, one should sprinkle that location with water purified by mantras.
Having sat down upon his seat, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) especially, the wise man should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Having worshipped the earth with the mantra, the preceptor should offer oblations all around;
there, he should wash the digging tool with the Astra-mantra.
Having covered it with cloth and darbha grass, one should touch the earth while reciting the Bhūsūkta;
facing the east, one should dig the ground with a spade while reciting the Kroḍavidyā.
Having drawn the Vāstumaṇḍala with mantras prescribed in the Vedas,
the wise preceptor should again worship it, beginning with the eastern direction.
He should proceed together with his retinue amidst the sounds of conchs and trumpets;
the wise man should then cause a pavilion to be constructed, or at least a water-shed.
Having adorned it with canopies and the like, with banners, arches, and water-pots,
[the site] should be long from east to west and long from south to north.
One should draw a mandala in its center that is either square or circular;
one may also have it fashioned as a wheel-lotus (cakrābja) which bestows the attainment of desired goals.
One should place the water-pot as before in the western part of the mandala;
however, the field for the *pālikās* is said to be in the eastern part of the mandala of the Lord of the Mandala. (17)
One should prepare the fire-chamber either in the west or the north;
likewise, the preceptor, having taken it, should place the *pālikā* in the south or the north. (18)
Having prepared the sacrificial ladle (pālikā), the small jar (ghaṭikā), and twelve shallow bowls (śarāva),
he should thereafter fill the pits with Palāśa leaves and Kuśa grass.
The best of preceptors should wash [the image] which is twenty-four finger-breadths in height;
the preceptor should then bind dūrvā grass and bilva fruit around the neck region.
Thereafter, one should fill it with earth and perform the laying of the lines;
in a square corresponding to the size of the *pālikā*, one should fill it with rice grains.
Upon that, one should place a vessel; to its east, the container for the seed-syllables;
and to the west, the moon-pitcher—thus should the expert in tantra arrange them.
Having prepared the gateway according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the worship of the gateway;
then one should worship, in due order, within the water-pot, the mandala, and the fire. (23)
Standing on the right side of the *pālikā* facing north,
the preceptor should afterwards cause the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) to be proclaimed together with the Brahmins.
One should worship the deities consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva using the sacrificial ladle;
having worshipped the Soma-vessel, one should perform the fire-oblation with the Soma-mantra.
Sesame, mung beans, barley, rice, black gram, millet, peas, mustard, wheat, horse-gram, wild millet, and dark grain. (26)
But even in the absence of seeds, a single radish is recommended;
having gathered this and placed it in a vessel, one should pour milk into it.
One should place them and wrap the *pālikās* with cloth;
one should then deposit the power (*śakti*) residing in the Soma-pitcher into the seed-vessel.
Afterwards, one should perform the consecration with medicinal herbs and mantras;
subsequently, one should fill it again and perform the offering of clarified butter.
He should again worship the seed-syllable and perform the sowing of the seed with the sounds of conchs and drums, and with songs and auspicious musical instruments.
One should perform the worship again, concluding with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
and especially offer sacrificial food (bali) all around the pavilion.
The wise scholar should honor the assembly and cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given;
having worshipped the pitcher and the maṇḍala, he should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 32 ||
Having performed special protection, the wise one should place it in a well-guarded location;
day by day, O best of sages, he should perform the offering of oblations and worship.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Planting of Sprouts," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O bull among sages, I shall now describe the practice of dwelling in water in brief."
On the third or even the fifth day prior to the commencement of the ritual action.
One should perform it for one day, or perhaps for one night;
or else, one should practice dwelling in water for a watch (yāma) or even for half a watch.
One should perform the consecration rite (kautuka) for the frontal part of the image and for the entire body,
especially for the preceptor and likewise for the officiating priests.
Especially during the Citrā yoga, and likewise with large images, one should perform the preliminary consecration of the shadow; however, in the absence of a physical image, one should use a mirror.
In its absence, however, one should take a kūrca, having adorned it according to the rules,
and have it conveyed along with the attendants, especially to a place on the riverbank.
In a river, or at the edge of a pond, or even near a mountain spring;
in the absence of these, specifically in a large vessel or even a water jar. (6)
Having constructed a water-shed in the middle of the water and a pavilion on the bank,
one should decorate it with canopies and the like, as well as with the ritual jars, mandalas, and sacrificial pits.
The mandala is said to be a svastika, and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is likewise a lotus;
having performed the worship of the doors and so forth, one should worship the pitcher and the mandala.
The worship with jars is declared to be for Vāsudeva in the maṇḍala;
then, one should indeed fashion a lotus in the fire using the Viṣṇu-mantra.
Having performed worship in this manner, one should place [the deity] within the water;
having thus prepared the bed, one should then set down the Brahma-pitcher and the others.
Then, having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should offer the oblation (bali) with the rosary and food;
first, after the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), one should perform protection on all sides.
One should cause the air to resound with dance, song, instrumental music, and the chanting of the Vedas;
one should pass the night in vigil with Purāṇas and peace-mantras.
At the time of installing the household image, one should perform the immediate consecration;
then, at the clear dawn, one should bring it to the pavilion on the bank.
Then, having established them in their respective places, one should worship the four locations in sequence;
one should then sprinkle all [the vessels], beginning with the Brahma-pitcher, upon the head of the Brahman.
One should perform the ritual bathing with twenty-five jars in succession;
then, the knower of mantras should invoke [the deity] with the mantra, or with the mūrti-mantra. (15)
Then, having performed a pure bath, one should consecrate [the image] with the Puruṣa-sūkta;
then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should offer food and cast the bali-oblation.
One should cause the deity to enter the abode and visualize him as before;
having fully decorated the pavilion, one should place [the image] facing west.
Having fashioned a maṇḍala of a wheel and a lotus together with a water-pot for the purpose of showing it,
the wise one should accomplish everything for the sake of opening the eyes.
In the place standing before the deity, upon a pedestal of rice grains,
one should place a vessel of ghee and honey, and deposit eight kinds of grain.
Having placed both a cow and a maiden near it, as well as a golden needle and a pair of scissors made of silver; || 20 ||
Having strewn [the ground], one should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the four directions;
having worshipped the pitcher and the maṇḍala, one should also cause the proclamation of the "day of merit" (puṇyāha) to be made.
Having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should place vessels of clarified butter and so forth;
then, opening the right eye with a rod smeared with clarified butter, [one should perform the consecration].
With the mantra "citraṃ devānām" and with the mantra "taccakṣuḥ," he should show the maṇḍala, the water-pot, the cow, and likewise the maiden.
All eight kinds of grain, as well as a *pala* of gold,
various types of flowers, and diverse fruits. (24)
One should cause all these materials to be given to the preceptor, as well as a garment for clothing and likewise a linen cloth. (25)
One should worship the God again and cause the proclamation of the Vedas to be heard,
as well as song, dance, instrumental music, and the Purāṇas and Drāviḍa texts.
All those who steal the rain of flowers are thieves, whereas contentment is the Supreme Person;
the best of preceptors especially rejoices at the bathing pedestal.
Having performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), one should perform [the rite] one hundred and eight times at most,
or with eighty-one pots, or forty-nine.
Clarified butter and warm water, as well as gems and fruit-water, iron cleansing, fragrance, and unbroken-grain water. || 29 ||
Barley-water, as well as arghya, pādya, ācamanīyaka, pañcagavya, curd, milk, honey, and decoction; || 30 ||
O Brahmin, these substances are prescribed for the three kinds of jars;
the sequence of extraction is intended to proceed from the east up to the Brahma-jar.
Having wrapped it with cloth, silk, and so forth, and provided it with a tuft of grass (*kūrca*) and a *caṣa*,
one should then apply a coating of clay colored with red powders.
Hari himself is present in the worship of the five elements;
one should perform the worship of the five elements especially during the consecration ceremony. (33)
Anointing with clay, bathing in water, the offering of lamps, the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), anointing with fragrant paste, sprinkling, and likewise the playing of musical instruments; || 34 ||
I shall describe the procedure for applying clay; listen as I explain it in brief.
[One should take] earth from a river, a pond, an anthill, a mountain, or a field. (35)

The earth from the temples of elephants and boars, that situated on the horns of bulls, and likewise the mud from sacred bathing places and the ocean—this is remembered as the twelvefold [earth]. (36)
Likewise, it should be taken in a copper vessel and placed in a separate vessel;
or else, a shallow bowl or a water-pot should be supported by some clay as prescribed.
Having established it upon a heap of grain, there shall be twelve compartments.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having worshipped the clay, the practitioner [should proceed]. || 38 ||
One should apply a coating of clay with the twelve-syllable mantra;
having enclosed it [with the mantra], one should worship it along with the preliminary ablution (upasnāna).
O Brahmin, one should perform the ritual bathing of the jar with the twelve-syllable mantra,
or with the Viṣṇusūkta, or even with the Puruṣasūkta.
One should worship by means of intermittent applications such as the preliminary bath and so forth;
thereafter, one should perform the powder-bath and likewise the pure-bath.

One should perform the ritual bath with a thousand streams as well as the lustration ceremony (nīrājana). Having established twelve lamps in jars in the space before [the deity], [one should proceed]. (42)
O Brahmin, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with a water-pot accompanied by musicians and bards, and one should worship it with full ritual honors.
The worship of the fire is prescribed by means of the rite of lustration (nīrājana);
indeed, a consecration devoid of the worship of the fire becomes fruitless. || 44 ||
For the purpose of pleasing the Maruts, one should perform a fragrant bath with sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and likewise agallochum. (45)
Uśīra, koṣṭhaka, kacora, and likewise rajanī;
elā, lavaṅgaka, takkola, and muram as well. || 46 ||
These twelve [mantras] have been declared in this mantra by the Supreme Lord;
having placed them in separate vessels and worshipped them, one should bathe [the deity] with the twelve-syllabled [mantra].
The practitioner who has mastered the tantras should perform the *saṃpuṭa* rite with worship;
for the sake of pleasing Ākāśa, he should proceed with Vedic recitation, instrumental music, and so forth. (48)
And the chanting of the four Vedas and so forth, the Purāṇas, auspicious songs, verses and stanzas, as well as mixed compositions, and likewise the recitation of the Pratyaṅgiras hymns. || 49 ||
O Brahmin, one should cause [the text] to be heard in the presence of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
one should worship the Lord with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, followed immediately by words of praise.
Having adorned it according to the rule, one should prepare a bed.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Consecration of Water," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall now fully describe the ritual of the deity’s repose, and immediately thereafter, the ritual of installation.
First, one should construct a pavilion adorned with banners, archways, and water-pots.
It was adorned for a long time with canopies, the previously mentioned jars, delightful portions,
various kinds of fruits, and flower garlands.
Surrounded by garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned with strings of pearls,
the wise man should construct an altar in the center of that pavilion.
One should prepare a bed on the ground of the platform made of palm leaves,
and fill it completely with five bhāras of rice.
Half of that [measure] should be rice, and half of that again should be sesame seeds;
having spread these over each cloth, one should place a blanket on top of them.
Having placed a mattress above that, and likewise a tiger skin on top of it,
one should then place a multicolored cloth and a covering cloth above that.
Having thus prepared the bed, provided with a soft mattress and accompanied by three pillows, according to the method prescribed in the scriptures; (p. 74) 7.
On its right side, one should fashion a mandala;
it may be a wheel-lotus, or one with many lotuses, or even for the sake of attaining desired success.
On the northern side of the bed, one should construct a pedestal for the water-pot;
having prepared the water-pot as before, one should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
One should place the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus-altar at the four cardinal directions;
then, in order, the intermediate directions [are marked] with triangles, hexagons, or pentagons.
This very same procedure shall apply to the installation of the primary image (mūlabera),
as well as to the installation of Nārasiṃha and especially that of Vārāha.
O Brahmin, [one should perform] this in eight fires; otherwise, it would cause harm.
Specifically, one should establish the Vedas at the four directions as the mouth.
One should place the Ṛgveda in the eastern quarter, the Yajurveda in the south, the Sāmaveda in the west, and likewise the Atharvaveda in the north. (13)
Thus, according to the prescribed ritual for the Guru, the wise man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
having worshipped the bed, he should place [the image] upon the bed.
One should perform the worship beginning with the doors; one should worship Hari in the water-pot (kumbha), Vāsudeva in the mandala, and that specific form (tanmūrti) in the image (bimba).
One should place the deity upon the bed and cover him with the finest linen cloths;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-offering (homa), which should be conducted by each of the officiating priests (ṛtvij). || 16 ||
One should indeed adorn [the site] with two [lines], or one may have it done with four;
and in the absence of officiating priests (ṛtvij), one should employ the preceptor (ācārya) and others. || 17 ||
One hundred and eight oblations constitute the highest [rite], while half of that (fifty-four) would be the middling one.
Furthermore, the wood of the aśvattha, udumbara, nyagrodha, and plakṣa [should be used]. || 18 ||
Palāśa, khadira, śamī, and apāmārga—
should even these be unavailable, one should offer fuel-sticks of palāśa.
One should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and ghee;
at the conclusion of the oblation, one should especially offer the fourfold food.
Milk-rice, rice with mung beans, kṛsara, jaggery, pure rice, rice with black gram, and likewise rice with turmeric; || 21 ||
There should be a special oblation of pulse-cakes (śimbānna) in an eight-pit fire-altar;
having then performed the placement-oblation (nyāsahoma), one should carry out the dissolution-placement (saṃhṛtinyāsa).
Having performed the triad beginning with drying (śoṣaṇa), one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of emanation;
one should carry out the emanation and withdrawal by means of the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
Then, having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
Then, having performed the placement of the tantras (tantranyāsa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) separately for each.
Having performed it in this manner according to the ritual procedure, one should also fasten the door-panel.
Having fastened it thus for three nights, one should fasten it with a great deal of effort. (43)
When the fourth day has arrived, one should perform worship at the four locations;
thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with jewels, gold, and rings.
O best of Brahmins, one should perform daily worship from that time forward with gifts of cows, land, gold, clothing, and especially by the giving of maidens in marriage. (45)
One should indeed celebrate a festival and perform worship with mantras.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall now describe the conduct of the virtuous; listen to that with careful attention."
I shall describe his specific conduct of the virtuous in detail. || 1 ||
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the wise practitioner, recollecting his guru, should chant the names of the Blessed One and satisfy Him with hymns of praise. (2)
Salutations to Vāsudeva, the divine one, the embodiment of all virtues; O Saṅkarṣaṇa, let there be salutation to you, whose form purifies the universe.
O Aniruddha, homage be to you, whose form is the cause of the universe! Homage be to you, O Keśava; thereafter, homage to you, O Nārāyaṇa! (4)
Salutations to you, Mādhava; salutations again and again to Govinda.
Salutations to you, the Soul of the Universe; let there be salutations to Madhusūdana.
O Trivikrama, salutations be unto you; salutations again and again to Vāmana.
Salutations be unto you, O Śrīdhara; salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa.
Salutations to you, O Padmanābha; salutations to Dāmodara as well. Salutations to you in the form of the Fish; salutations to you in the form of the Tortoise. || 7 ||
Salutations be to you in the form of the Boar; salutations to you in the form of the Man-Lion.
Salutations be unto Vāmana; salutations unto the triad of Rāmas.
Salutations be unto Govinda; salutations unto you, Hayagrīva.
Having thus praised according to the prescribed rite, one should resort to the riverbank;
then, having laid down a cloth of darbha grass, one should go outside at a distance from the water.
With the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) resting on his ear, he should go out during the day facing north;
at night, facing south, he should place a blade of grass upon the ground.
One should smear the right hand with wood, leaves, grass, and so forth;
then, grasping the tip of the penis with the left hand, one should move it externally.

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in a clean location, one should take earth according to the mantra; one should perform the washing especially with earth that has been specially extracted. (12)
One should perform [cleansing] seven times on the region of the anus and three times on the penis;
one should perform the washing of the hands by means of repeated intervals.
One should perform the purification of the feet with five [applications] and then carry out the ritual rinsing (ācamana);
one should drink [water] three times, wipe [the mouth] twice, and likewise touch the ten limbs.
One should touch [the body] specifically with the fingers and with the eyes and other senses;
then, having applied a coating of clay, one should perform the binding of the directions with clay.
One should perform immersion with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should enter the area of the riverbank.
One should sprinkle water over one's own head with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā";
then, having formed a handful of water, one should perform a circumambulation.
Having especially offered libations, one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana);
thereafter, one should wring out the garment and then mutter the Sāvitrī mantra.
Then, having performed the ritual attendance, he should lead [the guest] into his own house;
having washed his feet, the wise man should perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) as before. || 19 ||
One should kindle the fire afterwards and then perform the daily oblation;
having completed the daily rites before the rising of the sun. || 20 ||
Then, having entered the temple, one should perform two circumambulations;
having performed purification and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before, one should carry out the worship.
Upon reaching the doorway, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa);
then, having made three claps of the hands (tāla), one should enter with the right foot.
He should sit upon a seat on the right side of the deity;
turning toward the north-east, he should proceed facing the south.
O Brahmin, at the western gate the wise man should likewise act;
then, having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), he should perform the gesture of snapping the fingers (choṭikādarśana).
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) by means of the triad beginning with exhalation (recaka),
one should perform the dissolution-assignment (saṃhṛtinyāsa) using the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
Having superimposed the individual soul upon the supreme, eternal Brahman,
the wise one, remaining within, performs the threefold process beginning with drying.
Having established the divine abode, one should perform the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa);
having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās, one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa). || 27 ||

In the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should likewise understand the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with the great elements (mahābhūtas), as well as the pentad beginning with the mind (manas) and intellect (buddhi). || 28 ||
The placement of the syllables of the root mantra, whether as the six limbs or twelve,
from the head down to the feet, is proclaimed as the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (emission-arrangement).
The placement [of mantras] from the navel up to the heart is proclaimed as the *sthitinyāsa* (placement of maintenance);
that from the feet up to the head is called the *saṃhṛtinyāsa* (placement of withdrawal). || 30 ||
The celibate student, the householder, and the ascetic, respectively, are the head, the eyes, the mouth, the navel, the private parts, and the sandals. || 31 ||
The earth and other elements have their abode in the feet or even the head;
however, for others, this lotus is declared to be the abode.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands through the processes of emanation, withdrawal, and preservation—
beginning from the right and ending with the left— it is proclaimed as the "emanation placement" (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
By means of the reverse yoga, the reverse [method] is illustrated:
the placement starting from the index finger and ending with the little finger is proclaimed as the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the rite of emanation).
First there should be the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands, and then the ritual placement upon the body;
having performed the nyāsa in this sequence, one should perform mental worship.
One should worship with offerings such as meditation, water for honor, fragrance, and flowers;
the wise know that mental worship is superior, while external worship is inferior.
The external, however, goes to destruction; therefore, the mental is superior.
One should act in such a way for one's own sake, but one should perform worship for the sake of others.
The practitioner, who knows all the scriptures, should not worship Viṣṇu if he is not himself Viṣṇu;
the wise man, an expert in the Pañcarātra, should contemplate, "I am God. (38)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Rule of Right Conduct," in the *Aniruddha-saṃhitā*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
I shall now describe the procedure for propitiation; listen attentively.
Bhṛgu said:
O Lord, with which substances and with which ritual offerings (upacāras) should one worship the God?
The Blessed Lord said:
By initiated practitioners, as well as by attendants, with sweet waters, flowers, and various kinds of perfumes; (2)
With incense mixed with guggulu, with lamps provided with wicks, and also with garments, sacred threads, and various kinds of garlands. (3)
With songs, dances, instrumental music, hymns of praise, and circumambulations;
with vehicles, chowries, and the sounding of conchs and trumpets. || 4 ||
With rhythmic claps, palm-leaf fans, ritual baths with water from jars, lustrations accompanied by lamps, and likewise with offerings of water for honor and water for the feet; || 5 ||
With camphor and betel leaves, with gifts of cows and peace-vases,
and with foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked, along with great and other offerings.
By means of recitations, prostrations, gifts, and especially by burnt offerings (homa),
as well as by the presentation of oblations (bali), festivals, and various kinds of images.
(84) And with palaces and pavilions accompanied by their retinues,
and especially with festivals and the like, [honored] by Ananta, Garuḍa, and others.
By means of the worship of the mandala, as well as by the worship of the water-jars (kumbha), by the worship of the fire, and accompanied by the monthly worship; || 9 ||
Then, by means of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite, the festival of leaves and flowers, the offering of *damanaka* plants, and likewise the festivals of fruits; || 10 ||
By means of the prescriptions for expiation, as well as by the worship of Viṣṇu and others, by worship on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, and by worship on both full moon days; || 11 ||
By means of the glorious Jayantī festivals, as well as the worship of Kṛttikā, especially by the Āgrayaṇa offerings, and likewise by festivals of Vedic study; || 12 ||
By means of special spring festivals, as well as festivals for the month of Jyeṣṭha,
through the worship of Tulasī, and likewise with Pāṭala and Campaka flowers.
One should worship the God with these; otherwise, one becomes a doer of evil.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship well with these substances.
Through constant, occasional, and likewise optional great festivals;
for if this ritual is omitted, there will be danger to the king and the kingdom. (15)
One incurs great fault, which is the cause of total destruction; therefore, I shall now describe the ritual services (upacāras) in brief—understand them. 16.
(85) The yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action are its two kinds of means.
O Blessed One, from the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge arises. (17)
The supreme worship of Keśava is performed through the excellence of the yoga of action;
indeed, the worship of Keśava brings happiness to both the king and the kingdom. (18)
It pacifies all suffering and bestows the fruit of omniscience;
it grants the fruit of the knowledge of the Blessed One, brings pleasure to Viṣṇu, and is auspicious. (19)
By the grace of the God of gods, [this leads] to the destruction of all suffering;
therefore, one should perform the worship of Keśava with every effort. (20)
O best of sages, one should first perform the fivefold purification:
the purification of the elements, the purification of the substances, and likewise the purification of the place. (21)
Then follows the purification of the vessel, and fifthly, the purification of the image;
bathing and sipping water are distinguished as the purification of the body. (22)
Purification of the mind through truth and the yoga of meditation is taught here. Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings, and meditation is indeed the contemplation of Viṣṇu.
The purification of a place is prescribed through sweeping and smearing, as well as by burning, moistening, washing, and even by sprinkling. (24)
The practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should understand the purification of substances;
he should indeed wash the vessels with pure water until they are clean. (25)
The purification of the *bimba* is brought about by *tintriṇī*, sand, and water.
Having performed the purification in this manner in due order, one should then place the auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*). || 26 ||
Upon a cloth or even on a wooden plank, one should place the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings:
the vessel for *arghya*, the vessel for *pādya*, likewise the vessel for *ācamana*, the vessel for bathing materials, and the pure vessel. (27)
One should place [the deities] from Agni up to Brahmā upon the supporting base;
likewise, one should place fragrance and fruit in the *arghya* vessel, and *dūrvā* grass and sesame seeds in the *pādya* vessel.
Cardamom and cloves are for rinsing the mouth; sandalwood is supreme for bathing.
For purification with pure water, the ritual worship is likewise performed in this manner. (29)
The goddess Śrī should be the deity for the *arghya*; Vāgīśī for the *ācamana*;
the divine Pitṛ for the *pādya*; and likewise Varuṇa for the *snānīya*.
Purification in pure water, peace, the five deities of the bowl, the burning and the satiation, and the manifestation of the daughter of Surabhi. || 31 ||
One should perform the gesture of snapping the fingers and worship all the vessels in sequence with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, using the five Upaniṣads.
Having likewise worshipped the water-vessel with perfumes and flowers,
one should then perform the worship of the door, specifically at the doorway.
Having worshipped oneself, one should then fully honor the lineage of gurus;
one should likewise worship the Guru, the Supreme Guru, and the host of Siddhas.
O Brahmin, having first performed the worship of the doors, one should worship the Person of the Temple (Prāsādapuruṣa);
one should worship all the deities situated upon the pedestal with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (35)
Likewise, he [established] the four beginning with Dharma, as well as the four beginning with Adharma;
the four beginning with the Vedas, and likewise the four beginnings of the Yugas. || 36 ||
Above that are the three qualities (guṇas), and above those are the three mandalas.
The first support is Kūrma, and immediately after that is Kālāgni.
One should worship Ananta, Maṇika, Bhadrapīṭha, and Paṅkaja, as well as all the members of the retinue in their respective places. || 38 ||
And likewise Vāsudeva and the others, as well as Śaṅkha and the others;
all the hosts beginning with Kumuda, and similarly the guardians beginning with Indra. (39)
One should worship all these hosts of Viṣvaksena, headed by Caṇḍa and the others, with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth.
Then one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) for the ritual and the marriage-thread (kautuka) using the root mantra,
with various offerings or with one hundred and eight [repetitions].
O Brahmin, in a sacrifice performed for the sake of others, one should not allow this sequence of sixty-four or even the sequence of twenty-two to be deficient.
For one's own sake, sixteen or thirty-two steps are prescribed;
immediately following these are the invocation, the salutation, and the rising from one's seat.
(88) The offering of flowers, words of welcome, a seat, a footstool,
the water for honoring (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and likewise the water for sipping (ācamana)— the sequence for these shall now be described. (44)
Especially during the offering of the *arghya*, one should sound the bell and the conch;
O best of Brahmins, during the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should perform the recitation of the Veda as the musical instrument.
O best of Brahmins, at the time of offering water for the feet, one should likewise offer two conch shells, a kāhala trumpet, and the sound of a horn twice upon the lotus-feet.
Having performed the wiping with a cloth, one should apply sandalwood paste;
one should offer flowers individually, or likewise fragrant water for the feet (pādya).
In the offering of water for the feet (pādya), there should be a conch shell; for the water for sipping (ācamana), it should be without a conch shell.
One should offer the water for sipping three times, and after wiping the mouth twice, one should touch [the lips]. 48.
One should touch the eyes, the nose, and likewise the ears and the two shoulders;
having placed the *arghya* on the head, one should place the *pādya* on the two lotus-feet.
O Brahmin, one should place the rinsing water (ācāma) upon the hands; then, for the eyes and other [limbs], one should perform the wiping, and finally touch the head from side to side.
One should offer fragrant unguents and flowers upon the head and the shoulders;
one should also offer loose flowers and leaves three times at the two lotus-feet.
The offering of incense, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), betel leaf perfumed with fragrance,
the gift of even a single mung bean, as well as sandals, a bathing cloth, and a seat.
But at the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), one should give only the rinsing water (ācāma);
likewise for all the seats, and for the giving of garments and betel-leaf. (53)
One should always cause the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) after washing the feet and especially at the conclusion of a meal; likewise, one should provide clothing, collyrium, and ointments.
Having offered a seat for the bath, one should then perform the washing of the feet;
[offer] water for sipping (ācāma), a cloth for bathing, and again water for sipping.
The cleaning of the teeth, as well as the scraping of the tongue, the rinsing of the mouth and sipping of water, and likewise clothing, garlands, and ointments— 56.
Oral fragrance such as betel-leaf, as well as a mirror and the like, a shoulder-cloth, oil, and fragrant flowers; || 57 ||
One should offer cakes bound with a cloth for the eyes,
fan [the deity] with a palm-leaf fan, and properly perform the anointing with oil.
At the conclusion of the offerings of cakes and other foods, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācāma), offer betel leaf,
plantain, and hot water, and apply an ointment to the face.
Sandalwood for smearing on the face, musk-impregnated camphor, highly fragrant oil, and sweet, cool water. (60)
Then, having performed the pure bath (śuddhasnāna), one should cause a washed garment to be offered;
likewise, the water-offering (arghya), the turmeric bath (rajanīsnāna), and again the bath.
One should offer washed garments and provide vessels;
one should perform worship as before and present the *arghya* offering. (62)
One should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and fragrant unguents;
as well as a sacred thread, a sacrificial cord, and an upper garment. (63)
Offering garlands of flowers, the presentation of incense, the lighting of lamps, the recitation of the Vedas, and various kinds of hymns composed both in prose and verse; (64)
The common auspicious rite, as well as the Piśāca auspicious rite, the sung auspicious rite, and likewise dance and instrumental music. || 65 ||
The bath with a thousand streams, preceded by the jar-bath (kalaśasnāna),
should be performed twelve or nine times, according to one's means.

Ghee for the foot-washing, curd as the respectful offering (arghya), and thereafter milk; then water for sipping (ācāma), scented water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and decoction-water.
Just as it was taught regarding the ninth jar, hear now [the teaching] for the twelfth and beyond:
gems, metals, fruits, and flowers are placed in the center and in the four [directions] respectively. (68)
But even when materials are unavailable, it is recommended to perform at least one rite from that category;
likewise, for daily ablutions and for the consecration of a marriage-thread, the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is prescribed.
Bathing with powders of *niśā* (turmeric) is not desired on the site of the pavilion;
one should perform the offering of *arghya* at regular intervals.
The bathing with a thousand streams shall consist of three *anuvākas*;
likewise, there shall be consecration with the *viṣṇusūkta* and prosperity through the *śrīsūkta*. (71)
The earth is said to be [purified] by the Bhūsūkta during the ritual bathing;
it should be performed verse by verse, or the whole may be done with the eight-syllable or the twelve-syllable mantra.
At the conclusion of bathing, at the conclusion of eating, and at the end of the period for ornaments and the seat—
especially in the evening— one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
One should wave the lamp within the vessel once, twice, or thrice;
it should be accompanied by many lamps and arranged for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
It may be a pair, a fourth, a group of six, or indeed a group of eight, ten, twelve, sixteen, twenty, or even thirty. (75)
Having especially prepared the lamp-vessel with consecrated materials,
one should worship the deity with water for honor (arghya), flowers, and so forth, satisfying Him in the proper sequence.
The Lord of the gods should whirl [the vessel] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
he should then wipe his head and body with two washed cloths.
One should wear lower and upper garments and perform the wrapping of the head;
accompanied by song, instrumental music, and the like, one should proceed to the seat of adornment.
Having adorned oneself with ornaments, one should especially sit upon the seat. || 79 ||
p.
92) The best of those who know mantras should perform the preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings as before.
Then he should perform the worship of the doors and likewise the worship of the retinue. || 80 ||
One should likewise perform the worship of Viṣvaksena and the worship of the deities of the pedestal,
as well as the offering of the arghya and so forth, and likewise the water for washing the feet and the water for sipping.
Three types of offerings are prescribed for the rite of propitiation;
one should perform the bathing of the body using camphor powder.
In ancient times, Viṣṇu indeed declared that musk is for bathing the head;
likewise, one should apply an ointment to the body with mixed sandalwood. 83.
O Brahmin, there should be artificial ointments applied to both armpits;
one should perform the wrapping of the head with various kinds of perfumes and flowers. (84)
Having adorned it with garlands for the head, one should hang it from the base of the arm, shaped like a mace-staff and like a pericarp. || 85 ||
One should likewise offer a sacred thread and ornaments;
having applied a tilaka on the forehead, one should likewise apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka).
Betel-leaf, a mirror, incense, and likewise a lamp;
a vehicle, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, a banner, and the proclamation of auspicious fame. (87)
The sound of the Vedas and ancient [hymns], the resonance of conchs and trumpets, as well as song, dance, and instrumental music, preceded by the offering of the *mātrā* measures; || 88 ||
There should be circumambulation, prostration, and likewise the waving of lights (nīrājana).
Then, one should seat the Lord of Gods upon the dining seat together with three devotees of the Bhagavat. (89)

Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and immediately thereafter the honey-mixture (madhuparka); then further water for sipping, betel-leaf, and the gift of sesame seeds and cows. || 90 ||
Likewise, one should give a garment for the limbs, as well as honor and food—specifically milk-rice (pāyasa), mung-bean rice, and pure food mixed with milk-rice. (91)
Having offered a beverage, as well as water for drinking, water for rinsing the mouth and sipping,
and having performed the wiping with a cloth, one should apply fragrant unguents.
Having summoned the followers of the Pañcarātra, one should worship them with water for the hands (arghya) and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform the gift of the manual (tantradāna), preceded by the madhuparka offering.
Then, having offered the maternal gift (mātrādāna) and presented betel,
one should worship the rosary and perform the rite of recitation (japa).
Then, having entered the kitchen, one should perform the rite of oblation (homa).
Thus has the supreme worship been briefly described. 95.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Worship," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of sages, I shall now describe the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in brief."
Having reached the kitchen and worshipped the door, the practitioner [should proceed]. || 1 ||
O Brahmin, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (homa-kuṇḍa) to the south of the hearth;
it should be square, level, and provided with both the yoni and the navel.
Equipped with three girdles and provided with a pedestal and other such items,
he should take his seat upon the throne on the southern side of the sacrificial pit.
One should perform the ritual tracing (ullekhana) on the sides of the extensive [mandala], which brings prosperity;
with three lines facing east and likewise three facing north.
The eastern end should face south and north, while the northern end should face west;
thereafter, one should kindle the fire and then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should strew darbha grass there with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva;
one should strew it with darbha grass on the northern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The practitioner should arrange the vessels in pairs;
likewise, he should set out the vessel for clarified butter, the ladle, the sprinkling vessel, and the *praṇītā* water vessel.
The one most skilled in mantras should especially prepare the fuel and the ladle;
having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel in front, he should deposit the *pavitra* strainer therein.
One should fill it with water from a water-vessel and perform the ritual sprinkling there;
one should sprinkle the vessels with that water and properly perform the rite with them turned face upwards.
Furthermore, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and place the praṇītā vessel in front;
having performed the "floating" (utplāvana) as before with a blade of darbha grass according to the rule.
Having lifted it up level with the forehead, one should place it upon the girdle;
then, on the northern side of the fire, one should deposit the *brahmakūrca*.
The wise practitioner should worship Brahmā in due order with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and perfumes;
then, taking a vessel of clarified butter (ājya), the adept should pour the ghee into it.
Then, on the northern side of the fire, one should divide the embers;
having divided them, one should place them above and then kindle the darbha grass.
Having placed two tips of darbha grass there and kindled them again, he should show them;
then, having lifted up the vessel of clarified butter, he should join the embers with it.
Having taken it and placed it before him, one should properly perform the ritual of leaping;
having cast the *kūrca* grass forward, one should display the cow of Surabhi. || 15 ||
Taking the ladle with his left hand and a blade of darbha grass with his right hand (in the apasavya manner),
the wise man should heat it three times and then cast the darbha blades into the fire.
The learned Brahmin should place the enclosing sticks (paridhi), the clarified butter (ājya) to the south, and [the offerings] to the north;
he should place the after-offerings (anuyāja) and the Praṇītā water in the middle of the front.
Then, having performed the oblation of fuel-wood (idhmahoma), one should subsequently offer the āghāra libations.

One should first offer the support beginning with Anila (the northwest) and ending with Agni (the southeast); then the second support, beginning with Nairṛta (the southwest) and ending with Īśa (the northeast). (19)
To the left and right of Agni, however, the oblation is offered by means of Soma;
thereafter, one should present the Goddess and the God, which is the supreme union of the seasons.
One should also contemplate the fire produced from both [hands];
O best of the twice-born, having performed the rites beginning with the end of the *homa*, one should [offer] with clarified butter (*ājya*). 21.
One should offer sixteen oblations each with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice;
then, having performed the offering to the tongues of fire and ascertained one's own capacity, one should perform the fire-sacrifice.
I shall now specifically describe the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) in its proper sequence;
thereafter, one should kindle the fire and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having performed the sprinkling of water in due order and meditated upon the fire, one should worship it;
this may be done with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, or indeed with clarified butter alone.
One should perform the secondary oblation (parahoma) three times with the substances using the three root mantras;
or else, one may offer twelve or eight oblations and present the bali offering on all sides.
One should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for oneself and for the ancestors;
thereafter, one should strew darbha grass and perform the offering of three mouthfuls (kavala).
Immediately after the groups of the ancestors and the mothers, the preceptor should offer three morsels of food with his left hand to the Viśvedevas. (27)
One should first offer water and afterwards perform the sprinkling;
by this distribution among the ancestors, the God of gods is pleased. (28)
By the grace of the God of gods, it shall bring about all accomplishments.
I shall now explain the ritual of the bali offering; listen with attention to this concise account.
Having first performed the bali offering, one should thereafter conduct the festival;
[one should prepare] the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru), flowers, a bell, and indeed an incense burner.

Especially during the offering of the *bali*, the wise practitioner should present the oblation from the entrance of the womb-chamber up to the pedestal (*pīṭha*), amidst the clamor of the sounds of conchs and kettledrums.
In the ritual of bali-offering, one should present the offerings for the groups beginning with Kumuda and for those beginning with Indra separately,
three times each, using substances measured by the handful.
Having first worshipped with water-offerings (arghya) and other items, one should cast [the offering] preceded by water,
accompanied by the sound of a bell and joined with the music of the bali-offering.
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, as well as the treasure-vases Śaṅkha and Padma;
Bhadra and Subhadra, and likewise Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ.
One should worship Jaya and Vijaya at their respective gates,
as well as the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the pestle, and the sword.
The Śārṅga bow and the forest garland (vanamālā), stationed in the inner enclosure,
as well as Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana. (36)
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita;
as well as Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa. || 37 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation to Vāyu, Soma, and likewise Īśāna, who are situated in the third enclosure, and to Viśveśvara in the cardinal directions, as well as to the Kṣetrapāla.
One should especially offer the bali-offering for all beings upon the pedestal;
having thus given it according to the rule, one should then perform the daily festival.
Taking the image of Bali and placing it upon a vehicle, the guide [should proceed] with it accompanied by umbrellas and chowries, and provided with many lamps. (40)
Accompanied by numerous attendants and provided with song and instrumental music,
one should bring the Lord of the gods around the temple in a clockwise circumambulation.
One may circumambulate [the altar] once, twice, or even thrice;
having completed the circumambulation of the *balipīṭha*, one should take a stand on the eastern side.
The wise man should cause song, dance, and instrumental music to be heard by the God of gods; he should lead him to the temple and install him within the pavilion.
And one should worship [the deity] with offerings ending with the *nivedya*, as well as with the *arghya*, scents, and so forth;
namely, the *arghya*, the *pādya*, the *ācamana* water, scents, flowers, and incense. (44)
Having placed the lamp, the offering, the betel, and the vocal and instrumental music in their proper places, one should then propitiate Viṣvaksena. (45)
Having performed the worship beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the lamp, the wise practitioner should cause a single vessel of the food offering (*naivedya*) to be given to Viṣvaksena.
No one else should touch the remnants left over from that [offering] once it has been offered by the hosts of deities;
then, having performed a circumambulation and prostrated before Janārdana, [one should depart].
Then, having entered his own home, he should perform the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga).
If the preceptor (ācārya) is deprived of food, the worship of the deity is fruitless. (48)
Just as Hari eats from the mouth of Agni, so too does he eat from the mouth of one who serves the gods;
when the teacher is well-pleased, the God of gods is pleased.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire-Rite and the Offering of Bali," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Bhṛgu said:
"I desire to hear about the ritual bathing of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow."
O Brahmin, tell me the sequence of time and the expansion of the substances in their proper order.
The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one, I shall describe to you in detail the ritual bathing (snapana).
Bathing is declared to be of two kinds, distinguished as the higher (para) and the lower (apara). || 2 ||
However, it is said to be of three kinds; the lower [form] consists of twelve thousand, half of that, half of that again, and half of that once more. (3)
I have specifically declared three types, namely the supreme [mantra],
as well as those consisting of one, three, five, nine, and twelve syllables.
The seventeenth, the twenty-fifth, the thirty-sixth, and the thirty-ninth;
specifically the fortieth, and in sequence the eightieth and the eleventh. (5)
And likewise, there should be one hundred and eight [recitations]; thus it shall be twelvefold on the solstices, the equinoxes, and on both full moon days.
Especially on the twelfth lunar day, or when the moon is in the Śravaṇa asterism at the time of his birth,
or on the day of the ritual consecration, or during the offering of the damana plant and other such rites.
At the beginning and end of festivals, especially during the flower sacrifice (puṣpayāga),
as well as during the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) and the festival of flowers and fruits (puṣpaphalotsava).
In the worship of the four locations, as well as during rites for drought, when ill omens have arisen, in times of famine, and during affliction by disease; || 9 ||

In the performance of special sacrifices and also in the replenishing of ritual substances, the wise man should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed; otherwise, it would result in fault.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
the earthen one should have the shape of a ripe bimba fruit and be free from defects.
An *āḍhaka* is declared to be the best; half of that is the middling; half of that again is declared the lowest. A wise man should have these three varieties constructed. (12)
Twice that [measure] is called a *karaka*; twice that is said to be a *kumbha*;
and twice that is a *mahākumbha*—this is proclaimed as the standard of measurement.
Everything is determined by measurement; therefore, measurement indeed fulfills [the requirement].
There should be wrapping with thread for an earthen jar, but one should avoid it for metal.

The cloth, the tuft of grass, and the shallow bowl—these materials are common [to all]. Ablution is said to be of two kinds: that which is an auxiliary to ritual action (karmāṅga) and that which is independent (kevala). || 15 ||

In the case of a subsidiary part of the ritual, however, there should specifically be no *aṅkura* or *kautuka*; but in the case of the primary rite alone, there should specifically be both the *aṅkura* and the *kautuka*. || 16 ||

A twice-born man should perform the decoration of the pavilion as part of the ritual for festivals and the like, or solely on occasions such as the equinoxes, just as he would for the rite of consecration.
But indeed, O best of Brahmins, one should perform worship at four locations;
then the wise man should have a mandala constructed according to the desire of the patron.
In the row to the north of the pavilion, one should arrange the water-pot, the mandala,
and the ear-ring in order, starting from the east and ending at the west.
In the center of the pavilion, one should perform the installation of the water-pot;
first, one should perform the laying of the lines and the installation of the image.

O best of Brahmins, one should perform the laying of the foundation lines (sūtrapāta) according to the size of the water-pot (kalaśa), whether it be one, two, or three [pots], or in groups of nine and so forth. (21)
One should especially fill a corner of the chamber with a *prastha* measure of rice;
one should perform the consecration of the water-jars (*kalaśa*) in the western location of the jars.
Having likewise prepared the three paths, he should strew rice grains and then spread darbha grass there, facing eastward, while reciting the Parameṣṭhi mantra.
The preceptor should place the pitchers upon that very person;
having performed the rites of drying and so forth, he should worship them thoroughly with the arghya offerings and other requisites.

The preceptor, knowing the mantras, should place the jars facing downwards with the Viśva-mantra alone; afterwards, the knower of mantras should scatter unbroken grains (akṣata) with the Nivṛtti-mantra.
Having strewn darbha grass all around, the knower of mantras should cover [the vessel] with a cloth while reciting the serpent-mantra; thereafter, he should offer oblations on all sides.
At that time, the supreme preceptor should perform the consecration of the ritual materials;
O Brahmin, during the consecration of the materials, he should sprinkle them with the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya).
This ritual action is especially universal for all;
it includes the sprouting [of the seed], the tying of the auspicious thread, and likewise the consecration of the water-pot.
Either immediately prior to the day of commencing the ritual action or at that very moment, one should perform the entire procedure,
including the rite of worship at the gateway and the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
p.
103) Immediately following that is the worship of the fire within the reflection of the pitcher-maṇḍala;
then the bathing with the pitcher, and immediately after that, the bath with aromatic powder. || 30 ||
Then one should perform the pure bath (śuddhasnāna) as well as the night-bath (rajanīsnāna);
thereafter, the bath with a thousand streams (sahasradhārayā) and the lustration rite (nīrājana) follow.
Next, one should perform the rites for the pavilion and the seats, followed by the seating for the meal;
then, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and present the sacrificial offering (bali) on all sides.
O Lord! This ritual has been described in sequence for this auspicious [temple];
however, in the case of the single-liṅga (ekabera) arrangement, the ceremonial bathing (snapana) should take place right there.
But when there is an extensive arrangement of many rites, there should be a ceremonial bath (snapana);
likewise at a festival (utsava), and in the absence thereof, at the rite of the sacred thread (kautuka).
One should perform the ritual worship upon an image made of plaster, a wall-painting, or a cloth;
in the absence of those, on a mirror; and in the absence of that, on a tuft of grass.

O Brahmin, during the ritual bathing of the deity as part of the rite and during festivals, one should perform everything [as prescribed]. Now, I shall briefly explain the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the substances; listen attentively. (36)
The best knower of the tantras should pour into the northern jar either ghee, or else the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or simply fragrant flowers.
But on the third day, there should especially be leaves, flowers, and fruit;
and on the fifth pot, O best of Brahmins, there should likewise be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
(104) Fragrance, flowers, fruit, as well as leaves and grain; and likewise the five products of the cow—these shall now be described in relation to the ninefold [rite]. (39)
Alternatively, there may be ghee and so forth, or water with the nine gems, or even the nine perfumes and so on; these will now be described in the twelfth [chapter].
Alternatively, the ghee and other substances may be taken in two, three, or even four parts and so on;
immediately thereafter, water with dhātrī fruit and water with lodhra [are used].
Water with red sandalwood, the excellent water of turmeric,
water with *granthi*, *phala*, *vacā*, and *aśvattha* wood, and then water with grass.
Then water from the priyaṅgu plant, after that water from the muñja grass, then white mustard water, barley water, and likewise water containing all medicinal herbs. || 43 ||
Leaves, flowers, and water—these twelve are thus proclaimed.
Now, I shall describe the substances for the seventeenth jar in their proper order.
Ghee, warm water, jewel-water, fruit-water, iron-powder, fragrance, unbroken rice, and barley-water. || 45 ||

Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as curd, milk, honey, and astringent decoction (kaṣāya)—these shall be the seventeen [substances] in due order. || 46 ||
Now the placement of substances in twenty-five jars is described: O Brahmin, one should pour ghee and other substances into a group of nine among them.
Clarified butter, water for the feet, curd, and then the *arghya* offering consisting of milk;
thereafter, water for rinsing the mouth, scented water, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and decoction water. (48)
O Brahmin, one should sequentially place the substances, including water with *dhātrī* fruit, into the thirty-six pitchers; this is declared to be the ritual placement of substances (*dravyanyāsa*).
The supreme thirty-six jars are said to contain a set of nine substances;
alternatively, they may contain a set of nine beginning with ghee, or a set of nine beginning with fragrance.
Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and likewise agallochum; cardamom, cloves, black pepper, usīra, and koṣṭha as well. || 51 ||
I shall now describe to you the placement of substances (dravyanyāsa) in the forty-nine jars,
as well as the primary group of seventeen substances and their application in due order.
In the central pitcher, one should place either fresh milk alone or ghee;
likewise, in the six great pitchers, one should fill each with ghee alone.
O Brahmin, one should fill the four corners of the intermediate directions with curd; now hear the sequence for the placement of substances in the eighty-one jars.
Next, one should perform the excellent deposition of seventeen substances in their proper order;
this may be a collection of substances beginning with clarified butter, or even milk alone.
Or, O Brahmin, listen: one may offer pure ghee alone one hundred and eight times;
among those [offerings], there are thirty-two substances, and within those, four.
Incense, flowers, fruit, as well as roots, leaves, and sprouts; likewise, small mandalas and long bouquets. (57)
Now, that group of nine wheels is proclaimed to be long;
[the substances are] sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and snow-water. (58)
One should place [the flowers] in the four central jars, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth: the hundred-petaled lotus, as well as the jasmine, the mallikā, and the bakula. (59)
O Brahmin, one should place twelve [fruits] in front and a mirror in the middle;
likewise, the plantain, the jackfruit, the wood-apple, and the pomegranate.
In the twelfth pitcher of the southeast, one should place [the substances] in the center as before:
camphor, hrīvera, uśīra, and turmeric.
O Brahmin, in the twelfth [month] of Yama, in the midst of four water-pots,
there should be Tulasī leaves, Bilva leaves, and likewise two Dantī leaves.
One should place [the items] in a vessel in the southwest; in the west, there should be sprouts:
dūrvā grass, aśvattha shoots, bhadra, viṣṇukrānti, mahī, and gaja. (63)
In the northwest (Māruta), one should mention a cluster of flowers, as well as moss and agallochum;
in the east, the Ātharvaṇa priest, and in the north, they likewise prescribe [these offerings].
O Brahmin, the *punnāga*, the *pāṭala*, the *cūta*, and likewise the *āragvadha*—as well as the *kramuka* and the *nālikeraka*—are said to be [placed] in the northeast. (65)
*Tāla* indeed, *rola*, and *kramuka* are found in the middle steps;
the eleventh is declared to be *apara*, while the others are said to be threefold. (66)
One thousand, half of that, and half of that again—these three [measures] shall be;
O sinless one, I shall describe to you in detail the eleven jars.
Having placed one in the center and four in each of the directions, the fifth is recommended to be placed both in the four directions and in the center. (68)
It is taught that there are nine in the eight directions; hear now that there are twelve in the center. Eight groups of eight are taught, and four indeed in the middle.
O Brahmin, in the sequence of seventeen, there should be a central group of nine;
outside of that, in the eight directions, one should place the eight jars.
O Brahmin, one should place twenty-five jars in the middle group of nine;
there shall be sixteen jars on the outside—now hear about the thirty-six jars.
One should place four [units] in the four directions within the nine compartments;
listen, O brahmin of secret mind, to the forty-nine [squares]. (72)
O Brahmin, having placed the group of nine in the center, there would be five groups of eight in the directions;
they declare that to be the sequence for the eighty-one jars.
O Brahmin, one should arrange nine [deities] each in nine rows;
O Brahmin, the procedure for installation in one hundred and eight [deities] is now being declared.
"O Brahmin, one should arrange twelve [deities] in each of the nine rows.
O Brahmin, the procedure for the installation in the thousand-pitcher [rite] is now being declared. (75)
O best of Brahmins, one should place eighteen jars in the central regions of the field;
in the nine squares, one should place them two by two.
Outside of that, one should place five [vessels] in each of the eight directions;
and outside of that, in the hundred and eight jars, one should place them in the intermediate directions as well.
O Brahmin, one should place twelve [units] each in the nine rows;
one should place them all around in the various directions with exactly one hundred and eight [units].
O twice-born one, in this manner, with eighteen jars for each of the nine rows, there will be one hundred and eight jars plus sixty-four. (79)
One should arrange [the deities] from Brahmā to Īśāna in rows and columns;
the remaining thirty-six jars should be filled with powders of turmeric.
I have described two methods for the installation of a thousand jars;
O Brahmin, the installation of fifty jars is now being told.
O Brahmin, one should place [the mantras] around the one hundred and eight [deities], and forty-nine in each of the eight directions.
Now hear about the placement of fifty and twenty jars. || 83 ||
In the fields within the four squares, one should place forty-nine [deities];
outside of that, in the eight pitchers, one should place twenty-five.
And there should be two hundred jars of powder all around.
Now I shall describe the placement of substances for the thousand jars.
One should place the nine gems in the central eighteenth pitcher;
and by means of the application of pairs and pairs, one should deposit them into two pitchers.
One should place a single pearl on each of the forty external jars;
then, with the root mantra, one should fill the jar dedicated to Indra, which is the hundred-and-eighth, to completion.
One should place hrīvera, karcūra, uśīra, and likewise rajanī in the middle of the four jars, together with fire.
O Brahmin, one should place hribera around the eight external jars;
beyond that, in the eight directions, I shall describe to you the placement of the substances.
