The two types of *rajanī*, ginger, *muśīraka*, the three kinds of *utpala*, *kānta*, and *karcūra* constitute the group of eight. (90)
One should place the substances of affection within eight or twelve jars;
in the midst of the one hundred desired vessels, one should place a group of four upon the petals.
Having cast into the fire the two *tulasī* leaves and likewise the two *damanaka* leaves, one should indeed offer the remaining *tulasī* leaf.
O Brahmin, I shall describe to you the multitude of leaves on the outer eight-petaled [lotus]:
the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Vaṭa, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha. (93)
O Brahmin, one should place a mango, a wood-apple, and a vakula flower there in succession; this is declared to be the ritual placement of substances for each hundred [verses] in the southern octad.
In the central four-pitcher arrangement, however, one should place the *campaka*, the *vakula*, the *mālatī*, and the *śatapatra* in the directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya). || 95 ||
O Brahmin, one should place a hundred-petaled lotus in the eight external jars;
outside of those, in the eight directions, a profusion of flowers is prescribed.
There should also be a Nandyāvarta, a Punnāga, a Mālatī, and likewise a Mādhava;
there should be a triad of Utpalas and a Ketakī-cāraka.
One should fill each one individually, pot by pot, separately;
O Brahmin, I shall now describe to you the collection of fruits for the eight [deities] in the southwest. (98)
Likewise, one should place the plantain, the breadfruit, the *mātṛcūta*, and similarly [the other fruit] in sequence into the four pitchers in the middle, starting from the east. (99)
Outside of that, one should place plantains in eight jars; I shall now describe to you the arrangement of fruit-filled vessels starting from the eastern direction.
Likuca, vakula, pomegranate, citron, pārāvata, āmalaka, navāṅga, and viśva—these indeed [constitute the nine parts]. || 101 ||
One should fill this vessel in the same sequence as before;
in the western [direction], there should be only milk and only clarified butter. (102)
In the northwest, I shall fully describe the four substances: sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and agallochum; one should arrange these four in their proper order.
O Brahmin, in the remaining jars situated around the perimeter, there is only sandalwood water; now the substances for the exterior directions, starting from the east, are described in order.
Mura, māñjiṣṭhaka, karcūra, koṣṭha, or likewise campaka;
and elā, lavaṅga, and takkola—these are proclaimed as the substances in their respective order. (105)
In the gentle [quarter], one should fill a single pitcher with milk among the twelve;
likewise, the substances for the eighth and tenth [pitchers] are prescribed in order.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, curd, and likewise buttermilk;
sesame oil, mustard oil, coconut, ghee, and molasses. (107)
Learn from me the substances for the jars situated in the northeast (īśānaka) in their respective order:
jujube juice, sugarcane juice, and sugar-water.
One should place the *sādhaka* mantra upon the meritorious [deities] within the four jars;
in the jars containing the eight seed-syllables, one should fill them with the essence of sugarcane juice.
Now learn from me the substances to be placed, in order, in the pitchers outside, starting from the east:
sesame, parched grain, mung beans, rice, black gram, and vachā.
One should place wheat and *priyaṅgu* seeds respectively into the jars;
then, one should bathe Puruṣottama with the Sahasramūrti mantra. (111)
One should bathe the supreme jar with the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvan, and other [Vedic hymns], or with the eight-syllabled mantra, or even with the twelve-syllabled one. || 112 ||
The first sequence of extraction is held to proceed from the east up to the north-west (Soma);
the second extraction proceeds from the south-east (Āgneya) up to the north (Īśa). || 113 ||
From the beginning to the middle and the end, there would be the grasping of everything;
it would be either milk alone as a single part, or ghee might come into existence. (114)
Or else, one may offer a thousand [oblations] with coconut water alone;
now I shall describe the sequential placement of substances (dravyanyāsa) in a jar containing half a thousand [units]. || 115 ||

Ghee, fragrance, as well as flowers, leaves, roots, and fruits, and likewise the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and milk, [should be offered] starting from Brahmā in the east, ending in the northeast and the west. || 116 ||
Having placed curd in the northeast, one should bathe Puruṣottama.
Now I shall describe the inferior mode of bathing according to the sequence of placing the ritual substances.
O Brahmin, one should fill all the central jars with milk alone; and outside, on the eight squares numbered twenty-five, [one should place the remaining substances].

The arghya, pādya, ācamana, buttermilk, curd, ghee, honey, and astringent decoction are prescribed in sequence; the purification with earth and water should be performed as previously described. (119)
But even when materials cannot be obtained, one-sixteenth part of them is recommended;
for materials, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity, while for the circular ornaments, Garuḍa is the presiding deity. (120)
The remaining deities of the vessels are for the *sūtras*, while the Lord of Serpents (*phaṇirāja*) presides over the bowls;
Brahmā is the deity of the *kūrca* grass-bundles, and Dharma is the deity of the supporting base (*ādhāra*). || 121 ||
Vāsava is the presiding deity of garments, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of all things;
that man who bathes the Lord of Gods with jars filled with ritual substances [attains great merit].
Freed from all sins, he goes to the abode of Brahmā;
he attains incomparable prosperity and obtains the fruit of all sacred fords.
It shall indeed yield the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all gifts;
one does not return through the cycle of worldly existence—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one, I shall describe to you in detail the festival.
Know that every inauspicious event is accompanied by a festival that serves as its remedy.
Festivals are of three kinds: regular (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). That which is performed annually or monthly is the regular festival. || 2 ||
When a cause has arisen and come into being, that which results from it becomes the effect.
Bhṛgu says:
And likewise during the appearance of spirits and the like, in times of famine, and when afflicted by disease. || 3 ||
And upon the entry of an enemy army, or likewise when the sound of wheel-rims is heard in the sky, or at the resonance of divine drums, or upon the sight of a young fish; || 4 ||
Likewise, when the rainbow is seen in the eastern quarter during the night, or when a meteor falls in the western or central quarter, especially so. (5)
When the storehouse is consumed by fire, when a palace collapses, and likewise when walls, gate-towers, and the like, as well as sacred trees and so forth, fall down. || 6 ||
When a circular mark arises from anthills and the like, or when honey is obtained within it—especially for kings—upon the onset of diseases and other afflictions; || 7 ||
O Brahmin, when the affliction of the planets has arrived, arising from the defect of the new moon (kuhū), and when disease and other calamities arise for one's sons, wife, and so forth; || 8 ||
O Brahmin, in the event of drought or excessive rain, upon the killing of gods or Brahmins,
or upon the death of one's father or mother, one should perform penance for the sake of expiation.

O Brahmin, the festival is traditionally held to be of three kinds: the constant (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and that which one performs for the sake of desire is called the optional (kāmya).
The festival is said to be of three kinds, according to the distinction of superior and so forth:
the month is called the superior, and the fortnight is called the middling. (11)
(115) "Nine days, however, is declared to be the lowest; such is the certainty of the scripture.
[This applies] to a single day, three days, and likewise five, seven, or nine days. (12)
One should have it performed on the twelfth day, as well as in the fortnight or after a month;
however, one should not perform the rite of the banner on the first day or the third day.
Now I shall describe the time of the sacred ford (tīrthakāla); listen, O best of sages! [It occurs] during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 14 ||
On the king's birthday, or on the day of his consecration, or on the two full-moon days, or during the Śravaṇa month, or every month; (15)
O Brahmin, one should perform a ritual bath at a sacred ford on the day of consecration, or on one's own birth-day, or even on the day of the equinox.
One should perform the hoisting of the flag prior to the day of the ritual bath at the sacred ford;
in the rite of the nine-day festival, one should perform it on the twenty-first day.
One should perform [the rite] eighteen days prior to the day of commencing the work, or likewise on the fifteenth day, the thirtieth day, or after two months.
Or else, on a day of the week (vāra), that procedure is likewise described:
either preceded by the hoisting of a banner or preceded by the beating of a drum. || 19 ||
The threefold distinction is said to be preceded by the offering of the sprout;
O great sage, listen as I describe the procedure for hoisting the banner, which is a secret. (20)
O best of sages, prior to the day of raising the banner, on the fifth or seventh day, or on the ninth, or even on the eleventh day; (21)
The wise one should offer the sprouts according to the sequence previously described.
Sprout is said to be of three kinds: seed, shoot, and grain. (22)
If there are many nights, it shall be seed; if there are few nights, it is for sprouting.
Especially at the time of immediate [use], they prescribe rice.
There may be various types of vessels, such as pālikās, ghaṭikās, and shallow bowls;
likewise, [they are used] for the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) and the festival of the water-jars (kalaśotsava). || 24 ||
O best of Brahmins, during the consecration of a great image and during festivals of leaves, flowers, and fruits,
there are three types of aṅkurārpaṇa for the God of gods.
In all other matters, one should act according to the *pālikā* [measure];
O Brahmin, in the performance of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), each one shall consist of sixteen [units].
There may be twelve, or eight, or six, or four; or there may be only a single *pālikā*, or even twelve or eight. || 27 ||
The height of the Trivargapāli should be sixteen finger-breadths at most,
with a width of twelve finger-breadths, shaped like an unmatta flower.
A *pālikā* is described as being provided with two openings;
a *śarāva* is described as being provided with a single rim. (29)
The water-jar (ghaṭikā) should have five faces and be oriented toward the four directions and the center;
having washed it with pure water, one should fill the vessel with grass for the sacrificial offering (bali).
One should tie [a protective amulet] made of *rajanī*, leaves, and *dūrvā* grass around the neck;
likewise, at the time of collecting the earth, one should bring the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa).
Likewise, one should also extract Viṣvaksena or Hanumān,
accompanied by their various attendants, using a spade.
One should perform the ritual as before, including the decoration of the pavilion, the worship at the four locations, and likewise the worship of the doors and other parts. (33)
Then one should perform the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) and prepare a water-pot (*kalaśa*) as before;
O twice-born one, one should also draw either a mandala, a swastika, or a lotus within a wheel (*cakrābja*).
I shall describe the cloth specifically, and the work of painting in particular:
it should be ten cubits, eight cubits, or even seven cubits [in length]. (35)
The peak should be as wide as half its length and provided with a tail;
it should be polished, fitted with a bit, dried, and endowed with the proper characteristics.
The most skilled painter should paint it according to the rules of the treatises on art,
with half [the width] extended by half, and the crest made with a quarter [of the width].
One skilled in the arts should fashion [the image] with nine tālas, including the measures of height and width; he should paint the deity in the center of the cloth using five colors. (38)
Two-armed and golden-hued, resplendent with a crown and a casket, he is beautiful as he begins his flight through the sky, his wings outspread.
With his palms joined in reverence, the tip of his nose was dark blue;
he was pleasant to behold, yet his face was formidable with fangs, and his eyes were curved with a frown.
The left foot is raised, while the right stands behind;
Ananta is upon the left hip, and Vāsuki is the sacrificial thread.
Takṣaka is the waist-string, and Kārkoṭaka is the necklace;
Padma is on the right ear, while Mahāpadma is on the left.
Śaṅkha was on the region of his head, while Gulika was on his arm;
he was thus adorned by these eight beautiful and supreme serpents.
Having placed a parasol above and white chowries on both sides,
one should place two lamp-stands at the sides and a conch and a discus on either side.
Below [the central figure], one should draw a lotus, a full water-pot, and small bowls; the intervening spaces should be filled with dark black color.
Having thus painted the cloth, one should properly perform the consecration;
one should have the cord made from a collection of threads with a thickness equal to that of a thumb. (46)
O Brahmin, before the day of commencing the ritual and also at night, at the beginning of the night, the preceptor should bring the cloth-painting into the pavilion in front of the deity. (47)
Having shown the root-liṅga, one should elaborate [the ritual] in the presence of the deity;
having installed the water-pot (kumbha) as before on the northern side of the pavilion.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the southeast and a mandala to the east of the cloth-painting;
the mandala may be either a svastika or a bhūtāvāsa.
In the western part of that [area], one should perform the supreme installation of the image;
one should carry out the worship of the doors and so forth, and perform the ritual adoration of the four stations.
Afterwards, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and tie the protective amulet (kautuka) upon the cloth;
then he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the shadow over either a large cauldron or a water-jar.
One should perform everything using a mirror; in its absence, however, one should use a *kūrca* (bundle of grass).
Having established the secondary jar (*parikumbha*), one should then place the Brahma-jar.
O Brahmin, having placed it in water for one watch (yāma) or even for half a watch,
the practitioner should worship it in the pitcher with the Brahma-bīja mantra.
One should worship Indra and the other deities for protection over all the jars;
one should offer an oblation of black gram and rice in all eight directions.
O best of the twice-born, the wise one should join the Lord of all gods, who has been fashioned from clay, onto the cloth;
he should perform the opening of the eyes as previously described.
Then one should apply a coating of clay from the summit of a mountain;
having invoked [the deity] into a mirror, one should place it upon the bathing altar. (56)
One should perform the *snapana* (sprinkling) as before, followed immediately by the *cūrṇasnāna* (powder bath),
the *śuddhasnāna* (pure bath), the *mantrasnāna* (mantra bath), and subsequently the *nīrājana* (lustration).
The wise man should place the fastening cord for the cloth and the arrangement for the bed,
and he should set down a water-pot on the right side of the cloth.
Having placed the *vardhanīs*, the *parikumbhas*, and the eight auspicious vessels (*aṣṭamaṅgalaka*) all around the *pālikās*, one should worship the Lord within the central jar.
O Brahmin, one should worship Garuḍa depicted on a cloth with one's own vidyā;
then, having performed the rite of fire-offering (homa), one should carry out the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Then, having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods, one should present oblations (bali) on all sides;
and one should place Garuḍa, who resides within the water-pot, in the center of the cloth painting.
I shall describe the invocation of the deities accompanied by the striking of the drum;
this is especially significant when there is a banner, and it should be performed in its entirety during that night.
O Brahmin, when the banner is divided, there should likewise be the mounting of banners;
one should then depict Garuḍa in the middle of the cloth and perform the three paths.
Having thus prepared the bed, one should place the image of Bala there;
the wise practitioner should then install a water-pot to the east of the image of Bala.
On the eastern side of the pitcher, one should place a drum;
there, with a surrounding strewing of *darbha* grass, one should install Vāsudeva and the other deities. (65)
The learned man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and should fully worship that *bali* offering;
the learned man should also honor the drum together with the bell of white copper and other instruments. (66)
The conch, the kāhala, the jhallikā, and likewise the maddala, as well as the paṭaha, the timila, and the short maddalaka. || 67 ||
One should likewise place a set of bronze cymbals all around;
specifically, one should properly invoke all the gods into the water-pot.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, as well as Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna, along with Indra, Āditya, and the hosts of Maruts. || 69 ||
The eight Vasus, twelve Ādityas, and eleven Rudras, in their respective order—
the eaters of offerings such as Kumuda and the others previously mentioned—
[should be worshipped] in dwellings for the rites of the great festival of Hari.
Tell me, in due order, of the attendants of Hari in every direction of my preceptor, the teacher of all the gods.

I shall indeed describe, according to my understanding, the colors, forms, vehicles, weapons, retinues, mantras, and modes of worship for Kumuda and the others stationed in the directions of Indra and the rest— during the great festivals and other occasions of Hari, who is the source of all cosmic eggs, the lord of Śeṣa and Dhiṣaṇa, the four-faced one, the immeasurable, and the eternally blissful.
Vāsudeva, seated upon a lotus placed on the throne of the aggregates (skandhas),
whose vehicle is the wind whose speed is shaken by his own velocity;
I invoke the Lord of Birds, whose curved beak is eager to seize the king of serpents, at the beginning of festivals and other occasions.

Having thus recollected [the Lord], one should worship Him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; immediately thereafter, having likewise offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), the ritual substance, and the food offering (naivedya), and having presented water for sipping and joined palms in reverence,
one should provide a mouth-freshener for Hari, followed by conch-shells, drums, dance, song, and so forth, for the sake of satisfying the deities of the directions.
One should have [an image] made for the Lord of the Gods, who has arms terrifying with the thunderbolt,
who is dark-complexioned, and who is the cause of the destruction of the race of Dānavas.
Salutations to you, the former sovereign, whose vehicle is the celestial elephant, the husband of Pulomā’s daughter.
Thus, O Agni, you incessantly carry the oblation of the gods, or else lead the ancestral offering into the presence of the Pitṛs— you,
the smoke-bannered burner, whose belly is the sacrificial ladle.
Salutations be to you, Śoṇa, the Lord of the South-East. || 73 ||
To him who is thus the Time, who metes out equal punishment to the world, who possesses a blue radiance, whose vehicle is the lord of buffaloes,
whose weapon is the staff, and who is the son of Vikartana;
To Śyāma, whose vehicle is the terrifying lord of beasts, the sovereign of the corner, who possesses a gleaming and fierce sword;
O Nirṛti, who brings joy to the hosts of Piśācas, Rākṣasas, and Yātudhānas, let there be salutation unto you! || 75 ||
To you, Śyāmala, who rides upon a crocodile, whose hand holds a shimmering noose,
we offer salutations to Varuṇa, the giver of life.
Salutation to the Lord who is the protector of those whose direction is other [than their own]. || 76 ||
To the one who possesses the distinctions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, who holds the banner, who is smoke-colored, whose vehicle is the preeminent tall deer,
the lord of the corners [of the mandala], and the purifier of the worlds.
Salutations be to you, the wind, who possesses swift movement. || 77 ||
To him who is gold-colored, beloved of Śiva,
the lord of wealth, whose weapon is the mace,
the sovereign of the northern direction, and who dwells on Mount Kailāsa.
Salutation be to that one whose vehicle is the bull. || 78 ||
To him who is mounted upon a bull, who has matted hair and a crown, who is adorned with a skull and a digit of the crescent moon,
who wields a trident, and who dwells in the intermediate direction.
Thus, bearing in his hand a rosary and a water-pot that resemble the glow of refined gold, he— p. 124).
Salutations to you, the Self-Existent One, who mounts the supreme swan, and who desires to create the worlds.
O Great-minded One, let all musical instruments be sounded by those skilled in the art of playing them, whether in a village, a city, or even a town. 81.
One should adorn the entrance of the street with plantains, betel-nut trees, banners, and sprouts,
as well as with lamps, full water-pots, garlands of *darbha* grass, and archways.
The wise practitioner should offer the bali-oblation from Indra up to Īśāna;
the festival, the bali-linga, and the water-pot should indeed be placed facing the deity.
Having mounted [it], together with attendants, accompanied by a multitude of palm-leaf fans, joined by many banners, and attended by the playing of musical instruments; || 84 ||
Standing in the direction of Indra (the east) or other quarters of the village, facing the deity,
one should perform the smearing with cow-dung to the extent of one cubit.
Then, having prepared a seat of darbha grass and directed it toward the deity,
the practitioner should then invoke the god Indra and Kumuda as well.
One should likewise worship with the arghya, pādya, ācamana, fragrance, flowers, incense, bali, and betel leaf, preceded by the recitation of verses. || 87 ||
(125) Furthermore, the beating of drums accompanied by the clapping of cymbals,
as well as song, dance, and instrumental music, [should be performed] in all regions in due order. (88)
Kāntāra is in the eastern direction, Kauśika likewise in the south;
Kāmada is said to be in the west, and Tarkarāga in the north. (89)
In the southeast there shall be Kaulī, in the southwest Naṭabhāṣaṇa;
Takkeśī is in the direction of the wind (the northwest), while Cālāpāṇī is in the quarter of Śaṅkara (the northeast).
In the center, the fifth is proclaimed; in the location of the *pīṭha*, however, it is Mālavī.
In the eastern quarter there shall be Deśī-nṛtta, and in the south-eastern quarter Mallaka shall be.
In the south, however, is the game of the water-pot; in the southwest, the game of battle;
in the west, the game of the ball; and in the northwest, the game of the host.
One should know the Mārga [tīrtha] to the north, and Bhujaṅga in the northeast;
the Gaṇabhū is said to be in the Brahma [quarter], while Maṅgala is on the side of the Pīṭha.
The shield is in the southern quarter, while the circle of wheels is in the south-eastern (Nairṛta) direction;
situated in order in the eastern quarter, the sound arises in the south-east (Āgneya).
The Gāruḍa dance is in the western quarter, while laughter and dancing are in the northwest;
the Maṅgala dance is in the northern quarter, and the Mahānṛtta is in the northeast.
In the Brahma [quarter], however, all musical instruments should be placed according to one's preference in the vicinity of the seat;
in this very manner, one should offer the bali-oblation on all sides. || 96 ||
Standing to the south of the pedestal, one should perform the hoisting of the banner;
having installed the banner-pole, as well as the pillar and the sandalwood [image], [97]
The teak tree, the khadira, the jackfruit, or the pāṭala; likewise the betel nut, the coconut, the palmyra palm, and the bamboo. (98)
One should discard a hollow that is naturally dry, fallen, crooked, or curved;
it should be one hundred tālas, half of that, or even half of the latter. (99)
Some maintain that its height should be eighty *tālas*, or even half of that; it may also be equal to the height of the palace or the height of the gate-tower (*gopura*). (100)
The base should be thirty-two finger-breadths wide, with a hollow at the middle and the tip, excluding the opening;
one should fashion three tiers of pedestals, and the pedestal should have the shape of a yantra. The projection should be equal in measure, and one should fix the staff right there.
One should have the pedestal made of udumbara wood or else of aśvattha;
the staff should be made of bamboo or khadira wood, with the tip of the staff being of equal measurement.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass in a clockwise direction,
one should place a piece of *darbha* grass together with other *darbha* blades in front of it.

O best of Brahmins, one should lay it with its handle pointing north on the northern side of the pit; however, if there is a constriction, it should be done according to the requirements of the location.
In rites for the gods, one should have [the ground] prepared with lines running eastward and northward;
having washed it with pure water, one should perform the sprinkling with the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula. (106)
Having worshipped it with perfumes and flowers, one should extract [the mantra] by means of the yantra itself;
one may have it fashioned either with a fixed banner-cloth or even alone.
One should make the base of the pillar firm and properly construct the pedestal;
it should be three cubits, two cubits, or even five cubits in size. || 108 ||
One should likewise raise the hand [to measure the height], and above that, one should fashion three tiers (mekhalā).
Above those, one should fashion a lotus adorned with twelve or eight petals.
One should construct a pavilion or even a water-shed all around the pillar;
thereafter, the most excellent of preceptors should hoist the banner using a rope.
One should first perform the *puṇyāha* rite after worshipping according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should offer the sacrificial oblation preceded by the sprinkling of water from the jar.
In the presence of the God of gods, one should perform dances, songs, and so forth;
having circumambulated the processional path, one should cause the festival to enter.
But those people who hear the drum at the time of hoisting the banner shall not cross a river, nor travel more than a yojana by vehicle. (113)
When there is movement, one constantly incurs disease through delusion;
therefore, with every effort, one should avoid going outside. || 114 ||
(128) Thus has the ritual for hoisting the banner been briefly proclaimed by me.
This concludes the "Ritual for Hoisting the Banner" in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: O sinless one, I shall describe to you in detail the great festival.
First, the sowing of seeds, and likewise the hoisting of banners.
After the festival of the marriage-thread (kautuka), the commencement of the festival shall take place;
the ritual bathing of the God of gods occurs immediately after the initiation for the sacrifice.

Then follows the worship of the four locations, the performance of fire-offerings (homa), the offering of water at sacred fords (tīrtha) and the planting of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), as well as the ritual oblation (bali) for the village. || 3 ||
Likewise, there should be the consecration (adhivāsana) of the image for the festival procession and the pilgrimage site;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford (tīrthasnāna) following the flower sacrifice (puṣpayāga).
The lowering of the banner, the offering for dismissal,
and likewise the worship of Viṣvaksena— they know this to be the sequence of rituals.
On the seventh or fifth day from the day the festival begins,
one should perform the offering of the sprouts (aṅkura) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
On the evening preceding the day of the festival's commencement, the wise one should bind the *kautuka* (protective thread); that sequence shall now be explained to you. (7)
Having thoroughly decorated the pavilion with banners, arches, and water-jars,
as well as with betel-nut trees, plantain trunks, darbha grass, garlands, and so forth.
In the center of that, one should construct an altar and fashion the Viṣṇu-yantra;
the wise practitioner should place the water-pot (kumbha) in the northeastern direction of the pavilion.
As before, the wise one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) at the side of the fire;
he should then install the image to the west of the mandala according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed the worship of the doors and other parts, the wise preceptor should perform the worship of the four locations and have the auspicious thread (kautuka) made of gold.
It should indeed be joined with threads and cords, especially during festivals;
and particularly for the two goddesses, for the bali-offering, the ritual bathing, and the image.
Specifically for the preceptor and likewise for the officiating priests,
one should place [the offerings] together with betel leaves in separate vessels of rice.

Having placed [the hand] upon the head of the disciple, he should circumambulate the temple in a clockwise direction, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and provided with songs and musical instruments. || 14 ||
Having cast a heap of grain, one should place it upon the support;
thereafter, the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited. || 15 ||
Afterwards, one should worship the image and then worship the *pratisarā*;
the wise one, having taken up the thread with both hands, should hold it fast. (16)
One should tie [the cord] on the right hand of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
one should place it on the left hand of Śrī, and on the hand of the preceptor himself.
Having worshipped as before, one should offer cakes and other foods;
then, having offered food made with mung beans, one should present the bali offering on all sides.
Having prepared a bed, he should place [the deity] upon it;
then, together with all his attendants, he should perform the festival of the dawn hour.
It was joined with many lamps, accompanied by songs and instrumental music,
attended by the recitation of auspicious benedictions, and endowed with every kind of auspiciousness.
Having thus rotated [the deities], starting from the eastern enclosure of the street and ending with the western inner enclosure, one should install them within the pavilion.
Having displayed all the arts, such as dance and song, the wise one,
the best among those who know mantras, should begin the ritual bath at the commencement of the festival.
One should then bathe [the deity] with either one hundred and eight or eighty-one jars, and subsequently perform the powder-bath (cūrṇasnāna).
Having led [the image] to the seat of adornment and having adorned it according to the prescribed rite,
one should then place it upon the ground of the sacrificial pavilion.
O Brahmin, I shall describe in brief the ritual procedure for initiation into sacrifice, which includes the Śrībhūmi and is accompanied by the bali-offering and the image; listen attentively. (25)
One should construct a pavilion in front; if one cannot obtain a site in front, then as one pleases.
Having well-decorated the pavilion, it should be adorned with canopies and other ornaments. (26)
Adorned with banners, arches, and water-pots, and provided with jars of water and betel nuts, the wise man should have the maṇḍala constructed with various paintings on its walls.
The wise practitioner should place the water-pot on the northern side of the maṇḍala;
outside the perimeter of both the pot and the maṇḍala, one should construct the sacrificial fire-pits (kuṇḍa) all around.
Now hear the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) from the east up to the northeast:
they are triangular, circular, hexagonal, or octagonal, respectively in the intermediate directions.
O Brahmin, regarding the rite for eight sacrificial pits, hear now the procedure for four pits:
a triangle, a bow, a circle, and a lotus, in order starting from the east.
But in the primary ritual procedure, O best of Brahmins, one should prepare eight sacrificial pits;
one should first select the officiating priests for each pit individually.
One should place Garuḍa in the eastern part of the maṇḍala,
the Cakrarāja in the south, and Baliberaka in the west.
Having adorned the northern side of the Senaśa [temple], one should install either a mandala or a wheel-lotus (cakrapadma), which bestows the desired accomplishment. || 33 ||

Or one may have the Yantra known as Vāsudeva constructed according to one's preference; [one should prepare] the water-pot (kumbha), the mandala, and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), together with the secondary pots (parikumbha). 34.
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel beside the great *kumbha*,
accompanied by a secondary *kumbha* and endowed with the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgalaka*).
It was provided with small offering vessels, endowed with various kinds of fruits,
and joined with long clusters of betel nuts and coconuts.
One should place a pair of garments in the great pitcher, and another [pair] elsewhere;
[the latter] should be joined with a *kūrca* of sprouts and placed in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) together with a thread.
In each and every shallow bowl, one should place a coconut fruit;
having done this, one should especially perform the worship of the door.
One should worship the god Vāsudeva, who is free from ailment, in the main pitcher (kumbha);
one should worship the deities beginning with Vāsudeva in sequence in the subsidiary pitchers (upakumbha).
Having honored [the deity] with many offerings, or with the sixty-four groups,
one should perform the sprinkling and bathing in both the water-pot and the mandala.
One should offer oblations separately with specific ritual services into the fire; afterwards, one should worship within the mandala and thoroughly worship the supreme image.
Then, having performed the fire-offering (homa) rite with the mantras of Vāsudeva and the others,
one should offer oblations in the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) through the application of the principle of arising and non-decay.

One should perform the offering of the sprouts at the sacred sites (tīrtha) according to the sequence previously described; likewise, having offered the oblation (bali) along the pathway together with the sacrificial vessel (balibera). (43)
Accompanied by the *kumuda* and other groups [of attendants], and provided with song and instrumental music,
one should place the festival procession upon an elephant or a chariot.
Or specifically a palanquin, according to its form as obtained, provided with many attendants and equipped with numerous lamps. (45)
When the intermediate enclosure has been completed and one has reached the final enclosure of the pathway,
and having arrived at the site for the offering, one should present betel and sandalwood.
When the central region has been reached, one should perform the ritual play of the Gaṇas;
having done so specifically in this manner, one should lead [the deity] to the great pavilion.
Then, having seated [the deity] upon the lion-throne, one should worship with the water for honoring (arghya) and other offerings:
arghya, pādya, as well as ācamana, fragrance, flowers, and incense. || 48 ||
One should present a lamp, a lustration ceremony, and many dances;
then, having removed the garments and garlands, one should perform the ritual of bathing.
At the conclusion of the bath, one should place the Lord of the gods in the pavilion;
then, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the worship until the offering of food (naivedya).
In the first [case], a chariot is prescribed; in the second, it should be a palanquin;
in the third, Garuḍa is prescribed; and in the fourth, indeed a chariot.
In the fifth [year] there shall be a palanquin; likewise, in the sixth, an elephant;
in the seventh, a flower-carriage; and in the eighth, a horse-vehicle. (52)

In the ninth [day] there is the luster of an elephant; in the tenth, it becomes an elephant itself. Prior to the consecration at the sacred site (tīrtha), the day of death and so forth occurs. || 53 ||
Before the day of the hunt, there shall be immersion for water-sports; before the day of the water-sports, there shall be a visit to the garden. (54)
One should perform the river festival before going to the garden;
now, the measurement of rice prior to the day of the river festival is described.
One should then undertake residence in the forest prior to the Vrihimāna day;
furthermore, the procession of the Lord's image at the two appointed times shall be most excellent.
Or else, at one and the same time, according to the desire of the maker,
[he should be adorned] with unprecedented ornaments and garlands, as well as with unprecedented garments.
Just as curiosity arises regarding unprecedented gardens, vehicles, and other such things,
so too should one perform these special rites specifically until the day of the Tīrtha.
On the night preceding the day of bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the ford;
having beautifully decorated the pavilion, one should bring the image of the sacred ford there.
Having established the seat of grain, one should bring the image of the deity from the sacred ford;
then, having worshipped it with offerings such as the *arghya*, the wise one should install the water-pot (*kumbha*).

Having invoked the sacred waters (tīrtha) into the jar and worshipped them, the wise practitioner should subsequently present the sacrificial oblation (havis) and offer the bali-offering on all sides. || 61 ||
Having taken the powder of Rajani, the preceptor should place it in the mortar;
then, having washed both the mortar and the pestle, he should worship them.
First is immersion by the teacher, followed immediately by the courtesans; then there is rubbing with powder, or else the pentad or the triad [of these]. (63)
Having established [the image] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should indeed place a grass mat (kūrca) there;
having worshipped it with the Puṃs-mantra, one should perform the rite for a day of merit (puṇyāha). || 64 ||
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, one should perform the powder-bath;
the powder touched by the body of Vāsudeva is supremely purifying.
O Brahmin, water touched by one's feet becomes equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā;
likewise, Tulasī, sandalwood, and flowers remove all the sins of men.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause this to be given to devotees;
those who carry it or drink it attain the supreme goal.
The Avabhṛtha-bath:
Then, at the clear dawn, one should perform the festival of the day;
preceded by the purification of the city, one should offer the oblation (bali) as before. (68)
At the conclusion of the procession, one should sprinkle the Lord of Gods, preceded by the primary image, with the *kūrca* from the great jar while reciting the root mantra.
One should enclose [the deity] with worship and then enjoin it within the maṇḍala;
specifically, that which resides in the fire, preceded by the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 70 ||
Having first performed the expiatory oblation (prāyaścittāhuti) and the worship of the pitcher and the maṇḍala as prescribed before, one should subsequently perform the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
O twice-born one, having installed the image of the deity at the sacred ford (tīrthabera) with the best of Brahmins,
and at the conclusion of the festival, having taken it back, one should retain only the image of the deity at the sacred ford.
One should bring it to the site of the sacred ford (tīrtha) and have a radiance (prabhā) created right there;
having reached the site of the sacred ford, one should place it in the midst of that radiance.
Taking a vessel from the sacred ford, one should again join it with those waters;
having duly worshipped that sacred water, one should bathe the Lord with jars [of water].
But having reached the sacred ford (tīrtha) afterwards and immersed oneself there three times again,
those who bathe shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
One shall obtain the fruit of all gifts as well as the fruit of all sacred fords;
then, having settled [the image] in its own place, one should perform a pure ablution.
Then, having performed the mantra-bath, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having brought forth the seat of ornaments, one should worship until the end of the oblation (havis). || 77 ||
One should bring the deity to the temple along with all the attendants,
preceded by Brahmins chanting the Vedas, to the western side of the enclosure of the residence.
Accompanied by a festival procession, one should bring the image of the Tīrtha to the street;
then, having installed it in its own place, one should sound a conch shell at the doorway. (79)
Having established the festival in the pavilion, the wise one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed;
then, having led [the deity] to the seat of ornaments, he should offer abundant food.
When the tenth day has arrived, one should perform the flower sacrifice;
in the presence of the God of gods, one should carry out the recitation of the Vedas (vedapārāyaṇa).
The Saṃhitā and the Śākhā, and immediately thereafter the Āraṇyaka;
likewise the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Atharvaṇa itself. || 82 ||
Then one should honor the deities with garments, betel, and food;
one should cause the ritual bathing for the purpose of the flower-sacrifice to be performed according to the prescribed path.
First, one should tie the protective thread (kautuka) for the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
then, having reached the fire-mandala, one should perform the flower-mandala.
Alternatively, one may employ a wheel, lotus, or mechanical device according to the teacher's discretion;
then, one should place the image upon a lion-throne at the western side of the mandala.
The wise one should place the water-pot on the northern side of the mandala;
he should install Viṣvaksena in the northeast quarter of the deity.
To the south, one should place the King of Weapons (Hetirāja) surrounded by Brāhmaṇas;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the doors and the worship of the water-pot and the maṇḍala.
Thereafter, one should worship the images—eight, or even twelve;
specifically, six or four at each particular time. (88)

The water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), fragrance, flowers, a lamp, incense, food offerings (naivedya), betel leaf, and the gift of sesame seeds. || 89 ||
The Veda, the Śloka, as well as song, dance, and instrumental music—these are repeated again and again;
song is declared to be auspicious, while dance is indeed the Mārga-nṛtta.
Having gathered a profusion of flowers, one should place them separately in vessels; having set them down in close proximity, one should worship them with flower petals.
Having performed the rites of drying and so forth, one should worship thoroughly with the water-offering (arghya) and other materials;
namely, the fourfold set consisting of arghya, fragrance, flowers, and incense.
One should place [the offerings] with cloth alone and scatter them at the feet of the deity;
then one should perform the honoring of all the groups of artisan-servants.
One should cause divine garments to be offered with sandalwood paste and betel leaves; the preceptors and practitioners should then place them upon the head of the deity. (94)
The wise man should perform a circumambulation of the temple,
either once or twice, standing at the entrance.
Having summoned the people, the preceptor should satisfy the God with hymns of praise,
as well as all the gods and hosts of sages who have arrived for the purpose of service.
Having beheld the Lord of the gods, one should dismiss him to his own place;
having led the deity into the inner sanctum, one should establish him in his proper station. (97)
Taking that pitcher, one should place it upon the support;
having worshipped the primary image (mūlabera), one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the root mantra. || 98 ||
Then one should perform worship once more and display auspicious rites and so forth;
having offered the *pāyasa* (milk-rice), one should then honor the patron (*yajamāna*).
Having placed the teacher upon a vehicle, one should lead him into one's own home, like a deity, amidst male and female servants and the resonant sounds of musical instruments and conch shells. 100.
One should honor all the people with unadulterated offerings such as betel leaves and other gifts;
then, having entered the temple, one should again perform the ceremonial bathing for the festival.
O Brahmin, whether it be in an eighty-one-pitcher or a twenty-five-pitcher [arrangement],
one should enter the sacrificial pavilion specifically at the conclusion of the ritual bathing.
Having completed the remainder of the ritual action, one should offer the expiatory oblation;
specifically with sesame seeds, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should cause all the deities residing therein to go to their respective abodes;
having installed them in the inner sanctum as before, one should perform a great festival.
Having performed the offering for dismissal (udvāsanabali), one should lower the banner;
having worshipped [the deity] as before, one should offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.
Having invoked Garuḍa into the jar, one should perform the descent (avarohaṇa);
likewise, [one should descend] his staff, his cloth, his rod, and his radiance. (106)

The preceptor, having personally brought [the materials], should cause the wise disciple to give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of garments, gold, gems, and so forth; otherwise, he would become a doer of fault.
He should also provide five-fold ornaments, along with maidens, cows, land, and excellent wealth;
half of that should be given to the officiating priests, and to the singers according to their capacity. (108)
One should bring satisfaction through honors and other marks of respect to those who have come from other lands;
thus, he who performs the festival with devotion as enjoined by the scriptures [attains merit]. (109)
He attains incomparable prosperity and obtains the fruit of ten million righteous acts;
likewise, he gains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
One obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), the fruit born of many gifts of cows, and the fruit of many meritorious deeds; of this there is no doubt. || 111 ||
It brings about the destruction of all sins; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
One should perform ablutions twice a day, especially at the time prescribed for bathing.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Festival," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall now describe the procedure for the monthly festivals; listen briefly."
Especially on every twelfth lunar day, and on both equinoxes, month after month.
Among all the lunar mansions, Śravaṇa shall be the most excellent;
among the lunar days, the twelfth is the best, and among the days of the week, it is Friday.
One should especially worship [the deity] on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) month after month, during the yoga Vyatīpāta and the karaṇa Viṣṭi.
One should perform worship on the new moon day, the full moon day, or at the half-month;
however, one should especially perform the worship of the maṇḍala on the twelfth lunar day.
Especially on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should perform a ceremonial bath with water-pots;
it may consist of ghee, or milk, or even coconut water.

Then, according to the desire of the patron, the Guru should perform the worship of the four locations, especially during the Śravaṇa asterism, using either the aforementioned materials or other substances.
O Brahmin, one should place leaves, flowers, and other offerings upon the Mānasa-kṣetra;
and in the month of Māgha, under the asterism of Maghā, one should perform the offering of the damana plant.
In the month of Phālguna, under the [appropriate] lunar mansion, one should perform the planting of Tulasī;
in the month of Caitra, under the [appropriate] lunar mansion, one should perform the worship of Campaka.
In the month of Vaiśākha, under the asterism Śatabhiṣaj, one should worship with a lotus;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, in particular, one should perform the ritual for the festival of fruits.
O best of Brahmins, on the new moon day falling under the asterism of Anurādhā or even Śravaṇa,
one should bathe [the deity] with a thousand jars, or half that number, or half of those again.
One should perform it with one hundred and eight [offerings], or with fewer than that;
either with the aforementioned substances or with milk alone.
O Brahmin, one should worship with either pure ghee or coconut water during the month of Āṣāḍha, under its presiding asterism, using mango fruits as offerings.
O Brahmin, one should have a bed prepared during the Cāturmāsya period starting from the month of Śrāvaṇa;
when the moon is in the constellation of that month, one should worship with plantain fruits.
In that month, on the twelfth day, one should perform the ritual of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa);
and on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, one should celebrate the Jayantī festival.
In the month of Bhādrapada, under the asterism [Śravaṇā], one should perform the worship with lotuses;
in the month of Āśvayuja, under the asterism [Dhaniṣṭhā], one should worship with white lotuses. || 15 ||
In that month, one should especially perform the rites of laying down and raising [the deity];
in the month of Kārttika, under the lunar mansion of the month, one should perform the lighting of lamps.
O Brahmin, throughout that entire month one should perform the worship of Vṛścika;
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, under the [corresponding] asterism, one should apply fragrant unguents.
In the bright fortnight of that month, one should perform the study of the Vedas;
one should hold a festival for study lasting either ten or seven days. (18)
Or else, O Brahmin, one should perform it for five days, or three days,
or even twenty days, and cause all the gods to hear [the recitation].

One should always cause a festival to be performed by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and are conversant with the mantras of the deity's form, as well as the vehicle that was his own in a previous birth.
In that ritual, one should avoid the fire-oblation of the Kumbha-maṇḍala;
and in the month of Puṣya, under the asterism of that month, one should perform the smearing with turmeric.
In that month, however, one should especially observe the practice of eating forest food;
in the month of Māgha, one should perform the gift of sesame seeds and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors.
This is declared to be the "Monthly Rite" (māsakarma); its procedure is now explained:
O Brahmin, during the ritual of leaves and flowers, one should perform the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
O Brahmin, one should properly perform the fruit-offering and other rites of completion;
O Brahmā, in the ritual of fragrance-offering, one should properly perform the anointing.
First, the sprouting [of the seed], and likewise the decoration of the pavilion;
thirdly, the pure ablution, and fourthly, the worship of the gateway.
The worship of the four locations is declared as the fifth;
the sixth is the image for the marriage-thread ceremony (kautuka), followed by the preparation of the bed.
After that, the consecration of the bed and the protective rite (rakṣā) should be performed;
then one should perform the morning bath, and the ceremonial bathing with water-jars (kalaśa) shall take place. || 27 ||
The procedure for the worship of the door, as well as the veneration of the four locations,
the offering of food (naivedya), the ritual oblation (bali), and likewise the donning of ornaments.
O Brahmin, the offering of ornaments constitutes the "saṃpuṭa" (concluding casket) of the worship;
thereafter follows the sounding of the Vedas, the gift of verses, and likewise the waving of lights (nīrājana). || 28 ||
There should be song, instrumental music, and likewise dance, as well as oblations for the fire and offerings;
then one should perform a procession festival to bestow his grace.
One should perform the descent of the worship, and then perform the worship once again;
thereafter, having performed the pure bath, one should likewise carry out the installation in its proper place.
They know the sequence of ritual acts to be "the gift" and "the excellent giving";
by this very sequence of ritual acts, one should perform all rites. || 31 ||
The first is the measurement of the navel, the second is that which reaches between the thighs, the third extends to the knees, and the fourth is the measurement of the feet. || 32 ||
The measurement for flower-pavitra and leaf-pavitra has been fully proclaimed;
this same measurement is cited for the water-jars, the mandalas, and the sacrificial pits.
Thus the measurement for the gross [image] has been declared; for the two goddesses, the measurement based on the navel is prescribed.
For images in union with the gross [form], the measurement based on the navel is praised. (34)
The measurement in *tāla* for ornaments, weapons, and powers is praised; O observer of good vows, I shall now describe the specific measurement by means of filling (*pūraṇa*). (35)
The first pedestal should be as high as the ankles; the second, as high as the knees; the third, situated at the middle of the thighs; and the fourth, as high as the hips.
One should fashion [the altars] for the pitchers, the mandalas, and the sacrificial pits according to the measurement of Śiva:
namely, one Śiva, two Śivas, three Śivas, and four Śivas.
One should fill the secondary vessel (upakumbha) with exactly one prastha measure;
for the primary image (mūlabimba), however, the measurement is specifically declared to be as previously stated.
The preceptor himself should perform the worship with the Vāsudeva and other mantras;
O best of Brahmins, they declare that for the rite of offering (bali), the measure should be one handful.
O observer of noble vows, I shall now describe specifically the measurement for the plastering:
first, one should apply it as far as the region of the neck.
O Brahmin, one should smear the second [layer] starting from the navel down to the base;
O Brahmin, they declare the third to be from the navel down to the hips. (41)
One should smear [the image] from the eyes down to the feet;
the measurement for the two goddesses is said to extend from the neck down to the navel.
In the case of filling [the vessel], it should be one-quarter measure; for others, it should be a quarter-measure as well.
Before the offering of the *damanaka* flower, the wise practitioner should offer sprouts. (43)
Having thoroughly decorated the pavilion on the previous day at the onset of night,
one should have the water-pot, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit constructed as prescribed by the ritual rules. (44)
Having constructed a mandala of a wheel and lotus, or one called Bhadra, or even a yantra-mandala according to the desire of the patron, the Guru [should proceed]. (45)
The wise one should perform the worship of the doors and other parts, and the learned one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
the intelligent one should then have the ceremonial bathing performed using twelve jars of milk and other substances.
Having adorned that image, one should place it upon a seat;
then, one should worship Hari in the pitcher located at the western side of the pavilion.
In the mandala, one should worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment;
the wise one should honor the image and perform the rite of fire-offering (homa).
Then, having made the formal announcement, one should cast the *bali* offering in each respective place;
having placed the *kautuka* (protective thread) upon the rice grains, one should lead [the deity] around the temple in circumambulation.
One should place [the seal] joined with the sound of a drum upon the *ādhāra*;
having worshipped the deity with *arghya* and other offerings, one should bind it on the right hand.
Having performed worship once more, one should then offer cakes and other such foods;
having fetched sprouts of *damanaka*, one should wash them with pure water.
The wise man should have a long-leaved plantain tree fashioned by artisans using the very same method previously described.
Having placed [the items] separately in individual vessels, one should then perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
One should prepare a pedestal of rice grains between the deity and the pavilion. (53)
One should place the vessel upon it and perform the rites of burning and nourishing;
then, having displayed the cow, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
And with the *kirāta* and other mantras, one should cause [the deity] to descend by means of another;
then, taking that which was produced during the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), one should join it to the top of the water-pot (*kumbha*).
One should enclose [the deity] with worship and perform singing, instrumental music, and so forth; O Brahmin, they declare that the consecrated garland is not to be held with pride. (56)
Then, having placed [the image] upon the bed, one should perform protection on all sides;
thereafter, at the clear dawn, one should properly perform the ritual bath.
For the purpose of bathing the Lord of Gods, one should bring him upon the lion-throne using either one hundred and eight or eighty-one jars.
Having adorned [the deity] according to the rule, one should perform the worship of the four locations;
thereafter, one should worship the fourfold set beginning with the crown using the water-pot (kumbha).
Then one should offer [the vessel] into the *vardhanī* while it is enclosed by worship;
and in the presence of the deity, one should display all [performances] such as song and dance. (60)
Having paid homage according to the rule, praised the deity, and bowed down,
the best of teachers should thereafter place [the disciple] in the mandala like a jar.
O twice-born one, at that time he should especially cause him to enter the mandala, along with the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, and even those ending with the parched grain offerings. (62)
And with ornaments, powers, as well as those of the Lord of Birds, and with vessels such as the *arvī* and others, along with excellent incense and lamps; || 63 ||
Just as one would act regarding the primary image, so it should be with the sacrificial pit (homakuṇḍa).
Having performed this according to the prescribed rule, one should attend to the locations of the doors and other such features.
One should especially offer a bali with the respective substances to Caṇḍa and the others, who reside in the limbs of the ālaya and whose forms are of such a nature.
When the afternoon has arrived, the preceptor, having placed [the image] upon a vehicle and performed the circumambulation of the temple,
[should proceed] to the western end of the enclosure of the street.
Then, having seated him in the pavilion, one should perform the renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Having performed the pure ablution thereafter, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be bestowed.
One should cause the favor of ascetics, Brahmins, and others to be bestowed;
the man who does so with devotion goes to the abode of Brahmā. (68)
It yields the merit of eight horse-sacrifices and three Vājapeya sacrifices;
it effects the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all calamities. (69)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Installation of the Damanaka Flower," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
149) Now begins the twenty-third chapter. The Blessed One said:
O Brahmin, when planting Tulasī, one should likewise perform the planting of Damana; and when worshipping with Campaka flowers, one should carry out the ritual in that same manner.
Then one should perform the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), as well as the three auspicious rites (kautuka),
the ritual worship at night, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), and the adornment.
There shall be a sacrifice at three locations, as well as the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation;
furthermore, the ceremonial bathing should especially be performed with coconut water.
O Brahmin, in the rite of consecration (adhivāsa), the materials should be consecrated immediately, either with mere scented water, or especially in its absence.
But during the time of the procession, O best of Brahmins, a garland of flowers is highly recommended;
one should scatter flowers all around, O Brahmin, as if with a shower of rain.
O twice-born one, he should have all other rites performed as before;
however, in the absence of campaka flowers, the pāṭala is prescribed.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should especially perform the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) correctly;
one should cause the grace of that [deity] to be bestowed upon the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
For the *snapana* (sprinkling), however, specifically one should use only water with flowers, or else scented water, or even coconut juice. || 8 ||
O Brahmin, during festivals of leaves and flowers, one should adorn [the deity] with ornaments;
during all festivals of fruits, the filling [of the vessel] is prescribed. (9)
At all festivals involving perfumes, one should properly perform the act of anointing; especially during the Anurādhā asterism, one should celebrate the festival of fruits.
I shall describe the ritual for the festival of fruits; listen attentively to it in brief.
The plantain, the jackfruit, and the mango are proclaimed as the [principal] fruits. (11)
The *tvajārkṣa* fruit combined with a deficient seed-vessel is called *bījapūra*;
the *panasa* is said to be of various kinds, including that known as the small *panasa*.
O Brahmin, one should always avoid the small variety during the rite of filling;
the plantain is said to be of three kinds, and all three are indeed suitable.
Likewise, it is stated regarding the mango (*sahakāra*): the *hārīta*, the red, and the yellow varieties are suitable for filling;
and for the betel nut (*kramuka*), the *candrapūraka* is recommended.
For the filling [of the vessel], it should be green, yellow, or red;
likewise, there should be the invocation of the sprouts and the worship at the four locations. || 15 ||

Furthermore, the ritual of the auspicious thread (kautuka), as well as the morning ablution (prātaḥsnāna), the procedure for the worship of the door (dvārapūjā), and the rite of worship at the four locations (catuḥsthānārcana). || 16 ||

O Brahmin, on the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should complete the worship of the primary image, as well as the food offering (naivedya) and the ritual oblation (bali), according to the measurement of Śiva.
One should offer a bali-oblation with that same substance, and the rite of homa should likewise be performed;
it may be twice, thrice, or even four times as much in its proximity. (18)
One should perform [the rite] with mantras beginning with Vāsudeva and others, or with those beginning with the four Vedas,
or even with the triad beginning with the Śākhā, or with the third hymn of the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
One should specifically fill the limbs and so forth up to the measure of a fist;
one should specifically fill Śrī and the others up to the measure of a knee.
One should complete the images of the ritual fire, the deity, and so forth according to the measurement of a foot;
however, for the performance of the fire oblation (homa), each should be one [span], while for the rite of offerings (balikarma), it should be a single fistful.
At the conclusion, one should hold a festival and scatter offerings of fruit-filled baskets;
then, having established [the deity] within the pavilion, one should perform the ritual of formal renunciation (sannyāsa).
Then, preceded by worship, one should have [the image] shaved as before;
having performed the pure bath, one should then install it in the inner sanctum.
In the absence of jackfruit, however, one should fill [the vessel] with mangoes;
in the absence of mango fruits, one should fill it with *mocaka* fruits. || 24 ||
O Brahmin, one should worship [the deity] for three months or during the month of Āṣāḍha;
O best of Brahmins, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship with eight *bījapūra* fruits.
In the absence of those, O best of Brahmins, one should worship with fresh areca nuts;
and in the month of Āśvayuja, O Brahmin, one should worship all around with water-born flowers.

For the ritual bathing (*snapana*), however, water from the night is especially excellent; or else, it may be combined with powder for bathing, using jars filled with the aforementioned substances. (45)
One should perform the smearing as before, as well as the rites beginning with the germinating of seeds;
thus has the specific monthly festival been briefly described. (46)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Monthly Festival," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
O sinless one, I shall describe to you in detail the ritual of the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
It may occur either in the middle of the four-month period, or at its beginning or end. || 1 ||
The Cāturmāsya is declared to be threefold: the solar, the lunar, and specifically the Vaiṣṇava; thus it is proclaimed to be of three types.

The solar [observances] consist of the transits [of the sun] and so forth; the lunar [observances] consist of the first day of the lunar fortnight and so forth; and those beginning with the twelfth day are proclaimed as the Vaiṣṇava [observances]. || 3 ||
The Vaiṣṇava vow is declared to be the best, the Saura is said to be middling, and the Cāndra is declared to be the lowest; one should practice the best among them.
Therefore, one should perform this with every effort on the twelfth day;
for if the rite of purification is omitted, the daily worship perishes.
If the daily worship is interrupted, the kingdom shall meet with ruin;
that village will go to its destruction, and that sacred site shall come to naught. (6)
Therefore, one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) with every effort;
because it protects from falling, it is proclaimed as "pavitra."
The ritual of installing the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) may be performed for one's own sake or for the sake of others;
O Brahmin, it may take place with a single image or with many images.

However, in the case of a ritual image situated on a plastered wall or a cloth painting, the wise practitioner should perform the rite; he should have a pavilion constructed either in front of it or all around it.
It may be constructed with many pillars, or made of stone or brick,
or even consisting solely of wood, or even as simple as a mere water-shed (prapā).
Whether joined with a wall or not joined, or even joined with a corner wall;
whether provided with a base (adhiṣṭhāna) or provided with a pedestal (upapīṭha). || 11 ||
It may also be provided with foot-bindings or with stone slabs and the like,
joined with flaming archways, and adorned with banners.
It may also be provided with a gabled roof, adorned with a Garuḍa, joined with lions, or even without them, and it may have many doors. || 13 ||
Or it may consist of three, five, seven, or nine walls;
having constructed it according to this rule, one should smear it with lime.
One should especially create various paintings with numerous incarnations;
the best of the twice-born should have archways constructed in the four directions. (15)
One should likewise have [an image] made from aśvattha, or vaṭa, or plakṣa, or even bilva, or tāla, or veṇu, as prescribed by the rules. (16)
It may be equal in length to the door, or equal in height to the pillar;
it should be half as wide as its length, or even one cubit in measure. || 17 ||
O Brahmin, one should have a small temple constructed measuring one cubit in size;
it should be provided with three spikes and accompanied by the figure of Garuḍa. || 18 ||
At every archway, one should place a Garuḍa standing upright;
one should also apply a coating of cow-dung to the ground within the pavilion.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar; such is the prescribed rite.
The mandala is in the central part, while the water-pot is placed in the southern part.
The fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) should be in the north, or between the north and the northeast;
each one should be five cubits, four cubits, or three cubits in size.
That pedestal should be one cubit in measure, or else one palm;
or the height of the altar-base should be four finger-breadths.
The altar of the pavilion should be like the surface of a mirror;
having made the altar for the pitcher level, one should prepare either a sacrificial pit or one shaped like a lotus.
(157) It may be square or even circular;
it should be provided with three girdles and endowed with a navel and a womb.
Outside of that, in the eight directions, the wise man should construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas):
the quadrangular, the triangular, the bow-shaped, the semicircular, the circular, and the hexagonal.
One should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in sequence starting from the east, either in the shape of a lotus with eight petals or in the form of a wheel and so forth. || 26 ||
Alternatively, there may be four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), but one should not make fewer than this;
[the shapes] are triangular, crescent-shaped, circular, and lotus-shaped, in order starting from the east.
O best of Brahmins, one should arrange the festival on the western part of the sacrificial ground upon a throne beautifully adorned with wish-fulfilling trees.
One should seat the God upon the throne, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, adorned with flower garlands and endowed with steady radiance. || 29 ||
One should worship Garuḍa in the eastern quarter, Cakra in the south,
the son of Vāyu (Hanuman) in the west, and likewise Viṣvaksena in the north.
One should also place banners, arches, and water-pots at the entrance;
and having adorned it with canopies and the like, as well as with silken and cotton cloths.
One should wrap the pillars, adorning them with plantains and betel nuts,
as well as with various kinds of fruits and decorated with lamps and water-pots.
Adorned with mirrors, chowries, and beautiful parasols,
as well as with bells, crescent moons, and garlands of *darbha* grass. (33)
Having performed it in this manner according to the prescribed rule, one should then have the purificatory thread (pavitra) prepared,
whether it be made of linen, cotton, or even gold thread.
Whether it was prepared by a Brahmin woman or purchased at the marketplace, it may be either odd or even; however, in an odd-numbered set, there should be nine.
It is taught that there should be twelve pairs, or eight, or even four;
having washed them with pure water, one should dry them with the *praṇava*.
O Brahmin, in the Nirmāṇa-maṇḍapa, there should be a smearing with cow dung;
and the preceptor should bury a conch in the ground using the Vāyu-sūtras.
The measurement of the first face shall be [one unit]; the second shall be double;
the third is declared to be triple; and the fourth is fourfold. || 38 ||
The first [set] consists of one hundred and eight; the second is double that;
the third is said to be triple; and the fourth is fourfold. || 39 ||
Alternatively, one should then string together according to the prescribed rule a thousand beads, half of that, half of that again, and half of that once more as the first part.
The *antarāntaraka* indeed should resemble the egg of a bird;
it may have the shape of an *dhātrī* fruit or be like a large pearl. || 41 ||
It should be composed by connecting it at various intervals from afar;
the measurement for the pair [of deities] is proclaimed to be within the *kubha*, *maṇḍala*, and *kuṇḍa* [measures]. (42)
The measurement of the altar (vedi) should be five [units]; it is prescribed for the secondary jars (upakumbha). One may perform it as a triad, a dyad, or even in combination.
The first [measurement] should not be less than one unit; the second should be double that, and the third should be known as triple; the same applies to the *parikumbha*.
O best of Brahmins, even a single one would suffice for the *parikumbhas*;
O Brahmin, for the *karaka* and the *astra*, there may be either one or three.
Indeed, the sacred thread (adhivāsa) is praised when being measured;
its measurement for the pericarp in the mandala is the same as that for the filaments.
It is especially praised when it expands leaf by leaf;
it should be measured in syllables, and that which is equal to it is found in the field of Arka.
Thus it is declared regarding the navel-field; likewise, it is equal in the Maru-field.
It is declared to be equal in the Nemi-field; thus, in the third [field], there would be a triad.
In the second [day], one should know there is a triad, and in the next, there is only one;
having stood within the mandala of the lotus-wheel, the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) shall take place.
O best of Brahmins, in the many altars, one by one or three by three,
the measurement of the girdles for each of the pits should be performed individually.
O Brahmin, this pavitraka may be knotted with threads according to one's desire;
however, for all other rites, the measurement of a palm (tāla) is recommended. (51)
The measurement for the *bimbapratisaraṇas* is declared to be according to the size of the head of the image; this is traditionally held to be the first ornament.
The second [measurement] is knee-height, the third is foot-length, and the fourth is seat-height; that indeed is the measurement for the primary image (mūlabera).
O Brahmin, for the two goddesses specifically, a triad or a dyad [of mantras] is prescribed; the third is proclaimed to be the position at the navel and the knees.
The second foot, or even a single knee-foot, is praised at the measurement of one *tāla* for ornaments and weapons. (55)

The measurement of the faces of the attendants, beginning with Caṇḍa, has been proclaimed; their size on the pedestal shall be according to the measure of the [central] image, and the measurement of their radiance shall be the same.
O best of Brahmins, there should be a third set of three in the external sacrificial pits;
O foremost of sages, one may also cause two or even one to be made.
Many preceptors have been prescribed, and likewise many officiating priests;
there should also be many attendants for the excellent rite of the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
The officiating priests and those who have been initiated, all of whom are most virtuous,
should be placed above with gold and other materials, as well as with linen threads.
Having filled [the vessel] with a soft plaster, one should color it with saffron;
having placed [the ingredients] separately in a vessel, one should prepare them with flowers and perfumes. (60)
In one [mandala], there are those suitable for the *kumbha* (pitcher) rite by means of fire;
in another, those suitable for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); and in yet another, those suitable for the [solar] disc (*bimba*). || 61 ||
One should place all other suitable items into a single vessel,
perfumed with various fragrant scents and with fragrant flowers.
I shall now declare that sequence to you; attend closely at once. On the seventh or fifth day prior to the day of commencing the rite, || 63 ||
Then the wise one should perform the offering of sprouts according to the procedure prescribed for festivals;
indeed, he should offer the sprouts into the vessel for the three goals of life (trivargapālikā).
Having fully decorated the pavilion with archways and other ornaments,
and having performed the taking of the earth as before, one should fill the clay vessels (pālikās).
One hundred and eight is proclaimed as the best;
half of that is the middling, and half of that again is the lowest.
One should perform [the rite] sixteen, twelve, or eight times;
one should carry out the laying of the lines (sūtrapāta) in accordance with the size of the vessel (pālikā).
Having established [the deity] upon a pedestal of rice, one should place the Soma-vessel;
likewise, having first placed the seed-vessel, one should perform the worship of the door.
One should perform worship at the four locations and also have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited.
There should be worship of the sacred threads (*pavitra*) and the honoring of the Soma-vessel. (69)
O best of Brahmins, one should perform the pouring of ghee with the *saṃpāta* clarified butter;
thereafter, the wise man should carry out the sowing of seeds and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).
Then, having placed [the deity] in the secret place, one should worship on the following day;
when the eleventh day arrives, one should perform the cleansing of the abode.
And with water-jars filled with water, the practitioner should wash [the area], omitting incense;
he should then smear it inside and out with sandalwood paste and other substances. (72)
O best of Brahmins, one should smear the pavilion in the painted chamber,
having decorated it as before with banners, arches, and water-pots.
And with various flower garlands, strings of pearls, mirrors, diverse kinds of fruits, or clusters of plantain trees; 74.
The wise man should especially construct a maṇḍala in the center, provided with many groups of lamps as well as fruits, flowers, and other offerings, upon an altar.
