Either the yantra described in the Pauṣkara, or that of Viṣṇu, or the yantra called Vāsudeva as taught by Sātvata—[one should draw it] according to the prescribed method. (76)
Or a wheel-lotus, or a svastika, or else the attainment of desired success; or the diagram known as Vāsudeva, or likewise the Viṣṇu diagram.
On its right side, the wise one should place a water-pot (kumbha),
as well as a great pot (mahākumbha), a subsidiary pot (upakumbha), a surrounding pot (parikumbha), and a vardhanī vessel. (78)

Having placed it around the *pālikā*, one should arrange the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgalaka*), together with thread, cloth, the prescribed ritual procedure, and the *kūrca* grass-bundle. (79)
In each and every pitcher, one should especially place a coconut fruit,
or else a betel nut, a cluster, or even a coconut blossom.
One should place various kinds of fruits upon the altar;
furthermore, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should indeed be situated on the northern side of the pavilion, atop the altar.
The wise one should place a water-pot (parikumbha) and deposit eight kinds of grain;
[he should also adorn it] with clusters of plantain fruits and groups of coconuts.
One should likewise worship specifically with betel-nut clusters, bunches of bananas, and fruits of the jackfruit and mango trees, especially at the water-pot and the sacrificial pit. || 83 ||
On the western side of the altar, one should arrange the festival,
having placed [the image] upon a lion-throne that is fully adorned with ornaments.
Having thus performed the ritual according to the prescribed method, one should carry out the worship of the door;
the wise practitioner should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made and perform the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) correctly.
Either with eighty-one jars, or even with thirty-six pitchers;
or with pure cow’s milk, or indeed with coconut water. (86)
(164) At the conclusion of the bathing, one should specifically perform a bath with aromatic powders;
then, having performed a pure bath, one should consecrate [the deity] with the Nṛsūkta. || 87 ||
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should place [the deity] upon the seat of ornaments;
one should likewise perform the worship of the jars within the mandala. 88.
One should worship with numerous ritual services as if it were the image of a deity;
one should perform the full sixteen-fold worship for all the subsidiary jars.

Thus it has been declared regarding the weapon-vessel; this same procedure should apply to the subsidiary vessels. One should perform the sprinkling and bathing rites over the ritual jars, the mandala, and the sacrificial fire-pits.
One should worship in the great jar with the eight-syllable mantra,
and one should perform the ritual adoration in the mandala with the twelve-syllable mantra.
O best of Brahmins, one should worship Hari residing in the fire with the Viṣṇu-mantra;
however, during a festival, one should especially worship him with the Gāyatrī.

One should perform the worship of the mandala with numerous ritual offerings, placing Vāsudeva near the central pitcher (upakumbha) and Indra and the other deities around the secondary pitchers (parikumbhaka).
Through the union of the five colors, it is remembered as consisting of the five principles (pañcatattva);
Viṣṇu consists of the five principles, and Śiva consists of the five principles.
Brahmā consists of the five principles; the world consists of the five principles;
everything seen in the world, both moving and unmoving, consists of the five principles. 95.
Therefore, with every effort, the worship of the maṇḍala is supreme;
one should worship the Lord Vāsudeva, who is free from all affliction, within the maṇḍala. (96)
Having first performed the worship of the vessel (pātra), one should thereafter perform the worship of oneself (ātmārcana);
after that, the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha), and then the worship of the retinue (parivāra). || 97 ||
The supreme worship of the maṇḍala, beginning with the seat and ending with the food offering (naivedya), is performed;
one should then worship the Deity in the image with numerous ritual services (upacāras). || 98 ||
One should act likewise for the primary image and perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the principal sacrificial pit;
the knower of mantras should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru) in sequence with the mantra of Viṣṇu.
In the case of the directional pit (dikkuṇḍa), however, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should specifically perform the fire-oblation (homa);
but in the absence of the priests, the Preceptor (ācārya) himself should perform it.
The eight types of fuel-sticks are those of the *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, *audumbara*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *apāmārga*, and *aśvattha* trees. || 101 ||
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) are prescribed from the east up to the northeast;
likewise, milk-rice (pāyasa), rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara), rice with turmeric (haridrānna), and rice with mung beans (maudgika).
Bean-rice, pure sesame-rice, and curd-rice—these constitute the eightfold [offering];
as well as parched grain, wild rice, sesame, and mustard seed. (103)
Rice, mung beans, barley, and wheat shall be the eighth;
one should offer oblations in eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), using those respective materials individually.
One should perform the consecration of the *pavitra* on a spot in front of the deity;
having then prepared three paths, one should deposit a heap of grain. (105)
Half of that [measure] should be rice, and half of that again should be sesame seeds;
one should place a vessel upon it and worship it as if it were a pedestal (pīṭha).
Then, the best of those who know mantras should arrange the vessels for the ornaments;
the best of those who know mantras should perform all the rites, such as the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and others.
Sprinkling, striking, burning, as well as uprooting and filling;
worship with iron, earth, and the time of the Bhogin—[these are the rites]. || 108 ||

And "with contact"—thus is the tenfold consecration performed upon all the ritual offerings; the knower of mantras, most learned in the scriptures, should sprinkle them with the clarified butter from the sacrificial ladle.
One should apply fragrant ointments and incense the area with incense materials;
having placed it upon fragrant flowers, one should then cover it with a cloth.
Then, having performed worship once more, the wise one should tie the protective amulet (kautuka);
having tied it likewise upon the primary image, he should also tie it upon the preceptor.
Following the previously described procedure, he should place [the image] upon the bed;
the twice-born should pass the remainder of the night with song, dance, recitation of the Purāṇas, and other such activities.
Then, at the clear dawn, one should perform the daily rites;
having placed [the deity] upon the bathing altar, one should properly carry out the ritual ablution.
(167) With one hundred and eight jars, or with eighty-one jars,
or even with those containing the prescribed substances, or with milk alone; || 114 ||
Having performed the bathing ritual as before— using either entirely ghee or coconut water, ending with the waving of lights (nīrājana)— 115.
Having led him to the seat of ornaments and adorned him with various decorations,
he then seated the Lord, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, upon the lion-throne.

Having performed the worship of the doors and so forth, as well as the worship of the pitcher and the maṇḍala, and then having completed the rite of fire-offering (homa), one should perform the image-homa (mūrtihoma). || 117 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation for the announcement and worship the ornaments;
then, taking the ornament-vessel, one should bring it to the side of the water-pot.
At the time of joining the *pavitra*, one should perform the sprinkling and other rites in the proper direction;
having taken the *pavitra* with both hands, one should apply fragrant unguents.
Having performed the fumigation especially well, one should carry out the application of fire;
[one should likewise apply it] to the unmanifest, the sattvic, the mantra, and the very form itself.
The inconceivable and unmanifest Yoga is the contemplation of reality as it truly is.
Having invoked the crown and other ornaments, one should contemplate each ornament individually. || 121 ||
Having honored [the deity] with offerings of water for the guest and the feet, one should join [the vessel] to the top of the pitcher;
then, with the four [mantras] beginning with the Saṃhitā-mantra, one should worship Hari within the pitcher.
(168) It is taught [to be performed] with mandalas consisting of branches and so forth, with effigies for rites such as killing (māraṇa),
and with the three Anuvākas and the Viṣṇu-sūkta, using sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
One should adorn the water-pot with the eight-syllable mantra, the image with the twelve-syllable mantra,
Viṣṇu’s Gāyatrī, and the sacrificial pit with the six-syllable mantra.
One should worship him thoroughly with various ornaments and with offerings such as the *arghya*;
likewise, one should offer the *arghya*, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), fragrance, flowers, and incense. || 125 ||
One should then offer betel-leaf in that sequence, followed by those [offerings] at the end of the meal in order;
likewise, one should offer a lamp, the *nīrājana* ceremony, a Vedic verse, and a *śloka*.
Singing, dancing, instrumental music, and indeed the giving of gifts such as gold, clothing, and cattle;
likewise, hymns of praise, prostrations, and [the worship of] the image within the maṇḍala. (127)

The best of those who know mantras should join [the offerings] to all the secondary jars (upakumbha), beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Varuṇa in the northwest, according to the respective mantras. 128.
One should perform the protection over all the jars, according to one's desire, using either three, two, or even one [mantra], following the sequence starting from the east.
Even one [item] alone is said to be sufficient; three in the cloth-vessel and two in the water-pot;
afterwards, eight in the mandala, and immediately after that, in the pālikā.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), one should then cast the bali-oblation with the very same hymn (sūkta);
likewise, one should perform [the rites] in the mandala—the specific details of which are now being stated.
O Brahmin, one should perform the sacrifice starting from the west in the lotus-field;
indeed, one should apply the ornaments and other items at the western doorway. (132)
One should perform all other rites as before;
thereafter, one should worship the image, and the lotus should be as it was previously. || 133 ||
O twice-born one, one should bestow the fourfold [mantras] and apply them to the limbs (aṅga) and so forth;
likewise for the secondary limbs (upāṅga) and the marks (lāñchana).
Then [he should offer] ornaments and powers, as well as those of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa),
followed by the pedestal, sandals, vessels, incense, lamps, and so forth.
And likewise for the teachers and practitioners, as well as for their vehicles;
and similarly for the vessels for song and instrumental music, such as conch shells and the like. || 136 ||
One should offer the Veda, song, instrumental music, a lamp, and the supreme *nīrājana* ceremony;
then, from the offering of milk-pudding (*pāyasa*) and other foods up to the end, one should present betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*).
One should likewise perform [the rites] for the physical image and similarly for the sacrificial fire-pit;
one should offer oblations of clarified butter (ājya) for all of them, including the ritual services (upacāra). || 138 ||
And likewise for the girdles starting from the top and for their vessels, in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the sequence beginning with the east. || 139 ||
The wise practitioner should employ either three, two, or even one [of these]; he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the collection of substances previously mentioned.
O best of sages, one should assign the ritual images of the goddesses to their respective vessels; having praised them with hymns, one should scatter clusters of flowers.
Then, in the afternoon, the preceptor should likewise perform a procession festival,
accompanied by numerous attendants and provided with many lamps.
O best of Brahmins, one should first make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for nine days, seven days, five days, three days, or even for a single day. 143.
Just as one would do during a festival, one should have the Lord mounted upon his vehicle;
then, on the day of completion, at night, one should perform the ritual of formal dismissal (sannyāsa).
One should perform the worship as before and offer the expiatory oblation;
then, having performed the purification bath, one should cause [the deity] to enter the temple.
The preceptor himself should perform the rite of placing the sacred threads (pavitra) upon the devotees of purified soul belonging to all castes, beginning with the twice-born. 146.
In the same manner, one should cause the collection of *pavitrakas* to be given individually;
O Brahmin, by wearing the *pavitraka*, it becomes the remover of all sins. (147)
It shall indeed yield the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
When the following day has arrived, one should lead [the disciple] to the vicinity of the sacred ford.
Having reached a sacred site (tīrtha), one should perform the ritual bath at that site;
indeed, one should perform the concluding ablution (avabhṛtha) together with a festival.
The preceptor should cause [the disciple] to bestow cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth; then, having entered the temple, he should cause him to be seated in the pavilion. (150)
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should place him within the inner sanctum;
thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with jewels, gold, and rings.
One should fully honor the preceptor with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and garments;
half of that should be given to the officiating priests, so that it may truly become a festival.
It bestows all powers, it is everything, the primary and most excellent means;
it grants happiness to the king and the kingdom, and increases longevity and health. (153)
For all beings, the worship of the sacred thread (pavitrārādhana) of Vāsudeva is supreme;
and he who performs the worship of Viṣṇu’s sacred thread with faith [attains the highest state]. (154)
Freed from all sins and devoid of all suffering, he goes to the abode of Brahmā, attaining the supreme union with Viṣṇu. || 155 ||
I shall speak of the specific discourse; listen to this secret, O great sage, which is like the horse-sacrifice for Brahmins and the royal consecration for kings. (156)
Just as the svadhā is for the ancestors and nectar is for the gods, so is the water of the Jāhnavī for men, and Acyuta is for the deities. (157)
For thus, the supreme worship with the purifier (pavitra) of the God of gods involves the encircling of the temple at the time of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). 158.
It may be with a five-colored thread or with the aforementioned thread;
having likewise encircled the pavilion, one should similarly decorate the vessel. || 159 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Sacred Thread," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: I shall describe the festival of the year; listen, if you wish to hear it.
Likewise, there are two equinoxes and two solstices. || 1 ||
Jayantī and Kṛttikā, as well as the Āgrāyaṇa rite;
the festival of study and likewise the Pavitrārohaṇa ceremony. || 2 ||
If the annual worship is destroyed, the monthly worship is destroyed;
if the monthly worship is destroyed, the daily worship is destroyed. || 3 ||
But if the daily worship is destroyed, the king and the kingdom perish;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the prescribed ritual.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when it is joined with the Rohiṇī asterism, that [day] is called Jayantī; for by it, one conquers all inauspiciousness.
It should be joined with Wednesday, free from all defects,
occurring either on a specific lunar day (tithi) and asterism (nakṣatra) conjunction, or even under a single asterism alone.
Having prepared the sprout on the previous day, the wise one should bind the *kautuka* (protective thread).
That night, he should perform the ritual bathing with twenty-five water-pots.
O Brahmin, it may consist of milk mixed with the aforementioned substances, or milk alone,
or ghee alone, or even coconut water.
Having performed the worship of the doors and so forth, one should worship the pitcher and the mandala;
by means of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra alone, the mandala shall be known as Jaya.
Likewise, having offered either *paramānna* (milk-rice) or *bhūtāvāsa*,
and having performed the fire-oblation (*homakārya*), one should then place [the image] upon the bed.
Having prepared a bed like that of a child, adorned with soft coverings—
or alternatively, having first performed worship and likewise a bath with fragrant powders— 11.
One should especially offer milk-rice, mung-bean porridge, various kinds of fruit,
and specifically the fruit known as jambuka.
In the absence of a black image, one should perform [the rite] using an obtained image;
in its absence, it should be performed at the root (mūla), provided with the four locations.
Having fasted on that day, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at the conclusion of its worship;
prior to the offering of the food, however, one should perform the worship of the Moon.
On the lunar ground, there should specifically be a smearing with cow-dung;
having adorned it with lime powder, one should draw the orb of the moon.
The most excellent practitioner should not draw [the maṇḍala] according to the path taught in the *Pādmatantra*, nor that spoken in the *Pauṣkara*, nor even the half-moon shape. (16)
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as before, one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules, one should then perform the worship of the vessel (pātrārcana).
The seat, the invitation, and then the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācāma), as well as fragrance, flowers, incense, and likewise a lamp. || 18 ||
The preceptor should offer a hymn of praise, the lustration rite (nīrājana), and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as various kinds of fruits, while reciting the Soma mantra.
Having kept a vigil at night, one should perform a great festival at dawn and beautifully decorate the streets, setting up many arched gateways (toraṇas).
In each and every swing, one should especially place jars of curd and milk;
having tied them to each and every archway, one should strike them in the presence of the deity.
Having placed the black image upon a flower-made palanquin,
starting from the first enclosure up to the final enclosure of the processional path.
The preceptor should bring [the image] with all kinds of musical instruments, the chanting of the Vedas, and numerous attendants crowded with umbrellas and chowries. || 23 ||
With various playthings and those who provide oil and powder,
having conducted [the deity] in this manner according to the prescribed rule, one should install him within the pavilion.
Then, having performed the pure ablution, one should install [the image] in its proper place for one day, three days, or five, seven, or nine days. (25)
One should always perform the festival at midday or in the afternoon;
the man who performs it thus with devotion shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He obtains the fruit of many daughters, the fruit born of giving many cows, and the fruit of much dharma; of this there is no doubt. || 27 ||
The Festival of the Kṛttikā Lamps:
O best of sages, I shall describe the procedure for the Kṛttikā festival in brief.
One should perform the offering of lamps during the pair of Kṛttikā parvans. (28)
Whether the conjunction of the asterism is present or absent, or even on the lunar day alone,
when midday has arrived, one should properly perform the ritual bath.
Having performed the *aṅkura* rite as before, one should perform the *kautuka* rite at the commencement of the work,
using either twenty-six or twenty-five water-pots.
Or else, with seventeen [mantras], or even with those joined with the appropriate substances—
whether it be milk, cow’s ghee, or even fragrant water.
Then, having performed the powder-bath, one should lead [the deity] to the ornamentation seat;
having adorned [the deity] with bodices and other garments, and having anointed it with musk.
Having specially placed the primary image, adorned with ornaments,
within the pavilion, one should then perform the worship of the four locations.

Having offered the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) especially in the afternoon, one should perform the consecration of the lamps (*dīpādhivāsana*) in the center of the temple pavilion (*devamaṇḍapa*). (34)
Then, having prepared three paths, one should deposit a heap of grain;
taking nine new vessels, one should fill them with cow's ghee.
Having inserted a wick made of thread and placed it in the center,
the preceptor should then arrange eight shallow bowls in succession around its exterior.
Then, having ignited a lamp-vessel filled with ghee and wick from Indra up to Īśāna, one should join [the flame] to the wicks within the vessels.
One should worship the fire with the fire-mantras using offerings such as *arghya* and *gandha*;
then, one should worship Indra and the others in the eight bowls placed in the east and other directions using their respective mantras.
Accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and adorned with the sounds of laughter,
the preceptor, taking up the vessel, should present it into the hand of Viṣṇu.
When evening has arrived, one should perform the lighting of lamps,
specifically by installing lamp-stands at every door.
Betel nut, coconut, palmyra, and likewise bamboo, as well as the campaka and the celestial tree (devavṛkṣa), provided they are free from crookedness and hollows. || 41 ||
O Brahmin, having carved it straight according to the measurements of the stūpa,
its width should be half of that, or equal to the measurement of the door, or one hundred tālas in length.
O Brahmin, some desire the wall to be eighty *tāla*s in height, or even half of that;
it should be on all eight sides outside the enclosure. (43)
Having established the lamp-stands, one should light each respective lamp;
that which is placed in a vessel should be joined to the stand in the eastern direction, accompanied by musical instruments.
One should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) beforehand and worship those various staffs (daṇḍas) in the temple, the gate-tower, the enclosure wall, and likewise in the pavilion.
At a sacred ford, in a new garden, and especially at the site of a well;
in temples such as those dedicated to Śrī and others, and in the dwellings of the retinue.
Then one should offer lamps in the presence of the God of gods;
likewise, one should do so in every house and cause them to be carried through all the streets.
Then, having entered the pavilion and seated him upon the seat,
he presented all the performances, especially the dances, songs, and so forth.
Having performed the worship again in that manner, one should offer flattened rice and other foods;
specifically, one should cause cakes and such to be given to all living beings.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Festivals of Jayantī and Kṛttikā," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā of the Śrī Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: I shall describe the ritual for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
O Brahmin, on the day of Kṛttikā and the following days, it does not occur at the onset of night on the next day.
Having brought all the groups of temple maidservants, adorned with every kind of ornament,
to the kitchen door, one should light many lamps.
O Brahmin, all those carrying the vessels should proceed into the presence of the deity,
all of them arranged in rows and preceded by songs and instrumental music.
Having thoroughly decorated the pavilion,
one should bring the festive image into the interior of the pavilion and place it upon a seat.
O Lord, having shown the Great Dance to the God who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi and adorned with ornaments, one should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana).
The preceptor should cause [the rite] to be performed by a thousand, or half of that, or even half of that;
or by a hundred, or half of that, or even half of that.
And all those holding alms-bowls should stand in the presence of the deity; the preceptor, having adorned himself with an upper garment, a turban, and ornaments, [should likewise stand]. (7)
One should sit upon a seat on the right side of the deity;
having worshipped the vessels for the *arghya* offering and others, preceded by the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having performed the worship of oneself, one should then worship the God of gods;
having performed the worship of the lamp, the wise man should then cause the Vedas to be recited.
Taking the lamp-vessel, one should place it upon its support;
having worshipped the lamp-vessel and especially offered sacrifice to the deity.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should cause [the deity] to revolve above the head,
beginning with the right foot and ending with the left foot.
Accompanied by auspicious instrumental music and auspicious songs,
the preceptor, taking the vessel from the hand of a woman, took hold of it.

One should cause [the vessel] to circulate within the mouth of the God of gods and then release it; one should especially worship each individual vessel with offerings of water (arghya) and flowers. || 13 ||
Taking up the vessel once again, he should circumambulate the temple clockwise and,
accompanied by song and instrumental music, cast it outside the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha).
Displaying dances and other performances, the female attendants stood before the Lord; having worshipped the Lord of Gods, they should offer cakes and other foods.
Having placed the festival image upon the vehicle and led it in circumambulation,
starting from the inner enclosure and ending at the western enclosure of the street.
Then, having performed the ritual bath of purification, one should install [the deity] in the inner sanctum;
for if the rite of lustration (nīrājana) is omitted, all ritual actions become demonic.
p.
180) The Festival of Study:
I shall describe the festival of study as it was heard by me in brief.
In this Tantra, worship has been declared by the Supreme Lord to be threefold.
It is threefold: mental, physical, and vocal. Mental action is called meditation (dhyāna), while physical action is called karma. (19)
In this Tantra, Viṣṇu declared in former times that the Vedic hymn is the verbal praise;
there is no other praise superior to the Vedas, therefore one should cause the Vedas to be recited.
Having first performed the *aṅkura* rite and subsequently the *pratisara*,
the wise one should commence [the ritual] on the eleventh day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the tenth day, one should perform the *kautuka* (auspicious thread ceremony), and on the day preceding that, the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
Having first made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), this should be done for either five days or ten days.
Having placed the deity in the pavilion, the wise one should install the image of the devotee;
likewise, accompanied by the devotees, he should cause the Vedas to be recited.
Then, having offered the great oblation, one should offer cakes and other such items;
thereafter, one should perform the preliminary rite for the journey, and the vehicles should be treated as before.
When the day of completion arrives, one should worship Viṣvaksena.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Festival of Study (*adhyayanotsava*)," in the *Aniruddha-saṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
181) Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
The Blessed One said:
O Sage, I shall now describe the ritual procedure for the Āgrayaṇa; attend closely to it. It should be performed in the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya on an auspicious day.
The sowing of seeds should first take place under an auspicious constellation;
on either the third or the fifth day thereafter, one should perform the cutting of the grass.
Accompanied by all his attendants, he should proceed to the sacred field,
taking either Māruti, Vainateya, or Viṣvaksena with him.
O Brahmin, having placed the preceptor upon a palanquin, the wise patron,
having reached the sacred precinct, should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
One should worship the field with perfumes and other offerings using the *dharaṇī* mantra;
having sprinkled water upon the wooden stake (*śaṅkulā*), one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) all around.
O best of brahmins, one should properly perform the salting with milk-rice;
having prepared the old threshing-floor, the farmers should strike it.
The wise preceptor, together with the plowmen, should tie the auspicious thread (kautuka);
having placed the woman to be plowed upon his head, they should proceed to the temple of the deity.
Having placed [the vessel] filled with various kinds of fruits and accompanied by conch shells and other musical instruments near the deity, one should perform the worship once again.
O best of Brahmins, the wise one should show some grain in the right hand of the deity, having measured it by means of the foot of a tree. (9)
One should cause all the castes to give [the offering] in the presence of the God of gods;
one should especially purify it and cast it into a heap of grain.
One should dry all these in the sun and perform the threshing;
having applied a plaster to that spot, one should decorate it with lime powder. || 11 ||
Having washed both the mortar and the pestle,
the preceptor should worship them with perfumes and flowers, and then place grain into the mortar.
It was accompanied by the threshing performed by the best of the twice-born, as well as by auspicious singers,
groups of temple maidservants, or various Brahmins.
Having winnowed away the husks with a winnowing basket, one should wash them with pure water;
having purified them all once more, they should be mixed with a preparation of jaggery.
O twice-born one, one should fill [the vessels] with marīca and cumin seeds in the presence of the deity;
having installed the Lord, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, within the pavilion.
Having offered [the deity] either as one endowed with the four locations or as the image alone,
one should worship the Lord of Gods in the primary image.
Then, having performed the bali-homa, one should offer it to Viṣvaksena;
one should cause it to be given to all castes, especially to the Brahmins and others.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should offer supreme food (paramānna);
by this specific *āgrayaṇa* offering, the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice shall be attained. || 18 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should apply oneself to that rite;
if one should omit it through delusion, the destruction of grain is certain.
O Brahmin, at both equinoxes as well as at both solstices,
the wise man should cause the ceremonial bath to be performed, preceded by the rite of sowing auspicious sprouts.
On the preceding day, one should perform the rite of the auspicious thread (kautuka) as well as the worship of the four locations;
having performed the consecration of the bed (śayanādhivāsana), one should lift [the image] in the morning.
Then, having performed the daily rites, one should perform the worship of the doors and other parts;
having worshipped in the pitcher and the maṇḍala, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the image.

If there is a single-liṅga stone image, one should perform the ritual bathing right there; however, when there are many images, one should especially perform both the bathing and the tying of the protective thread (kautuka).
But in its absence, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the ceremonial bathing during a festival using either one hundred and eight jars or eighty-one jars.
Or with ninety-nine, or with thirty-six jars, or with twenty-five pots, or else with seventeen vessels. (25)
Whether joined with a single substance or even with many substances,
the consecration of the water-pot (kalaśa-adhivāsana) should take place during the first part of the night.
O Brahmin, if the bathing takes place at night, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at that time;
according to what was previously stated, there may be many substances, or there may be a single substance, which is ghee.

O Brahmin, [one should offer] either milk alone, or coconut water, or else [water] combined with the five substances (pañcadravya), or indeed combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 28 ||
The leaf, the flower, and the fruit—these three substances have been declared [as offerings].
However, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is especially praised when accompanied by five specific substances.
Then, having performed the powder-bath with pure water immediately thereafter,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and bring forward the seat for adornment.
Having adorned [the image] according to the rule and having offered it, one should worship it to the end;
then, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should install it in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). || 31 ||
Taking the festival image, one should properly conduct the procession;
it may be carried on an elephant, in a chariot, or in a palanquin.
At the conclusion of the procession, one should take the deity and place him within the pavilion;
having exhibited the dances and other performances, one should worship him with offerings ending with the oblation (havis).
Then, having placed [the deity] within the inner sanctum, the wise one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given;
he should cause a water-pot to be presented for each of the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Those who drink the water from Hari’s holy site should drink it as if it were the water of the Gaṅgā;
those who carry it on their heads, that act becomes equal to bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā.
Thus, the supreme procedure for the annual festival has been briefly explained.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for Annual Festivals," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: In the month of Puṣya, during the asterism of that month, one should perform a bath at night.
Having performed the rite of the sprout (aṅkurārpaṇa) and likewise the decoration of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), || 1 ||

There shall likewise be the ritual for the worship of the doors, as well as the veneration of the four locations, the ceremonial bath, the laying to rest, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). || 2 ||
Having performed everything as before, one should proceed according to the previous ritual; taking the essence of the night (kumkuma) and mixing it with fragrance, one should grind it.
Having placed [the materials] in each vessel, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) as before;
at the time of the consecration, [one should fill them] from the neck down to the base.
One should smear the pitchers, the mandala, and the sacrificial pits with a handful [of earth];
then, at the clear dawn, one should smear them again with fragrant substances.
One should enclose [the mantra] with worship and perform the smearing correctly;
first is the measurement of the navel, and second is the measurement of the waist.
The third [measurement] is the height of the knees, while the fourth is the measurement of the feet;
one should smear the radiance-base (prabhāpīṭha), which is the height of the two goddesses up to the navel.
In the case of the water-pots, the mandalas, and the sacrificial pits, the first measurement is one fist;
the second is double that, and the third should be triple.
The fourth [mandala] is declared to be fourfold in the primary image as before;
likewise, it is the same for all other rites and for the remaining cases as before.
One should perform a great festival at the beginning and establish [the image] in its place;
one should practice the gift of sesame seeds during the first half of the month, but not in the latter half.
All rituals, beginning with the sowing of sprouts, shall be performed entirely as previously described;
thereafter, one should especially offer sesame seeds to the Brāhmaṇas.
One should perform the offering to the ancestors with a ball of food mixed with sesame seeds;
in the month of Māgha, one should perform the worship of the ancestors on the day of the lunar mansion of that month.
If a vessel is not obtained, one should especially worship with *pāṭala* flowers;
the leaf, flower, fruit, water, and fragrant unguent are to be offered as before.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Gift of Sesame," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
187) Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
I shall describe the special sacrifice; understand it in brief. It is to be performed when an ill omen has occurred, as well as upon seeing a bad dream.
In the event of drought, as well as in the event of excessive rain, when a planetary conflict has arisen, and when joined with the defect of the new moon (kuhū-doṣa). || 2 ||
When the affliction of malevolent planets has arisen, as well as when there is fear of a king, upon the invasion of a foreign army, and likewise during the torment of diseases; || 3 ||
Thus, for the sake of pacifying the affliction, one should perform the worship of Keśava;
having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as before, the wise person should bind the protective thread (*kautuka*).
On a Friday, an auspicious day, one should properly perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) using either seventeen,
twelve, or nine jars.
One should cause it to be made with one part, or three parts, or even five parts.
The single part may consist of milk, or clarified butter, or indeed fragrance.
The leaf, the flower, and the fruit—these are proclaimed as the three-fold [offering].
Likewise, there is the five-fold [offering] consisting of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Curd, milk, honey, sugar, and ghee—
these are declared as the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta) in this Tantra by the Supreme Lord.
p.
188) One should then perform a bath with these [substances], whereby one becomes integrated within the worship.
Having then performed a bath with powdered substances, one should carry out the mantra-bath. (9)
Having recited the three *anuvākas*, the *bhūsūkti*,
and the *sūkta* itself twelve times, one should properly perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
Having duly worshipped one, three, or likewise five, seven, or nine [deities], one should present the great sacrificial offering.
The Blessed Lord said: I shall declare the procedure for sprinkling; listen attentively to it as well.
[This applies] when there is contact with one who has not been initiated, and likewise when there is contact with one who is untouchable.
O best of Brahmins, [this applies] during birth and death, when a woman in her courses is present, when [the site] is defiled by Caṇḍālas and others, or by dogs, jackals, donkeys, and the like.
The same applies to touching [the image], as well as to a temple or a divine icon, when worship has been neglected for a long time, or during excavation and cremation by fire. (14)
Especially when there are internal outflows, when the inner sanctum is defiled on all sides, when conflict has arisen, and when the place is crowded with people. || 15 ||
When there is association with thieves and the like, or even in cases of moving or falling,
as well as in the confusion of tantras and likewise in the confusion of scriptures.
And likewise in worship without mantras, as well as in worship at an improper place;
in worship performed without proper conduct, and likewise in worship performed by one who is impaired. || 17 ||
Especially during the worship of Kāṇā, [the rite fails] due to those afflicted by leprosy or epilepsy;
likewise, it is so when there is contact with the divine image or when the temple has been defiled. (18)
When the occasion for sprinkling arises, one should properly perform the sprinkling,
as well as the rite of the sprout, the auspicious thread (kautuka), the ceremonial bath, and the worship of the water-pot.
The worship of the four locations, as well as the act of laying to rest,
the offering of food, the oblation, and the sprinkling of the pitcher.
And one should perform everything immediately according to the path seen in the scriptures;
on a particularly distinguished day, the ritual of germinating seeds (aṅkura) should take place on the preceding day.
The rite of the auspicious thread (kautuka) is likewise prescribed, as well as the act of providing a bed,
the bestowal of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and the festival that follows thereafter.
The feeding of the twice-born and likewise the gift of grain—thus has the supreme ritual of sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) been briefly described. (23)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Sprinkling," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
(p. 190) Now begins the twentieth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall declare the expiation; listen attentively.
Purity is said to be threefold, pertaining to speech, mind, and action. (1)
Purity of speech is declared to be truthfulness, and purity of mind is the contemplation of Viṣṇu; such threefold action of the body toward the Lord is called pure. (2)
If the practitioner is devoid of bathing, everything shall become fruitless;
if he is unable to perform the mantra-bath, he should drink water from a sacred ford.
If one is deficient in the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana), one should mutter the mantra a hundred times while practicing breath control (prāṇāyāma);
if one is deficient in the maintenance of the perpetual sacred fire (nityapāvaka), one should perform the feeding of Brahmins.
Any undertaking devoid of the scriptures, mantras, and ritual procedures is useless;
therefore, one should perform everything with every effort according to the path of the scriptures.
O best of Brahmins, if it is devoid of mantra, the practitioner perishes;
if it is especially devoid of the ritual substances, the performer will certainly bring about his own destruction.
O best of the twice-born, if it is devoid of ritual action, that village shall come to ruin;
however, when it is endowed with materials, mantras, and ritual action, that rite becomes fruitful.
But even in the absence of ritual materials, one should worship with mantras alone;
in the absence of materials, there should be flowers; and in the absence of flowers, [one should worship] with the mind alone.
(191) However, if one is devoid of faith and devotion, everything indeed becomes fruitless;
likewise if the pavilion or the inner sanctum arises from anthills and the like. (9)
Having caused that spot to be excavated, one should fill it with other earth;
then, having performed a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), especially with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
In the case of fire damage, and especially when there is a need for re-consecration,
the wise practitioner should produce a new image whenever the existing one is beset by defects.
Having performed the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) as before, one should then perform the worship;
in the case of damage by thieves or other such causes, one should likewise perform it correctly.
If movement should occur due to the force of water from rivers and the like,
the preceptor should install the Lord of the God of Gods and the image elsewhere.
After three years have passed, one should move [the image] from the village and so forth;
if one moves it out of delusion, there will be the destruction of the king’s kingdom and wealth. (14)
Therefore, with every effort, one should not cause it to move;
for through obstruction and through movement, the king himself perishes.
When temples, gate-towers, and other such structures fall or shake,
one should perform a ceremonial bath, a peace-offering fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), and likewise worship at the four sacred sites.
Whether for one day, three days, or five, seven, and nine days, one should perform all [these rites] according to the application of gravity or lightness. || 17 ||
Even by touching the sun, one is purified by sprinkling;
likewise, upon touching a woman in her courses, one should properly perform a ritual bath. (18)
If the image of the deity has been defiled by dogs, jackals, and the like, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
The same applies if the divine image has been touched by those afflicted with consumption, leprosy, epilepsy, or similar ailments.
The ritual bathing and the feeding of the twice-born should be performed according to the sequence of eighty-one;
however, if the worship with lamps is omitted, the ritual of adoration at night must be doubled.
If one night is omitted, however, one should perform double the penance on the following day;
indeed, the expiation is prescribed at the end of the second day. || 21 ||
One should perform the ablution with twelve jars and carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma);
O Brahmin, after a year has passed, one should properly perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
O twice-born one, O best of brahmins, beginning from the fourth day until the end of the month,
one should perform [the rites] in this sequence even when the worship is omitted.

From that time forward, one should perform daily the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the fire-oblation for peace (*śāntihoma*), the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*), the feeding of the twice-born (*dvijabhojana*), and the ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*). || 24 ||
If it is deficient by two months, one should perform the rite of sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa);
but beyond that, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the worship of the four locations.
After seven or eight months, however, one should perform the oblation of sesame seeds;
after a year, O Brahmin, one should properly perform the consecration.
In one who is devoid of such preliminary rites, every ritual act becomes demonic;
therefore, one should perform them while avoiding [the omission of] dwelling in water and the opening of the eyes. || 27 ||

If the rites such as plowing and so forth are omitted, all the ritual actions will become demonic; however, if the entry and the offering of oblations (bali) are omitted, that ritual action will be fruitless. || 28 ||
If the ritual installation of the ritual peg (śaṅku) is omitted, the destruction of the site will certainly occur;
if the sowing of the seed-syllables (bīja) is omitted, the destruction of the seed will occur upon the earth.
If the depositing of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) is omitted, that sacred field will lead to emptiness;
if the planting of the seed-syllables (aṅkurārpaṇa) is omitted, it swiftly brings about misfortune.
If the rite of dwelling in water is omitted, the destruction of the performer will certainly occur;
if the rite of opening the eyes is omitted, the destruction of the eyes will certainly occur. || 31 ||
If the ritual bathing is omitted, there will be a loss of the site;
if the fire-offering rite is omitted, every undertaking will perish. (33)
If the worship of the mandala is deficient, that ritual act shall become fruitless;
however, if the installation is deficient, one should perform the installation again. (34)
The best of preceptors, who at the outset performs the rites for the purpose of establishing [the foundation],
he alone— and no other, even if wise— should perform the entire ritual.
If there is a confusion of duties among teachers, the king destroys his kingdom;
it would be as if the movement [of the earth] were possible through the force of the waters of rivers and the like. || 35 ||

O best of the twice-born, one should design the city, village, residence, and so forth elsewhere in a place free from obstacles; the planning, including the measurements and other details, should be carried out as previously described. (36)
One should fashion the image in such a manner, and likewise the villages and other structures;
having first observed the auspicious signs, one should have them constructed when the omens are favorable.
But when an ill omen has occurred, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma);
it may be done with either the Sudarśana mantra or the Nārasiṃha mantra. || 38 ||
Then, having performed the worship of the site (vāstupūjā), one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should provide a meal for the twice-born and perform the installation of the ritual peg (śaṅku).
On the eastern and western sides of the gnomon’s base, one should mark points with its shadow;
by means of the tip of the shadow alone, one should determine the cardinal directions.
Then, having performed the excavation, one should fill it with sand;
having made it firm with hands and feet, one should sprinkle water upon the stone slab.

One should determine the sanctum and other parts according to the measurement of one's own finger-breadths; or else, one may determine the base (adhiṣṭhāna) as being joined with the secondary seat (upapīṭha).
Above the frieze, one should especially perform the ritual placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa), whether in the center of a village or likewise in a city. (43)
But if this preliminary rite is omitted, that primary rite will become fruitless;
therefore, one should perform each respective rite with every effort. (44)
One should bring everything to completion simply by feeding the twice-born;
one should establish villages and other settlements according to the path taught in the Pāñcarātra.
By the power of the Pañcarātra, every defect is destroyed;
one should perform all activities, such as plowing and so forth, according to the Pañcarātra.
If one is devoid of the daily rites, however, one should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa;
for if the Pavitrāropaṇa is omitted, the month-long worship perishes. (47)
If the monthly worship is neglected, the daily worship perishes;
if the daily worship is neglected, the destruction of the village will occur. || 48 ||
If the daily worship has been neglected,
one should perform all peace rites for five days, three days, seven days, or nine days.
O best of Brahmins, having first made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform worship at four locations;
one should also perform the ritual bathing every day and provide food for the twice-born.
But when a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is bestowed, every fault is destroyed;
by giving, everything is consumed [by fire]; therefore, giving is preeminent. || 51 ||
Everything is obtained through Dharma; therefore, Dharma is preeminent. This is so both through the two-fold practice of the duty of giving and through the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
For it is indeed obtained specifically; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā of the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
196) Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
The Blessed One said:
I shall describe the procedure for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa); listen as I explain it concisely.
The deposition of the embryo is prescribed for the deities, the Brahmins, and others.
One who is devoted to the Pāñcarātra should perform the ritual placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) specifically in the center of a village or likewise in the abode of the gods.
Otherwise, the preceptor incurs a fault along with the artisan;
one should fashion the womb-vessel according to the measurement of the *tāla*.
One should arrange the construction according to that measurement;
one should prepare nine pits, either with stone or even with brick. || 4 ||
When an auspicious moment has arrived during the night, the conception [of the ritual] is performed;
one should then carry out the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), the sequence of which I shall now explain to you.
Then, having performed the ritual bathing and adorned [the image] according to the rules,
and having offered the sprouts (aṅkura), one should tie the protective thread (kautuka) separately.
The wise one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) with seventeen jars in succession;
the wise one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made and should wrap [the image] with a cloth.
Having set aside a heap of grain, one should place half of that amount of rice;
having added half of that again as sesame seeds, one should cover it with new cloths.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the mantra itself, the preceptor should take up the womb-vessel and place it upon the bed. (9)
On its right side, the wise man should place a water-pot;
having invoked the God and the Goddess, he should worship them according to the path of the scriptures.
Having taken the substances for the womb, one should place them in the center of the cooked rice (bhakta),
as well as gems, metals, minerals, seeds, roots, and groups [of medicinal herbs].
One should specifically place the eight types of earth beginning with that of Brahmā in the northeast;
having poured the residual clarified butter over them, one should worship according to the previously mentioned procedure.

It should be produced according to the prescribed rite and wrapped right there; one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rule and offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) on all sides. || 13 ||

When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should deposit the vessel containing the embryo [the consecrated water] upon that [earth] which has the ocean as its garment and is adorned with mountains for breasts.
Resting within the womb of the Goddess, who is the support of all worlds,
it is endowed with signs made of metal and accompanied by a multitude of garlands and other ornaments.
Thereafter, one should fill that pit with sand, flowing water, and heaps of stones possessed of those same qualities, accompanied by dancing and instrumental music.
At the time of delivery from the womb, one should worship with auspicious symbols (svastikas);
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
Afterwards, one should honor the artisan with wealth, grain, cattle, and other such gifts; for if the laying of the foundation is deficient, that village shall meet its destruction. (19)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the ritual placement within the womb (garbhanyāsa) using either the eight-syllabled or the twelve-syllabled mantra alone.
The wise one should cause the ceremonial bathing to be performed with the Puṃsūkta mantra itself;
he should perform the rite for the womb-vessel with the Śrīsūkta mantra itself.
The wise one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the six-syllabled mantra;
however, if it is devoid of the mantra and the ritual manual (tantra), every rite becomes demonic.
One should perform protection on all sides with the Sudarśana mantra;
one should place Hetiśa in the inner sanctum with the Svarṇa mantra.
One should duly worship Indra and the other deities of the directions in their respective places.
Thus has the supreme procedure for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) been correctly explained. 24.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Deposition of the Embryo," in the *Aniruddha-saṃhitā*, within the Great Upaniṣad of the *Śrī Pāñcarātra*.
p. 199) Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
The Blessed One said:
O great sage, the consecration of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha),
as well as the temple, the inner sanctum, and the pedestal for the image, shall now be described.
The body of the Lord itself indeed consists of four parts:
the doors, the enclosures, the deities, and everything up to the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha). || 2 ||

A shadow-form (chāyāmūrti) fashioned from stone, metal, or other materials is installed by one who knows the mantras, specifically during the rite of consecration, using the respective mantra for each.
The beds, seats, vehicles, and especially the dwellings and other such items of the god, who is proportionate in limb, as well as his retinue; || 4 ||
That which is endowed with all common characteristics is prescribed for the pedestal,
and likewise for the temple, in a manner appropriate to the Lord and positioned in front of him.
Having constructed a pavilion according to the available space— either on the left, the right, or the west— it should be provided with sixteen pillars.
It is provided with four doors, adorned with four archways,
equipped with door-pitchers, and decorated with garlands of darbha grass.
In the center, one should prepare a nine-square altar with a face one cubit high,
and around it, in the four directions, one should arrange four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
The bow, the circle, and the lotus are [the shapes] in order starting from the east;
or else, there may be a single pit, which in the eastern direction is square. (9)

Having caused a pavilion to be constructed, one should perform the consecration according to the prescribed rules; prior to the day of the consecration, one should carry out the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Or one may perform it on the third day from the day of the ritual commencement;
if it is to be done immediately, then with rice grains, flowers, or seeds that have begun to sprout.
Prior to the day of the consecration, one should arrange for the water-dwelling;
having invoked [the deity] into the jars together with the mirror and the tuft of grass, one should perform the rite.
Having extracted it from a large quantity of water into a wooden trough or a cauldron, [one should keep it] for one night or even for a full day and night. || 13 ||
One should perform the ritual immersion (*adhivāsa*) in the midst of water for a duration of three *ghaṭikās*,
according to the procedure for water-immersion prescribed in the scriptures on installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having performed the ceremonial bath according to the sequence of eighty-one [verses],
and having performed the opening of the eyes, one should then apply clay in due order.
Having prepared a bed upon a grass mat, one should meditate on the Lord;
having placed it in the center of the altar, one should scatter rice there.
One should place two *bhāras* of rice and half that amount of sesame seeds;
in their midst, one should set down the *kumbha*, the *karaka*, and the *parikumbhaka*.

Having approached the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha), which is endowed with the eight auspicious symbols and adorned with small pitchers (pālikā), one should likewise prepare a water-shed (prapā). || 18 ||
Once the offering pedestal has been cleansed according to the method prescribed in the scriptures, one should wash the seat fashioned by artisans with pure water.
When the circumambulation with fire has been performed using bundles of blazing *darbha* grass,
one should sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and then bathe it with the nine-fold [mixture].
Then, having wrapped [the deity] with a cloth, one should worship it in due order;
thereafter, one should perform the door-sacrifice (dvārayāga) around the maṇḍala in sequence.
One should sit upon a seat in the western part of the altar;
then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should carry out the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). || 22 ||
One should perform the ritual preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings, and likewise sprinkle the altar;
then, one should invoke Viṣṇu, his attendants, and the deities into the primary image (*mūlabera*).
Having invoked [the deity] into the center of the pitcher and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should meditate upon it,
specifically performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra of Viṣṇu’s attendant.
Having worshipped them according to the rule, one should place Indra and the others around [the altar];
then, having approached the side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the rite of oblation (homa). || 25 ||
One should perform the purificatory rites, such as scraping and so forth, according to the previous sequence;
then, with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, one should offer oblations using the mantra of Viṣṇu’s attendants.
For each [offense], one should perform one hundred and eight expiatory oblations with clarified butter, honey, curd, and milk-rice, respectively. (27)
Then, having offered sacrificial fuel and other materials in the four directions in due order—
namely from the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees respectively— according to the sequence.
And in the absence of what has been mentioned, one should likewise use fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood in all cases,
with the mantra of Viṣṇu’s attendant, in the four sacrificial pits according to the sequence.
One should offer oblations into the pit in the east and perform the fire-sacrifice of the principles (tattvahoma);
thereafter, one should present the sacrificial food and perform the offering of the bali.
Having stayed outside the pavilion and other structures, he should feed twelve or eight Brahmins at the *balipīṭha* according to his capacity.
Having laid [the image] down in the pavilion accompanied by dance and music,
one should rise properly at dawn, bathe, and recite [mantras] according to the prescribed rite.
Having commenced the daily worship, one should worship the water-pot (kumbha) in the pavilion;
thereafter, one should present the sacrificial oblation and perform the rite of fire-offering (homa).
One should offer sixteen oblations each of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice;
one should present the bali offering on all sides and perform the ritual dismissal of the archways.
Taking the door-pitcher, one should join it with the surrounding pitchers.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, the preceptor, together with the Brahmins,
taking the installed water-pot, proceeds clockwise around the temple. (36)
One should cause it to be proclaimed with the sound of all musical instruments, such as dance and song;
having approached the side of the pedestal, one should perform the rite for a day of merit (*puṇyāha*) there.
One should worship [the deity] on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in the proper sequence;
then, taking water with the ritual grass-bundle (kūrca), one should sprinkle it upon the top of the pedestal.

One should contemplate the Lord who has Viṣṇu as his attendant upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭhaka); having sprinkled it with the secondary water-pot (parikumbha), one should perform the viewing of the eight auspicious signs. || 39 ||

Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). One should offer oblations (bali) in every direction and establish [the deity] upon the altar of offerings (balipīṭha). || 40 ||
One should visualize the Lord of Viṣṇu’s attendants upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha);
[one should visualize] the Lord of Viṣṇu’s attendants belonging to the Lord of Gods, who has become the Lord.
One should subsequently honor the preceptor and also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests.
Thus has the installation of the offering pedestal been briefly described. 42.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Bali-Pedestal," in the Aniruddha-Saṃhitā, which is a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
204) Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Bhṛgu said:
In former times, the installation of the god Viṣvaksena was ordained;
out of a desire to show favor, I shall now describe that procedure in detail.
The Blessed Lord said:
Now the characteristics of the installation of Viṣvaksena shall be described. Having constructed a pavilion in front of the deity, exactly as previously detailed in its entirety, || 2 ||
Or, in a location encompassed by the cardinal and intermediate directions,
one should construct a pavilion on the third day, preceded by the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Prior to the day of the consecration, one should arrange for the ritual residence in water;
all the rites of the water-residence are enjoined by the scriptures on consecration.
Having performed the opening of the eyes, one should carry out the ritual bathing and other rites;
then, having prepared the bed, one should perform the sacrifice at the door.
Having established [the deity] in the center of the altar, one should place the great jar;
specifically, having approached Viṣvaksena, one should place him within the middle of the jar.
Likewise, one should worship Indra and the other deities in their respective directions using water-pots (parikumbhas),
and one should honor them with the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) and the pālikā vessels.
One should arrange the fire-pits for Indra and the other deities in the four directions in their proper order;
alternatively, one may prepare a single pit that is square in shape.
One should worship the fire-seed (agnibīja), which has been consecrated by rites such as scratching [the hearth] and so forth;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice in sequence. (9)
Having offered oblations of clarified butter with the mantra of Viṣvaksena in due order,
one should then perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should also offer a hundred oblations for atonement with the five Upaniṣads,
mixing ghee with sesame, rice, and barley, and performing the homa.
One should perform the fire oblation there with one hundred and eight offerings using the mantra of Viṣvaksena, and one should carry out the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering preceded by the giving of the bali-oblation;
then, one should cause [the image] to rest upon darbha grass in the northeast portion of the pavilion.
At the clear and pure dawn, one should perform the daily worship;
one should worship the deities in the water-pot, preceded by the offering of oblations.
Having approached the side of the sacrificial pit, one should perform the rite of oblation;
specifically, sixteen offerings of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, each offered individually. (15)

Then, having offered the expiatory oblations of sesame and rice—one hundred and eight of each—followed by the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the path prescribed in the scriptures; || 16 ||
When the auspicious moment has arrived, having obtained the permission of the Brahmins,
one should take the jar that has been set out and sprinkle it upon the head of the deity.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra of Viṣvaksena, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*,
one should duly perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and then present the food for the deity;
afterwards, one should honor the preceptor according to the extent of one's wealth. || 19 ||
Thus has been briefly declared that which is established by Viṣvaksena.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Installation of Viṣvaksena," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: O great sage, I shall describe in detail the established status of the devotee.
These are constructed, respectively, from wood, metal, stone, and so forth. || 1 ||
Especially during the consecration ceremony, and for devotees according to the sequence,
one should construct a pavilion specifically in front of the deity.
First, one should construct a pavilion in the desired locations;
this may take place on the third day, preceded by the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having resolved upon dwelling in the water as prescribed by the scriptures on installation,
one should perform the preliminary consecration at dusk and adorn [the deity] with special ornaments.
Whether it be a wall made of plaster or clay, or like a cloth painting, or as in a mirror—
having performed the ritual bathing, one should carry out the sacrifice at the door. (5)
Accompanied by the worship of the water-pot (kumbhapūjā) as enjoined by the scriptures on consecration,
one should perform the naming of the devotee’s image with mantras beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ."
One should employ this mantra and contemplate each respective state,
having performed the worship according to the rule as enjoined in the scriptures on consecration.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and perform the rite of oblation (homa).
One should perform it in four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), or in a single pit as previously described.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, each in the number of one hundred, using the mantra consisting of the devotee's name followed by "svāhā."
One should perform the homa of the principles (tattva-homa) and carry out the ritual placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa).
Then, having performed the pacificatory homa (śānti-homa), one should offer the sweet substances and so forth in their proper sequence.

Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial oblation (havir), and then the water-pot and other items in their proper order; one should offer the bali-oblation on all sides and consume the remainder of the caru.
Having laid [the image] in the pavilion, especially upon its belly,
one should perform the daily worship at the clear and pure dawn.
Afterwards, one should present the sacrificial offering and perform the rite of homa;
specifically, one should offer sixteen oblations each of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
And when the auspicious moment has arrived, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the path seen in the scriptures, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas. (14)

Taking the jar that has been established, one should sprinkle [the devotees] with their respective vidyās, using the names of the devotees as mantras, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ. (15)
Having established [the deity] according to the rule, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
The installation of devotees such as Śaṭhakopa and others is thus proclaimed. || 16 ||
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor according to one's means. Thus has been correctly explained the installation of the image of Bhakta. 17.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Installation of Devotees," in the Aniruddha-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
The Aniruddhasaṃhitā is completed.
